review.auditor: Coordinator full-body routing review
review.rationale: Read all 99 lines. The tables pose questions and route to named comparisons; they supply no scientific answers, study findings, measurement rules or treatment recommendations. Introductory text gives reading instructions. Acronym expansions are link labels, not new explanatory teaching. Target existence does not verify the linked comparisons.

review.auditor: Codex coverage audit; not expert sign-off
review.rationale: Read the entire source delta against the prior complete review. Changes are internal links, terminal whitespace or the central-dogma sentence compressed without a new teaching requirement; all internal education Markdown targets exist. Linked new concepts retain their own unread status. Prior assessment: Read the public general-teaching mechanism, interpretation and common-confusion sections; inspected candidate records and searched canonical names/aliases for missed owners. Clinical/legal source verification and corrections are tracked separately. The missing explanations were implemented in the access proposal and checked against official sources and actual component renders. Structured query gaps remain separately open in schema-gaps.json. Supplemental general teaching, worked examples and scope sections have also been read; newly identified requirements remain separately open. Personal-case sections are excluded. The November 9 canonical-owner follow-up reads FDA forms/charging/industry guidance, the applicable published control rule and registry enrollment definition, plus NCI trial-method guidance. It adds the residual general distinctions without asserting a new cutoff, authorization rate, treatment probability or clinical eligibility determination.

remaining: Clarify safety and monitoring purposes; remove individual drug-suitability guarantees.

evidence.explanation: An assay is tied to a treatment label, but the record narrows the purpose to selecting responders.

points.requirement: Retain both treatment and device labeling, specimen and decision-rule context.

evidence.explanation: Retains both labels and the disease, specimen, biomarker and decision rule, and limits group labeling to its documented scope.

remaining: Explain exact intended use and group-label scope without implying every same-target assay or drug is covered.

evidence.explanation: Mentions drug-label ties and non-interchangeability.

points.requirement: Separate a label-matched test result from individual benefit and complete clinical suitability.

evidence.explanation: Separates a report drug list from authorization, rejects assay interchangeability by gene name alone and states that positivity does not promise response.

remaining: Correct both canonical glossary and technology explanations.

evidence.explanation: The current wording treats the test as universally required before prescribing.

points.requirement: Distinguish an invalid, inadequate or failed test from a valid negative result.

evidence.explanation: Explicitly separates failed/inadequate/invalid results from a valid negative; uses verified control-procedure criteria rather than treating no result as marker absence.

points.requirement: Scope follow-up to asymptomatic people after curative early-breast treatment and distinguish finding recurrence/new cancer from treating it.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A smoke alarm can detect a problem earlier without showing that a proposed inspection programme changes its outcome. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Follow-up after curative treatment for early breast cancer asks several questions: recurrence or a new breast cancer, treatment effects, ongoing therapy and support needs. Screening an asymptomatic person for distant recurrence is a different question from investigating a symptom or finding. Earlier detection alone does not establish longer life or better quality of life.

NICE NG101 recommends annual mammography for 5 years, with women continuing annually until they enter the national screening programme, and a written plan with access to the specialist team. ASCO's 2026 update uses risk-based follow-up intensity and permits less frequent mammography for a defined older, lower-risk group after an initial period. It still advises against routine distant-metastasis imaging or conventional blood-marker surveillance in the overall asymptomatic post-treatment population. Supplemental MRI or other breast imaging is a separate, individualised risk and anatomy discussion.

The 2006/2013 ASCO calendar is historical: examinations every 3 to 6 months for 3 years, every 6 to 12 months in years 4 and 5, then annually. Its first mammogram after breast conservation was 1 year after the initial mammogram and at least 6 months after radiotherapy. Those dated recommendations should not be presented as the latest single calendar. The 2026 recommendations and their evidence limits are distinguished below from the older trials and from experimental molecular surveillance.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: GIVIO randomised 1,320 women younger than 70 with stage I to III breast cancer to intensive testing or clinically indicated testing alongside follow-up. Added testing included bone scans, liver ultrasound, chest radiographs and laboratory tests. At median 71 months, 132 of 655 (20%) versus 122 of 665 (18%) had died; no significant survival or reported quality-of-life difference was found. That trial also found no significant difference in time to recurrence detection. Rosselli Del Turco's separate 1,243-person trial added six-month chest radiographs and bone scans. It found more isolated intrathoracic/bone metastases (112 versus 71) and earlier detection, without a significant five-year mortality difference (18.6% versus 19.5%). The two detection results should not be merged into one claim.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Follow-up after curative treatment for early breast cancer asks several questions: recurrence or a new breast cancer, treatment effects, ongoing therapy and support needs. Screening an asymptomatic person for distant recurrence is a different question from investigating a symptom or finding. Earlier detection alone does not establish longer life or better quality of life.

NICE NG101 recommends annual mammography for 5 years, with women continuing annually until they enter the national screening programme, and a written plan with access to the specialist team. ASCO's 2026 update uses risk-based follow-up intensity and permits less frequent mammography for a defined older, lower-risk group after an initial period. It still advises against routine distant-metastasis imaging or conventional blood-marker surveillance in the overall asymptomatic post-treatment population. Supplemental MRI or other breast imaging is a separate, individualised risk and anatomy discussion.

The 2006/2013 ASCO calendar is historical: examinations every 3 to 6 months for 3 years, every 6 to 12 months in years 4 and 5, then annually. Its first mammogram after breast conservation was 1 year after the initial mammogram and at least 6 months after radiotherapy. Those dated recommendations should not be presented as the latest single calendar. The 2026 recommendations and their evidence limits are distinguished below from the older trials and from experimental molecular surveillance.

points.requirement: Treat hallmarks as a versioned research framework, not a diagnostic checklist, stage, clinical test standard or set that every individual cell must independently satisfy.

evidence.explanation: The exact reader paragraph carries this learning requirement at its stated model, sample, measurement or inference scope: Treat hallmarks as a versioned research framework, not a diagnostic checklist, stage, clinical test standard or set that every individual cell must independently satisfy.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: The hallmarks are a versioned research framework, not a diagnostic checklist, stage, clinical assay standard or a demand that every cell independently perform every capability. The 2000 proposal contained six capabilities. The 2011 account retained six, added two emerging capabilities and described two enabling characteristics. In the 2022 account, the two emerging capabilities joined the eight core capabilities.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Capabilities can depend on cooperation with surrounding cells. To measure one, specify the process: division, death, invasion, vascular relations, metabolism or immune function. An RNA program is not a direct measurement of every capability or metabolic flux, and there is no universal hallmark unit or cutoff selecting treatment. In a fictional mutation-rich report, an enabling characteristic alone neither establishes distant disease nor proves those mutations caused the behaviour. A framework diagram organises concepts and provisional additions; it does not measure them in a specimen.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immune surveillance concerns immune control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds that immune pressure can alter which cancer populations persist. Shankaran’s genetically defined mouse experiments support lymphocyte and interferon-gamma contributions to control and selection. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Luksza followed 70 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas from 15 people longitudinally over ten years, comparing primary and recurrent tumours and modelling neoantigen quality and clonal fitness. Long-term survivors had stronger primary T-cell activity and recurrent tumours with fewer high-quality neoantigens under the model. This is human cohort and modelling evidence, not a vaccine experiment or direct observation of every selection event. Treatment and sampling history and model assumptions remain relevant.

points.requirement: Define an experimentally supported survival/growth dependency rather than gene presence, mutation or high expression. A cancer dependency does not by itself guarantee greater need than every normal cell or a therapeutic window.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A dependency is supported by a growth or survival effect when a function is perturbed in a defined context. Oncogene addiction concerns dependence on an activated driver; synthetic lethality concerns a conditional interaction between two losses; non-oncogene addiction concerns a normal support function under cancer-associated stress. A mutation, stain or high RNA level does not by itself establish any of them or a therapeutic window relative to normal cells.

This historical dose-group observation is neither prescribing advice nor a comparative-survival estimate.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A synthetic-lethal design compares the relevant single losses with the paired loss. A backup-pathway analogy is useful but does not make every interaction simple redundancy. Most drug combinations are not established synthetic-lethal pairs; a tumour’s existing loss plus one intervention differs from inducing two losses experimentally. PARP and ATR inhibition should not be called a universal synthetic-lethal pair; each experiment must establish the interaction in its specified context. In Smith’s 2024 laboratory panel, ATR inhibition impaired homologous-recombination repair and sensitised repair-proficient cells to rucaparib; matched BRCA-mutant and corrected cells were among the models. The authors called this induced synthetic lethality. It is model evidence, with no patient-benefit claim.

evidence.explanation: The exact reader paragraph carries this learning requirement at its stated model, sample, measurement or inference scope: Define tumour-suppressor roles in growth restraint, genomic maintenance or damaged-cell removal, and loss as a functional consequence rather than a gene-name label.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Tumour suppressors can restrain growth, maintain the genome or help remove damaged cells. Knudson’s retinoblastoma model proposed two events, with an inherited first event or two acquired events. Different changes can disable the useful copies, but two-hit loss is not a universal law for all suppressors. Haploinsufficiency means one useful copy supplies insufficient protective dosage; Fero’s challenged p27-heterozygous mice retained an unmutated, unsilenced remaining copy.

points.requirement: LoB concerns high-end blank/background response at a specified probability; blank noise, contamination and nonspecific signal require a distribution rather than one reading.

evidence.explanation: Semantic comparison at stated source or fictional-premise scope; hash and containment checks are separate from entailment.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: The limit of blank describes an upper background response at a specified probability. A limit of detection concerns an amount that can be detected under stated false-call and detection-probability conditions; LoD95 specifies 95 per cent detection in the tested workflow. It is not a line above which every repeat must be positive, nor 95 per cent certainty that a person has disease. A limit of quantitation requires stated quantitative accuracy, including bias and imprecision goals. The limits answer different questions and have no universal spacing; they may coincide under a particular method and its criteria.

evidence.explanation: Semantic comparison at stated source or fictional-premise scope; hash and containment checks are separate from entailment.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: A clinical decision threshold answers a different question from analytical detection or quantitation. Clinical sensitivity counts positive results among people meeting a defined reference condition; it cannot be converted directly from a laboratory detection limit. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Fictional assay example: the blank-response axis describes background readings, while a separate known-input axis has LoD95 at 2 units. At that input, the assumption leaves about 5 per cent of repeated tests undetected. A signal near 4 units is detected but remains below an assumed quantitation limit of 8 units. It therefore does not establish an exact 33 per cent rise from 3 to 4. These invented amounts, curves and limits belong to this example; neither the spacing nor the missed-repeat fraction is a personal disease probability.

points.requirement: Use repeated blanks and low-level samples across specified conditions to assess detection and quantitative error.

evidence.explanation: Semantic comparison at stated source or fictional-premise scope; hash and containment checks are separate from entailment.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Evaluate repeated blanks and low-level specimens across the conditions the claim covers. Each finite set of repeats needs representative clinical specimens or suitably equivalent reference inputs. Record the analyte, amount or concentration units, specimen matrix, input, workflow boundary, assay version and acceptable false-positive, false-negative and quantitative-error rates. Matrix means the material surrounding the analyte; reference material with a known added analyte amount needs justified equivalence to the clinical specimen. A limit measured on purified material is not automatically a collection-to-report limit. Contamination, nonspecific signal, calibration bias, poor recovery, unrepresentative targets, different lots or operators and inadequate input can change performance. Calibration-slope sensitivity, analytical detection capability and clinical sensitivity are different uses of the same word.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Imagine runners approaching a hurdle. A runner who leaves observation has an unknown later outcome; one who experiences a competing event cannot subsequently have the chosen first event. The analogy is about event definitions, not the idea that all departures have the same prognosis. Death precludes a later first recurrence, while a missed visit does not. Ordinary censoring still requires an appropriate assumption about unobserved outcomes. Deaths-censored Kaplan-Meier instead constructs a net-risk quantity from the cause-specific hazard. Interpreting it as the causal risk in a world where nobody dies needs additional assumptions; it is not the observed real-world recurrence probability.

points.requirement: Define cumulative incidence as event probability by time in the presence of competing events and resolve Aalen-Johansen as its standard nonparametric estimator.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: For cumulative incidence, each target-event increment is event-free survival immediately before that time multiplied by the target-event count divided by the number still at risk. Sum those increments through the chosen time. The survival factor falls after every relevant first event, including competing deaths. This is the competing-risk form of the Aalen-Johansen calculation. The target-event cumulative incidence, the cumulative incidence of all competing first events and the probability of remaining free of all those events sum to one. A cumulative incidence curve does not require Fine-Gray regression.

points.requirement: Retain all rows of the ten-person, no-loss, five-year fictional example, including risk sets 10/8/6/4/2, deaths and recurrences, and the 25% versus 20% and 62.5% versus 40% calculations.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Consider a fictional five-year cohort of ten people with no loss to follow-up. At year 1, two die without recurrence: eight remain, event-free survival is 0.8 and the cumulative incidence of death is 0.2. At year 2, two of eight recur. Their conditional fraction is 25%, but their cumulative-incidence increment is 0.8 × 2/8 = 20%, leaving event-free survival 0.6. At year 3, two of six die: the death increment is 0.6 × 2/6 = 20%, giving 40% cumulative incidence of death and 0.4 event-free survival. At year 4, two of four recur: 0.4 × 2/4 adds another 20% recurrence incidence. Two people remain event-free at year 5. The five-year probabilities are therefore 40% recurrence, 40% competing death and 20% neither. In contrast, censoring deaths in recurrence-only Kaplan-Meier gives 1 − (1 − 2/8)(1 − 2/4) = 62.5%. Four recurrences among ten with complete observation are 40%, not 62.5%.

points.requirement: Define cause-specific hazard among those free of all events and the use of competing-event censoring in a cause-specific Cox model without equating it to a recurrence-probability estimate.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A cause-specific hazard is the instantaneous event rate among people still free of every relevant event. Coding a competing event as censored in cause-specific Cox removes that person from this risk set; it does not turn the fitted rate into a recurrence probability. This observed-rate definition does not require assuming independent latent times to competing events. Ordinary loss to follow-up raises a separate censoring assumption. Fine-Gray models a subdistribution hazard linked to cumulative incidence, using a different risk-set construction that retains people with competing events mathematically. A subdistribution hazard ratio is not a risk ratio or a calibrated personal probability. The two hazard ratios can differ without contradiction; choice follows the scientific question, and neither association alone proves a biological mechanism.

More competing events and longer follow-up can create more opportunity for a gap, but neither supplies a universal correction factor or an individual-risk rule.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Imagine runners approaching a hurdle. A runner who leaves observation has an unknown later outcome; one who experiences a competing event cannot subsequently have the chosen first event. The analogy is about event definitions, not the idea that all departures have the same prognosis. Death precludes a later first recurrence, while a missed visit does not. Ordinary censoring still requires an appropriate assumption about unobserved outcomes. Deaths-censored Kaplan-Meier instead constructs a net-risk quantity from the cause-specific hazard. Interpreting it as the causal risk in a world where nobody dies needs additional assumptions; it is not the observed real-world recurrence probability.

points.requirement: Cause-specific and subdistribution hazard ratios are not interchangeable; different values for the same treatment do not by themselves contradict each other.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A cause-specific hazard is the instantaneous event rate among people still free of every relevant event. Coding a competing event as censored in cause-specific Cox removes that person from this risk set; it does not turn the fitted rate into a recurrence probability. This observed-rate definition does not require assuming independent latent times to competing events. Ordinary loss to follow-up raises a separate censoring assumption. Fine-Gray models a subdistribution hazard linked to cumulative incidence, using a different risk-set construction that retains people with competing events mathematically. A subdistribution hazard ratio is not a risk ratio or a calibrated personal probability. The two hazard ratios can differ without contradiction; choice follows the scientific question, and neither association alone proves a biological mechanism.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: For cumulative incidence, each target-event increment is event-free survival immediately before that time multiplied by the target-event count divided by the number still at risk. Sum those increments through the chosen time. The survival factor falls after every relevant first event, including competing deaths. This is the competing-risk form of the Aalen-Johansen calculation. The target-event cumulative incidence, the cumulative incidence of all competing first events and the probability of remaining free of all those events sum to one. A cumulative incidence curve does not require Fine-Gray regression.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Consider a fictional five-year cohort of ten people with no loss to follow-up. At year 1, two die without recurrence: eight remain, event-free survival is 0.8 and the cumulative incidence of death is 0.2. At year 2, two of eight recur. Their conditional fraction is 25%, but their cumulative-incidence increment is 0.8 × 2/8 = 20%, leaving event-free survival 0.6. At year 3, two of six die: the death increment is 0.6 × 2/6 = 20%, giving 40% cumulative incidence of death and 0.4 event-free survival. At year 4, two of four recur: 0.4 × 2/4 adds another 20% recurrence incidence. Two people remain event-free at year 5. The five-year probabilities are therefore 40% recurrence, 40% competing death and 20% neither. In contrast, censoring deaths in recurrence-only Kaplan-Meier gives 1 − (1 − 2/8)(1 − 2/4) = 62.5%. Four recurrences among ten with complete observation are 40%, not 62.5%.

points.requirement: Define an analysis population as the prespecified/data-defined people entering an analysis, with different sets answering different questions.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An analysis population specifies who enters an analysis and how people are grouped. Randomisation protects the comparison in expectation, rather than making observed baseline groups identical. Selecting people afterwards can undo that protection. Think of comparing two school programmes using everyone assigned or just those who completed: completion can depend on the programme and on factors related to the outcome. Per-protocol criteria are prespecified adherence and violation rules, not simply a preference for a tidier result. Those retained are commonly compared in their assigned groups; check the actual protocol. As-treated groups follow actual treatment received, with an explicit rule for non-starters. Safety sets commonly require at least one dose and group by treatment received; definitions remain study-specific.

points.requirement: Intention-to-treat retains everyone randomised in assigned groups, including non-completion, switching and non-start; missing outcomes remain a separate problem.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: ICH E9 permits limited, justified exclusions from a full analysis set. For an eligibility violation, its safeguards include measuring the criterion before randomisation, objective detection, equal scrutiny across groups and exclusion of every detected violation of that criterion. Excluding non-starters can preserve the principle only under suitable conditions, such as the decision to start being unaffected by knowledge of assignment. Prespecification alone does not remove treatment-related selection bias. An intention-to-treat label keeps assigned groups; it neither means everyone completed treatment nor supplies missing outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: ICH E9 permits limited, justified exclusions from a full analysis set. evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional trial with complete follow-up, arm A assigns 100 people: 80 complete treatment and 16 recur; 20 stop and ten recur. All assigned A participants therefore have 26/100 recurrences, or 26%. Arm B also has 26/100. Restrict A to completers and the comparison becomes 16/80 = 20% against 26%, an apparent six-percentage-point advantage created by this selection. No measured frailty difference is specified, and equal observed rates do not prove a zero treatment effect in the population. Removing people changes the question as well as the denominator.

points.requirement: Verify the 475-trial modified-ITT review and its reported 80% post-randomisation exclusions at the study's actual selection and definition scope.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Abraha and Montedori reviewed 475 trials reporting modified intention-to-treat. Eighty per cent excluded participants after randomisation, under varied definitions; their search ended in December 2006. Hollis and Campbell examined reports from four journals in 1997: among 119 mentioning intention-to-treat, 12 excluded non-starters, three did not analyse all participants as allocated, and 89 (75%) had missing primary outcomes. These are distinct, potentially overlapping features, not one combined exclusion count. Check the actual inclusion rules, arm-specific exclusions, reasons and missing-outcome methods rather than trusting the label.

points.requirement: Define Bayesian inference and prespecified adaptation separately; Bayesian need not mean adaptive and adaptive need not mean Bayesian.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A weather forecast is an analogy for updating uncertainty: a starting forecast is revised when new observations arrive. In a trial, the prior describes parameters before the data, the likelihood describes data under the model, and Bayes theorem produces the posterior. The prior, likelihood and target effect must be stated. A 95% credible interval contains 95% of posterior probability under that model. A confidence interval is defined through the coverage of its procedure across repeated samples; a p-value measures compatibility with a specified null model. None is a model-free probability that a medicine works. Sensitivity to plausible priors and likelihood assumptions matters.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Prespecified adaptations can alter sample size, stop for benefit or futility, change allocation or change eligibility. Bayesian and frequentist methods can each support adaptive designs; a Bayesian analysis need not adapt anything. A platform can add or drop arms without using response-adaptive assignment. FDA’s 2019 guidance recommends planning and evaluating operating characteristics, including power, false-positive probability, estimation and trial conduct. Simulations explore plausible null and alternative scenarios and operational assumptions. Neither an appealing ethical rationale nor simulated performance guarantees that every participant receives a better treatment.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A weather forecast is an analogy for updating uncertainty: a starting forecast is revised when new observations arrive. evidence.supportingExcerpt: A confidence interval for the mean effect differs from a prediction interval for an underlying effect in another comparable study under the model. Neither is a personal prognosis interval. These estimates can be uncertain, especially with few studies, and no I-squared cutoff alone makes pooling safe.

points.requirement: Define non-inferiority as excluding worse-than-prespecified-margin performance, with potential simplicity/shortness/harms advantages requiring their own evidence.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Think of replacing a bridge with a lighter design. An agreed limit on lost performance defines what must be ruled out, while the uncertainty around the estimate determines whether it has been ruled out. The analogy does not establish exact equality or safety. Superiority seeks evidence on the favourable side of no difference at the specified inferential level. Non-inferiority rules out the unacceptable worse side; equivalence instead requires excluding unacceptable differences in both directions. A statistically detectable loss smaller than the accepted margin can coexist with non-inferiority.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A vehicle control contains the carrier without the active treatment; an untreated condition asks a different question if the carrier has effects. A positive control checks that the assay can detect a known relevant response, while a negative or non-targeting control estimates background under its design. Another independent way to disrupt the same function can support a mechanism, and a rescue restores a function to test whether that reverses the response here. Off-target effects, incomplete restoration and model context limit interpretation. These are questions for matched model, timing and readout; no one control proves specificity or patient benefit, and agreement between similar readouts is not automatically independent mechanistic confirmation.

evidence.explanation: Semantic comparison at stated source or fictional-premise scope; hash and containment checks are separate from entailment.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Concealed chance assignment is different from predictable alternation between A and B. Allocation concealment hides the next assignment during enrolment; blinding concerns who knows the assigned treatment afterwards and may not be feasible for every intervention. Report sequence generation, allocation, who was blinded, assigned-group analyses, exclusions, dropout, missing assessments, treatment changes and unequal follow-up. Chance can balance measured and unmeasured factors on average without guaranteeing identical groups in one trial. Random assignment is not random sampling from a population: consenting eligible volunteers remain selected.

points.requirement: False discovery proportion is false rejections V divided by total rejections R, defined as0 when R=0.

evidence.explanation: Semantic comparison at stated source or fictional-premise scope; hash and containment checks are separate from entailment.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Write V for false rejections and R for all rejections: the false discovery proportion is V/R, defined as zero when R is zero, and FDR is its expectation. Family-wise error is the probability of at least one false rejection; the two coincide when every null hypothesis is true but generally differ otherwise. Benjamini-Hochberg sorts all m valid p-values, compares rank i with (i/m)q, finds the largest passing rank and selects everything through it. The original control result assumes independence; positive-dependence extensions and procedures for broader dependence have their own conditions. Correlation is not permission to ignore the procedure's assumptions.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Agretopicity compares two predicted binding scores for the same stretch of protein: the mutant peptide carrying the tumour's altered amino acid, and its wild-type counterpart from the normal genome, each scored against a person's human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I molecules by prediction software. Duan and colleagues named the numerical difference in NetMHC scores between mutated and unmutated sequences the differential agretopic index (DAI). Duan subtracted the wild-type NetMHC score from the mutant score. Some groups use a ratio instead, and sign conventions and subtraction order differ between papers, so a DAI value cannot be compared across pipelines without reading each one's definition.

Earlier primary-reading depth and acceptance limits are not upgraded.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Two separate ideas sit behind the measure. First, a mutation at a position the HLA groove grips can create a new anchor residue and change binding, potentially changing presentation; Duan and colleagues found that neoepitopes mutated to create new anchor residues, together with greater predicted rigidity of the peptide and HLA complex, identified protective neoepitopes with relatively high accuracy in mouse tumours (the CMS5 and Meth A mouse tumours). Second, reasoning rather than a finding of the cited papers: a peptide that normal tissue never displayed well may not have had its reactive T cells removed by self-tolerance, so a high value is sometimes read as a proxy for an intact T-cell repertoire against that target.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Two separate ideas sit behind the measure. First, a mutation at a position the HLA groove grips can create a new anchor residue and change binding, potentially changing presentation; Duan and colleagues found that neoepitopes mutated to create new anchor residues, together with greater predicted rigidity of the peptide and HLA complex, identified protective neoepitopes with relatively high accuracy in mouse tumours (the CMS5 and Meth A mouse tumours). evidence.supportingExcerpt: Ghorani’s retrospective human analysis included 66 lung adenocarcinomas and 72 melanomas from The Cancer Genome Atlas, plus three immunotherapy-treated cohorts containing 131 melanoma patients in total and 31 with non-small-cell lung cancer. Mean DAI correlated with overall survival in three of five cohorts, with the reported effect for clonal rather than subclonal peptides. The authors reported evidence of superiority over nonsynonymous mutational and neoantigen burden in these analyses, not a universally superior clinical predictor. Mean DAI also correlated with immune-infiltration measures in melanoma (P = 0.027) and lung adenocarcinoma (P = 0.024), whereas mutational and neoantigen burden did not. The association with survival was not uniform: P = 0.068 in the TCGA melanoma cohort and P = 0.003 in one treated melanoma cohort. These population associations and the animal protection findings are different evidence tiers. Neither prospectively demonstrates that selecting a vaccine by DAI improves clinical outcomes.

points.requirement: Contrast inherited non-rearranged NK receptor families with rearranged TCR specificity.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Contrast inherited non-rearranged NK receptor families with rearranged TCR specificity.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Natural killer (NK) receptors are encoded in the germ line rather than assembled by the T-cell receptor’s somatic rearrangement process. They integrate complementary activating inputs with inhibitory signals; this is more complex than adding fixed on/off switches. Inhibitory motifs can recruit SHP phosphatases and suppress early activation, while several activating receptors signal through adaptors. Repertoire, receptor variants, prior education, cytokines and the target context matter. Some receptors also occur on T cells, and HLA-related recognition can depend on the bound peptide.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: NKG2D is activating and recognizes stress-related MICA, MICB and ULBP ligands; it also occurs on CD8 and gamma-delta T cells. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Inhibitory KIR2DL1 and KIR2DL2/3 recognize subsets of HLA-C; KIR3DL1 recognizes the Bw4 epitope on class-I molecules. Activating KIRs also exist, with variant-dependent ligands: curated examples include KIR2DS1/HLA-C and KIR3DS1/peptide-free HLA-F. CD94/NKG2A is inhibitory and reads peptide-loaded HLA-E; CD94/NKG2C is activating and bound HLA-E with lower affinity than NKG2A in the recombinant-protein study. CMV seropositivity was associated with NKG2C-rich repertoires in healthy donors. These are defined receptor-ligand findings, not interchangeable switches.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Explain self-HLA-dependent education/licensing, reduced responsiveness without a matched ligand and cytokine modulation.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Education tunes responsiveness. NK cells with matched self-HLA inhibitory interactions can be more responsive to later activating stimuli, while unmatched cells can be hyporesponsive. In Juelke’s human-cell experiments, cytokine-stimulated hyporesponsive cells acquired competence when they acquired KIR in the presence of its cognate MHC. This is not a fixed panel present identically on every NK cell. Removing one inhibitory HLA interaction is not necessarily removal of all restraints or a sufficient activation signal.

points.requirement: HLA or B2M loss can lift inhibitory signals but killing still requires appropriate activation; avoid claiming every HLA-loss target is killed.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: HLA or B2M loss can lift inhibitory signals but killing still requires appropriate activation; avoid claiming every HLA-loss target is killed.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some inhibitory NK receptors recognize self HLA class I, while activating receptors respond to other features. Reduced self display can weaken an inhibitory input, but the NK cell, its prior education, activating signals and target context still determine the response. NK cells can also contribute antibody-dependent killing through Fc receptors. Donor-derived or engineered NK-cell products need their own compatibility, persistence and safety assessment rather than a blanket claim that matching or rejection never matters. The principle comes from mouse experiments: lymphoma cells selected for loss of H-2 were less malignant at low dose and were rejected by a non-adaptive mechanism, which suggested that natural killer cells are effectors in a defence system geared to detect reduced self MHC (Kärre et al., 1986); that does not guarantee the same outcome for any human tumour. MHC class I molecules are ligands for killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (Parham, 2005): two-domain KIR2D receptors bind HLA-C alleles and three-domain KIR3D receptors bind HLA-A and HLA-B alleles, and the KIR family includes activating as well as inhibitory members (Mariuzza et al., 2025). CD94/NKG2A binds HLA-E, and HLA-E surface expression was enough to protect target cells from lysis by CD94/NKG2A-positive NK clones (Braud et al., 1998). NKG2D binds class I-related proteins including MICA, MICB and ULBP1 to 3 (Mariuzza et al., 2025), and engagement of NKG2D activated NK and gamma-delta T-cell cytolysis against epithelial tumour cells expressing MICA (Bauer et al., 1999). No single activating receptor dominates, since NK cells integrate synergistic signals from several (Long et al., 2013), and responsiveness depends on prior education: in human cell experiments, cytokine stimulation let hyporesponsive NK cells acquire KIR and function when the cognate MHC was present (Juelke et al., 2009). Loss of one HLA allele is not loss of all class I. Loss of beta-2 microglobulin removed surface class I in one of four relapsing melanoma patients (Zaretsky et al., 2016), and because HLA-E is assembled with beta-2 microglobulin, the KIR and NKG2A restraints would be expected to lift together; that last step is an inference not tested in the cited abstracts. A flow-based cytotoxicity assay that stains target and effector nuclei separately and distinguishes live from dead nuclei has been validated with NK-92 cells, CAR-T cells and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (Rabinovich et al., 2019). Target death is not a count of effector cells that released granule contents: surface CD107a marked NK cells that degranulated after stimulation with MHC-devoid targets and correlated with lysis, and also marked a large subset that did not secrete cytokine, so different readouts count different cells (Alter et al., 2004). CD16 is a low-affinity Fc receptor for IgG that mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells (Liu, 2022), a route separate from missing-self recognition. Neither assay readout shows tumour entry or clinical benefit.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: HLA or B2M loss can lift inhibitory signals but killing still requires appropriate activation; avoid claiming every HLA-loss target is killed.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Flow cytometry measures receptor proteins on defined viable populations; KIR/HLA genotyping identifies possible pairs; tissue protein or RNA tests ask about ligands; a controlled NK-target assay measures killing. A fictional target lacking all measured HLA restraints but lacking measured activating ligands need not be killed. An antibody engaging CD16 supplies a further hypothesis to test. Receptor expression, degranulation, target death, tumour entry and patient benefit remain separate measurements.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: INTERLINK-1 tested monalizumab plus cetuximab against placebo plus cetuximab after checkpoint therapy and platinum progression in recurrent/metastatic head-and-neck cancer. This negative comparison does not support a general claim of clinical success for NKG2A blockade.

points.requirement: Anergy and exhaustion are distinct programmes, not compulsory successive stages or interchangeable labels for dysfunction. points.requirement: Explain peptide/class-II recognition, dendritic-cell priming, cytokine-dependent differentiation and transcription-factor programs.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Explain peptide/class-II recognition, dendritic-cell priming, cytokine-dependent differentiation and transcription-factor programs.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: CD4 T-cell subsets are differentiation programmes shaped by antigen recognition, cytokines and gene regulation. Conventional naive CD4 cells recognize peptide-HLA class II during priming, often on dendritic cells. Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper and regulatory programmes have characteristic signals, transcription factors and outputs, but these are not permanent job titles or mutually exclusive functional tests. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Th1 programmes are associated with IL-12 and interferon-gamma signalling and the transcription factor T-bet. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Th17 programmes include ROR-gamma-t and IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 outputs. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Follicular helper programmes include BCL6 and the CXCR5 receptor that supports follicular location, and help germinal-centre B cells, including through IL-21. evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Describe Tfh BCL6, CXCR5, IL-21 and germinal-center B-cell help; qualify human CXCL13 and steering cytokines by source.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: In untreated human breast tumours, Gu-Trantien found CXCL13-producing Tfh cells mainly in tertiary-lymphoid-structure germinal centres and an eight-gene signature associated with survival or preoperative-chemotherapy response. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Regulatory programmes help restrain responses and maintain tolerance. FOXP3 is a central regulator, and TGF-beta/IL-2 support induced differentiation in specified experimental systems. IL-10, TGF-beta and CTLA-4-associated interactions can contribute to regulation in context. These are not exclusive outputs of one programme, and the human FOXP3 studies above explain why marker presence needs a separate suppression assay.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Describe FOXP3-associated regulatory programs, TGFb/IL-2 context and suppressive outputs without treating any single stain as a functional test.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: A transcription-factor stain is a clue to a programme, not a function test. points.requirement: Explain T-cell antigen recognition, IFNg signaling, induced PD-L1 and PD-1-mediated restraint of the response.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Explain T-cell antigen recognition, IFNg signaling, induced PD-L1 and PD-1-mediated restraint of the response.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: The sequence proposed by Taube and colleagues and mapped in more detail since is a loop. A T cell recognises a tumour peptide on HLA and releases interferon gamma; the interferon acts through the Janus kinases JAK1 and JAK2 in nearby tumour and immune cells; PD-L1 rises; PD-L1 binds PD-1 on the T cell and damps it. In melanoma cell lines, Garcia-Diaz and colleagues found that the interferon gamma, JAK1 and JAK2, STAT1, STAT2 and STAT3, IRF1 axis primarily regulates PD-L1, with IRF1 binding the PD-L1 promoter, and biopsies from patients with melanoma showed enrichment of that interferon signature and of STAT and IRF1 target genes in tumours that responded to anti-PD-1 treatment.

points.requirement: Distinguish induced expression from tumor-intrinsic constitutive expression independent of local T-cell induction.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Distinguish induced expression from tumor-intrinsic constitutive expression independent of local T-cell induction.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Evidence from tissue. In human melanocytic lesions, 98% of PD-L1-positive (B7-H1-positive) tumours had tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes compared with 28% of PD-L1-negative tumours; positive melanocytes sat almost always immediately next to lymphocytes, and interferon gamma was detected at the interface but not in PD-L1-negative tumours (Taube and colleagues). The same colocalisation appeared in inflamed benign naevi, which fits PD-L1 as a response to tissue inflammation. In triple-negative breast cancer, Gruosso and colleagues described an immunoreactive group whose tumours had granzyme B-positive CD8 T cells inside cancer-cell regions, a type 1 interferon signature and elevated IDO and PD-L1, the pattern adaptive resistance predicts; that is an association in tissue and not a direct test of the loop. The alternative, called innate or constitutive resistance, is PD-L1 driven by the cancer cell's own signalling regardless of T cells.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Define survival through failed recognition, access or function and connect elimination/equilibrium/escape without making every tumor follow a fixed sequence.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: The claim. Immune surveillance concerns recognition and control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds selection of the populations that persist. Elimination, equilibrium and escape are conceptual processes that can coexist or occur independently. Their assignment requires evidence of control, restraint or outgrowth and its mechanism; they are not a compulsory calendar for every clinical cancer. The immune system therefore both protects against cancer and shapes the cancers that emerge.

evidence.explanation: This exact reader passage represents the specified distinction, measurement, study or qualified inference: Define survival through failed recognition, access or function and connect elimination/equilibrium/escape without making every tumor follow a fixed sequence.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immune escape can involve loss of a targeted antigen, altered HLA alleles or processing, defective inducible signalling, inhibition after entry or impaired access. Anagnostou found loss of putative neoantigens in checkpoint-resistant lung tumours with accompanying T-cell evidence. McGranahan described allele-specific HLA loss in lung cancer evolution. Montesion’s commercial pan-cancer genomic series contained 83,644 samples with HLA-I loss of heterozygosity in 17%; this assay-defined pan-cancer observation is not a breast-specific prevalence. Allele loss differs from reversible expression change or a B2M defect affecting class-I surface display.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Several things happen at once around an operation. Reviews describe a stress response in which injury and stress release catecholamines, prostaglandins and cortisol, and in which a short pro-inflammatory phase is followed by a prolonged anti-inflammatory phase; natural killer (NK) cells are severely affected in that period, and sympathetic stress factors, mediators including interleukin 6 and transforming growth factor beta, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells have been proposed as mediators (Horowitz and colleagues; Angka and colleagues). Wound healing adds repair signals, and anaesthesia and pain control add their own possible effects: the breast cancer anaesthesia trials were built on the premise that the surgical stress response, volatile anaesthetic and opioids impair host defence and that regional anaesthesia with propofol ameliorates all three. Most of this mechanistic evidence comes from blood measurements in patients and from mouse models, so whether the changes alter recurrence in people is a separate question that randomised trials answer best.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A common route for blood-borne effector T cells involves recruitment, adhesion and exit from a vessel, movement through stroma and contact with relevant cancer cells. An excluded distribution records where cells were found. It does not establish why they stopped. A cell that has reached a target but is inhibited has a different measured problem, although access and functional failures can coexist.

Chen and Mellman’s 2013 framework describes seven linked steps: release of cancer antigens; their collection and presentation; T-cell priming and activation; trafficking; entry into tumour tissue; recognition of cancer cells; and killing. Further antigen release may support another round. In conventional T-cell recognition, a displayed peptide-HLA complex and a suitable T-cell receptor are separate dependencies.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Harlin found six chemokines, including CCL5, CXCL9 and CXCL10, preferentially in T-cell-containing human melanoma metastases, with supporting migration experiments. In melanoma models, Mikucki found that CXCR3 supported intravascular arrest and extravasation of transferred CD8 effectors. These findings identify defined recruitment and vascular dependencies, not a universal explanation for every abnormal vessel. Spranger’s human melanoma association and mouse experiments connected tumour WNT/beta-catenin activity with deficient dendritic-cell recruitment and absent T-cell infiltration, a desert-like problem rather than necessarily an excluded rim. In their 2015 commentary on the mouse experiments, Spranger and Gajewski describe reduced CCL4 expression and failed recruitment of Batf3-lineage dendritic cells. This is a defined melanoma mechanism, not a universal explanation for every excluded tissue pattern.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Hammerl’s spatial analysis of 681 TNBCs distinguished excluded, ignored and inflamed groups. Excluded samples showed collagen-10 deposits and TGF-beta/VEGF programmes; ignored samples showed either dense CD163-positive myeloid cells or WNT/PPAR-gamma programmes. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are lymphocytes found in sampled tumour tissue, including T- and B-cell populations. The breast stromal TIL method estimates the area occupied by a defined mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within eligible tumour-associated stroma on H&E sections. Higher pretreatment scores were associated with better outcomes in the cited early triple-negative breast cancer cohorts, but those associations do not guarantee an individual outcome or establish extra benefit from pembrolizumab. Intratumoral location, stromal area, immune-cell counts and cells expanded for TIL therapy are different measurements or uses.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Fixed sections and morphology or selected stains can measure identity, compartment and abundance; viable-cell assays ask about phenotype and function. Dissociation loses native location, culture can select populations and tests consume finite material. Keep cells per square millimetre, specified cell fractions, stromal-area percentages and assay-specific function distinct. TIL therapy is a manufactured expanded-cell product: a tissue count does not establish product yield, composition, potency or treatment success. Sampling, damage, mixed compartments, unsuitable markers and culture selection are different failure modes, and descriptive pathology, research function and clinical treatment selection require different validation.

items.title: Breast MRI: enhancement, extent and research volume

review.auditor: Coordinator source-first reading and field comparison; not independent expert, learner or language approval
review.rationale: Seven later bodies read fully and six original/later exact diffs read. Unchanged original teaching is reused by identity, not claimed independently reread. The frozen 153 rows retain 99 original and 131 later substantive obligations plus 22 non-credit dispositions; one transcription erratum is explicit. All 160 section signatures reproduce. Claims use 26 complete abstracts, 33 targeted article-body paragraphs and specified official/PDF passages, not whole-paper reads. Current ASCO2026 guidance is separate from historical schedules and experimental molecular surveillance. Source figures are schematic; no viable-cell conversion, microscopic exclusion or scan-guided treatment benefit is inferred. Personal-context routing is excluded; older assertions outside selected fields are not blanket recertified.

points.requirement: Define breast MRI through magnetic/radiofrequency imaging rather than a count of viable cells.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) records tissue-dependent signals using a magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses. In contrast-enhanced breast MRI, intravenous gadolinium changes those signals. Dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging (DCE) acquires images before and at specified times after contrast. Enhancement depends on delivery, vascular and tissue distribution, and acquisition; its shape, distribution and time course help interpretation. Benign tissue can enhance too.

MRI can describe regional extent and changes during treatment. A change in contrast signal does not establish pathological complete response (pCR), which concerns examined tissue. Residual disease can be inconspicuous, while nonmalignant tissue and treatment changes can enhance. Image-derived lengths and volumes need their own acquisition and calculation definitions.

Their quoted anchors and the recorded source limits are part of the assessment; mere link presence is not the proof. Source scope: Definition and source-scoped overview read against the specified official text and named study abstracts. Acquisition, interpretation and useful clinical strategy remain separate. points.requirement: Carry the marker-through-landscape analogy with its limit: brightness and functional labels do not establish cancer-cell identity.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Think of a contrast marker passing through a landscape. A brighter region records how that examination sees the marker and tissue, not a label attached to every cancer cell. Background parenchymal enhancement (BPE) is enhancement of normal fibroglandular breast tissue, described as minimal, mild, moderate or marked. It is separate from the amount of fibroglandular tissue and from mammographic density. Non-mass enhancement (NME) describes enhancement without a mass or focus, distinguishable from the background; benign, high-risk and malignant processes can overlap in that appearance. Neither a bright area nor an NME label supplies histology.

items.title: Breast ultrasound: an image made from echoes

points.requirement: Define diagnostic breast ultrasound as returning acoustic signals describing structures/selected flow, without assigning histology or complete exclusion.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Diagnostic ultrasound sends high-frequency sound pulses through a transducer and reconstructs images from returning echoes. Gel helps transmit sound between probe and skin. Echo timing and strength, the selected plane and examination settings contribute to the displayed structures; moving the probe changes the view. It uses no ionising X-rays. This diagnostic use is distinct from therapeutic ultrasound.

Breast ultrasound can examine a focal breast or nodal finding, distinguish fluid-containing from solid findings, and guide a needle towards a target. Shape, orientation, margins, internal echoes and posterior behaviour are interpreted together. A simple cyst, a complex finding and a solid finding are not interchangeable diagnoses. Sampling adds tissue evidence; the live image guides the procedure but does not replace examination of the sample.

points.requirement: Carry the room-echo analogy and beam/time/boundary scope; diagnostic sonography is distinct from therapeutic ultrasound.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The room-echo analogy explains the observation: a beam travels into tissue and returns from boundaries. Under a common assumed sound speed, a later return is placed deeper than an earlier one. That relationship does not identify cell type. A selected image plane is neither a histological section nor a survey of the whole body. Grayscale images primarily describe echo patterns; Doppler uses frequency changes from movement to describe blood-flow direction or speed. Its displayed colours depend on the mode and settings, rather than staining malignant cells. Flow is not itself proof of malignant activity.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Diagnostic ultrasound sends high-frequency sound pulses through a transducer and reconstructs images from returning echoes. Gel helps transmit sound between probe and skin. Echo timing and strength, the selected plane and examination settings contribute to the displayed structures; moving the probe changes the view. It uses no ionising X-rays. This diagnostic use is distinct from therapeutic ultrasound.

Breast ultrasound can examine a focal breast or nodal finding, distinguish fluid-containing from solid findings, and guide a needle towards a target. Shape, orientation, margins, internal echoes and posterior behaviour are interpreted together. A simple cyst, a complex finding and a solid finding are not interchangeable diagnoses. Sampling adds tissue evidence; the live image guides the procedure but does not replace examination of the sample.

points.requirement: Define immuno-PET through a radiolabelled antibody/derived binder and distribution, not a guarantee of target-exclusive uptake or therapeutic benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Immuno-PET uses radiolabelled antibodies or antibody-derived binders. Full immunoglobulin G (IgG), antigen-binding fragments (Fab), minibodies and single-domain nanobodies differ in size and pharmacokinetics. The format can affect penetration, clearance, retention and normal-organ background; there is no universal best format. A label makes the binder traceable, not a perfect detector of every target site.

The radionuclide must suit the product's imaging time course. Dijkers' 89Zr-trastuzumab study examined a full antibody over several days; Keyaerts' 68Ga-HER2 nanobody study imaged at earlier times. These are product-specific examples. Antibody imaging can concern a tumour-associated target or immune cells. CD8 binder imaging belongs here; granzyme-B peptide or peptidomimetic imaging is a different tracer class and has its own record.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Imagine sending a labelled binding tool into the body. Some remains in blood, some reaches accessible sites, and some fails to bind or clears. It did not randomise a scan-guided treatment strategy.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Granzyme B is an enzyme released by cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells. Experimental PET tracers use labelled peptides or peptidomimetics to target granzyme-associated activity. This is distinct from CD8 antibody-derived binder imaging and does not by itself establish recognition of a particular tumour antigen, identify which cell released the enzyme or prove a durable response.

Larimer's 2017 proof of concept used mouse models and examined human biopsy specimens; it was not a human PET trial. A 2026 review describes 68Ga and 18F tracer approaches and early human feasibility while noting standardisation and validation needs. In Shen's 2024 phase 1/2 study, 68Ga-grazytracer imaging in 24 patients with mixed solid tumours or lymphomas explored distribution, safety and response associations after immune treatment. It did not randomise a scan-guided treatment strategy.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Immuno-PET uses radiolabelled antibodies or antibody-derived binders. Full immunoglobulin G (IgG), antigen-binding fragments (Fab), minibodies and single-domain nanobodies differ in size and pharmacokinetics. The format can affect penetration, clearance, retention and normal-organ background; there is no universal best format. A label makes the binder traceable, not a perfect detector of every target site.

The radionuclide must suit the product's imaging time course. Dijkers' 89Zr-trastuzumab study examined a full antibody over several days; Keyaerts' 68Ga-HER2 nanobody study imaged at earlier times. These are product-specific examples. Antibody imaging can concern a tumour-associated target or immune cells. CD8 binder imaging belongs here; granzyme-B peptide or peptidomimetic imaging is a different tracer class and has its own record.

points.requirement: Define low-dose X-ray breast patterns including masses/calcifications, without claiming direct identification of every cancer cell.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Mammography records how X-rays pass through a positioned, compressed breast. Fat and fibroglandular tissue contribute different image appearances. Compression reduces tissue overlap, thickness and motion. Standard digital mammography produces projection images; digital breast tomosynthesis acquires multiple angles and reconstructs thin sections. These computed sections are different from tissue that has been physically removed, prepared and stained.

Screening asks about cancer in people without symptoms; a diagnostic examination investigates symptoms or an imaging finding and may use additional views. Neither label establishes that cancer is present. Masses and calcium deposits are findings whose pattern and distribution matter. A calcification is not itself proof of malignancy or a measure of viable cancer after treatment. A biopsy adds examination of sampled tissue.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Imagine viewing a stack of translucent layers: features at different depths can overlap in a projection. Mammography measures X-ray transmission, not reflected sound. Tomosynthesis uses several projections to reconstruct sections and reduce the effect of overlap; it does not stain cells or guarantee that every lesion becomes visible. A schematic with overlapping shapes and separated reconstructed sections illustrates the geometry, without identifying any shape as cancer. A prepared stained tissue section supplies a different, sampled observation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Mammography records how X-rays pass through a positioned, compressed breast. Fat and fibroglandular tissue contribute different image appearances. Compression reduces tissue overlap, thickness and motion. Standard digital mammography produces projection images; digital breast tomosynthesis acquires multiple angles and reconstructs thin sections. These computed sections are different from tissue that has been physically removed, prepared and stained.

Screening asks about cancer in people without symptoms; a diagnostic examination investigates symptoms or an imaging finding and may use additional views. Neither label establishes that cancer is present. Masses and calcium deposits are findings whose pattern and distribution matter. A calcification is not itself proof of malignancy or a measure of viable cancer after treatment. A biopsy adds examination of sampled tissue.

points.requirement: Define PET-CT as named radiotracer distribution plus X-ray anatomy, without malignancy-specific or microscopic-exclusion guarantees.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Positron emission tomography (PET) detects photons produced when a positron emitted by a tracer annihilates with an electron. Detected photon pairs inform reconstruction of the activity distribution. The tracer molecule and its handling in the body determine the biological question; PET is not a label that marks every cancer cell. Anatomical imaging can help locate and interpret the distribution.

Normal tissues and inflammatory processes can accumulate some tracers, while some malignant lesions produce little detectable signal. The field imaged, background, lesion size, acquisition, reconstruction and tracer biology limit detection. Whole-body terminology does not establish a microscopic disease census. Uptake measurements have a named tracer, time, unit and calculation; they are not percentages of malignant cells.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
PET/CT combines positron emission tomography with computed tomography. PET reconstructs radiotracer activity; CT adds anatomical information and can support attenuation correction. Registration helps relate the two, without guaranteeing an exact match in moving tissues. A low-dose CT used for localisation and attenuation correction is not automatically a full diagnostic CT with its own acquisition and contrast protocol.

Tracer identity remains part of the scan identity. 18F-FDG concerns glucose handling, whereas an antibody or other target-directed tracer asks a different question. Normal physiology, inflammation and malignancy can contribute uptake. Structural and activity findings can also disagree. Interpretation retains anatomy, history, preparation, comparison images and, where indicated, tissue evidence.

SUL uses lean body mass; SUVmax is a voxel maximum, while SUVmean averages a defined region. These values are not percentages of target-positive or malignant cells. PERCIST uses specified SUL-based response measurements; that framework does not make all SUV summaries interchangeable. Raw numbers from different tracers or protocols do not supply a controlled biological comparison or a universal malignancy cutoff.

points.requirement: Keep RECIST target selection, five-total/two-per-organ limits, ordinary longest versus nodal short axes and dimensions distinct from total tumour volume or all disease.

evidence.explanation: Up to five/two-per-organ target selection and ordinary/nodal axes are distinct from total volume or an all-disease census.

points.requirement: PR uses baseline; target PD uses nadir plus relative and absolute increase. New/non-target disease can change overall response; preserve the fictional 100/60/73-mm assumptions and rule-specific calculation.

evidence.explanation: Baseline for PR, nadir with relative-plus-absolute increase for target PD, and outside/new disease remain separate.
The fictional 100/60/73-mm exercise retains its assumptions and both progression increases, rather than treating below-baseline as no progression.

points.requirement: Distinguish iUPD/iCPD and possible pseudoprogression, reassessment timing and clinical-stability criteria from automatic permission to continue treatment; trial data handling is not an individual care rule.

evidence.explanation: iUPD/iCPD data rules, generally 4-8-week reassessment, stability and protocol exceptions do not automatically permit personal treatment continuation.

evidence.explanation: SUL normalisation, peak ROI, input/reference suitability, the Table 7 percentage and absolute change, and other disease conditions remain distinct from anatomy or tissue clearance.

evidence.explanation: Imaging and tissue assessment have different criteria; undetected disease, durability and clinical outcomes remain separate.

evidence.explanation: Selected baseline ROI/reference conditions, liver threshold, technical comparability and the proposal's advised post-chemotherapy interval retain their exact framework and treatment-specific limits.

points.requirement: ELISpot counts spots from cells secreting a chosen molecule under defined stimulation; it does not watch killing

evidence.explanation: Coordinator semantic comparison: ELISpot counts spots from cells secreting a chosen molecule under defined stimulation; it does not watch killing Exact current passage is retained in the batch proof packet; this field evidence is draft-local, not main or expert acceptance.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Fictional arithmetic: wells with 100,000 input cells give 30 spots after peptide stimulation and 5 spots with vehicle. Background-subtracted, that is 30 minus 5 = 25 spots per 100,000 cells, or 250 spot-forming units per million input cells. This is an arithmetic summary and not a positivity cut-off, replicates, positive controls and a prespecified response rule still apply, and in mixed PBMCs it is not the frequency of a particular T-cell subset. If the cells came from an expanded culture, the number describes the cultured cells and not the responding fraction of the original blood draw.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: What the evidence does and does not support: the interferon gamma ELISpot is described as measuring the difference in the number of cells secreting the molecule with and without peptide, and interferon gamma is produced predominantly by natural killer and natural killer T cells as well as Th1 CD4 and CD8 effector T cells, so a mixed-cell spot does not by itself name the responding cell (Wykes and Renia protocol). In HIV vaccine research robust ELISpot responses were induced in a phase IIb trial that lacked efficacy, which challenged the assay's predictive power (Streeck 2009), and a validation in cynomolgus monkeys for responses to viral vector antigens (Yang 2022) validates that preparation and species and not cancer efficacy. Peptide added to cells can bypass the tumour's own processing and presentation, so a peptide response needs a separate bridge to natural tumour recognition.

A negative result remains bounded by the number and condition of input cells, the stimulus, chosen secreted molecule, culture history and response rule; it is not a census of every responding cell in the body. Assay reproducibility and a cancer-treatment benefit claim need separate evidence.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: What the evidence does and does not support: the interferon gamma ELISpot is described as measuring the difference in the number of cells secreting the molecule with and without peptide, and interferon gamma is produced predominantly by natural killer and natural killer T cells as well as Th1 CD4 and CD8 effector T cells, so a mixed-cell spot does not by itself name the responding cell (Wykes and Renia protocol). In HIV vaccine research robust ELISpot responses were induced in a phase IIb trial that lacked efficacy, which challenged the assay's predictive power (Streeck 2009), and a validation in cynomolgus monkeys for responses to viral vector antigens (Yang 2022) validates that preparation and species and not cancer efficacy. Peptide added to cells can bypass the tumour's own processing and presentation, so a peptide response needs a separate bridge to natural tumour recognition.

points.requirement: Expanded culture result describes cultured cells, not the original draw

evidence.explanation: Coordinator semantic comparison: Expanded culture result describes cultured cells, not the original draw Exact current passage is retained in the batch proof packet; this field evidence is draft-local, not main or expert acceptance.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

evidence.explanation: Coordinator semantic comparison: Expanded culture result describes cultured cells, not the original draw Exact current passage is retained in the batch proof packet; this field evidence is draft-local, not main or expert acceptance.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Fictional arithmetic: wells with 100,000 input cells give 30 spots after peptide stimulation and 5 spots with vehicle. Background-subtracted, that is 30 minus 5 = 25 spots per 100,000 cells, or 250 spot-forming units per million input cells. This is an arithmetic summary and not a positivity cut-off, replicates, positive controls and a prespecified response rule still apply, and in mixed PBMCs it is not the frequency of a particular T-cell subset. If the cells came from an expanded culture, the number describes the cultured cells and not the responding fraction of the original blood draw.
