items.title: Drug targets and mechanisms of action

review.auditor: GPT-6.1 Sol coordinator; semantic and source assessment at stated primary/inference scope, not blind, expert, learner or language acceptance
review.rationale: Full later lessons and complete original teaching differences assessed. The earlier 197 parent rows are retained: 176 teaching obligations, 19 bibliographic rows and 2 personal-case pointers excluded; 11 subclauses refine parents without extra points. Exact reader paragraphs carry definitions, controls, measurement limits and fictional examples. Two detailed ASTCT 2026 clauses remain source-open. No point is earned from citation presence, a source hash or an unapplied proposal.

points.requirement: Target = molecule/structure acted on; mechanism = how action produces effect; target name != reachable/driving/functional.

evidence.explanation: Target identity, accessible exposure, mechanism, dependence, tissue selectivity and human benefit are separate claims.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

evidence.explanation: Target identity, accessible exposure, mechanism, dependence, tissue selectivity and human benefit are separate claims.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

evidence.explanation: Target identity, accessible exposure, mechanism, dependence, tissue selectivity and human benefit are separate claims.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

points.requirement: Four panels: purified binding, engagement in relevant cell, effect measurement, benefit and harm evidence; reaching the compartment alone is insufficient; molecular shapes schematic.

evidence.explanation: Purified binding, relevant-system engagement, functional effects and clinical outcomes form separate evidence layers.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Target engagement and the evidence ladder. Target engagement asks whether a compound interacts with its intended target in the relevant system. Binding to a purified protein does not show that the compound enters the cell or reaches its target in a tumour, and engagement is also not a change in the target's function, a downstream effect or clinical benefit. Each question needs its own measurement: engagement first, then a measured biological effect, then a check of the causal explanation with controls, then clinical evidence.

evidence.explanation: Purified binding, relevant-system engagement, functional effects and clinical outcomes form separate evidence layers.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Reading a thermal-shift result. The cellular thermal shift assay was introduced to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples through ligand-induced thermal stabilisation (Martinez Molina et al. 2013). The readout is the soluble target signal remaining after heating, plotted either against temperature at a fixed compound concentration or against concentration at a fixed temperature, so degrees Celsius and concentration units sit on different axes and the two designs ask different bounded questions. A shift of the compound curve against a matched control supports engagement under those conditions; indirect stability or protein-complex effects can also change the signal, so it is not an inhibition or occupancy percentage, and no universal shift cut-off is given here. The heated aliquots are consumed, so a record should carry the compound, concentration, exposure time, temperature series, cell or tissue system and controls. In an isothermal-shift study with a pan-kinase inhibitor, a large share of non-kinase proteins shifted in cells, which the authors read as in-cell profiling being more likely than lysate profiling to identify indirect binding targets; they recommend lysate profiling to identify targets and in-cell profiling to verify intracellular engagement (Ball et al. 2020).

points.requirement: PK = absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; dose vs exposure (named substance, named place concentration-time); route/organ function/interactions/product change exposure.

evidence.explanation: ADME and measured concentration-time exposure are distinguished from administered amount and pharmacodynamic effects.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Dose, exposure and effect are three different things. Dose is the administered amount; exposure is a named substance's concentration over time in a named place, which route, organ function, interactions and product properties can change for the same dose; and effect is a separate measurement, because effects or injury can persist after exposure falls and detectable drug does not guarantee productive engagement. Pharmacokinetics follows absorption (including how much of an oral dose reaches the circulation), distribution (plasma is not the unbound concentration inside a cell), metabolism (active metabolites may add their own exposure) and excretion, summarised by clearance, the removal relative to concentration, in volume per time. FDA labelling guidance lists the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) at the approved dosage, time to steady state, accumulation ratio, clearance, volume of distribution and half-life; this AUC is an exposure area and is unrelated to the area under a prediction curve that judges tests.

evidence.explanation: ADME and measured concentration-time exposure are distinguished from administered amount and pharmacodynamic effects.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Read the measurement card as well as the curve. Record the dose, route, analyte, sampled compartment, assay, population and sampling interval. Concentration can be in ng/mL, maximum concentration in the same units, concentration-time area in ng·hour/mL, half-life in hours and clearance in litres per hour. Sampling should capture the phase of interest: a sparse late sample cannot reliably recover an unobserved early peak. Pharmacodynamics measures biological effects separately. First-pass metabolism can reduce oral bioavailability; protein binding and active metabolites also matter.

Measure death separately from slower growth, because a viability signal can fall when cells divide less or change metabolism; pair a suitable death assay with long-term survival or colony formation, and record concentration, time and denominator, remembering that colony formation measures reproductive survival and not the way cells die. Synthetic lethality is not oncogene addiction, which is dependence on an active driver: in Src-, BCR-ABL- and EGF receptor-dependent cells, unequal attenuation of survival and pro-apoptotic signals after the driver is inactivated contributes to death (Sharma et al.). It is also not synergy, since a score above a reference model does not identify which losses interact. In the BRCA/PARP example, homologous recombination is a DNA repair process and HRD means deficiency of that process. Trapping PARP on DNA and inhibiting its catalytic activity are different perturbations, while repair restoration or changes in replication stress can change sensitivity. The first impairment can pre-exist, so a two-loss interaction does not require two drugs.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Rescue, restoration and what each test can show. A rescue experiment restores a relevant function and asks whether the predicted harm falls; that strengthens attribution, but a failed rescue is not automatic disproof, because the restored function may not be expressed, localised or timed adequately (a reading rule, not a result from these experiments). A real example of functional restoration involved secondary BRCA2 mutations, often described as reversions. Ovarian cancer lines PEO1, PEO4 and PEO6 came from one BRCA2 mutation carrier: PEO1 was BRCA2 deficient and sensitive to cisplatin and a PARP inhibitor, while a secondary BRCA2 mutation that cancelled the inherited one arose in the patient (PEO4, PEO6) and, under cisplatin and PARP-inhibitor selection of PEO1, in the dish, restoring BRCA2 and resistance. Function was shown by homologous recombination assays after transfecting wild-type or mutant BRCA2 cDNA into reporter cells, and transient siRNA depletion (two siRNAs against a non-targeting control) re-sensitised the restored clones and PEO4 (Sakai et al. 2009). That is a secondary-mutation restoration plus knockdown in one patient's lineage, not a designed rescue of a knockout, and depleting a protein is not the same as inhibiting it with a drug. BRCA and PARP evidence is experimental: BRCA1 or BRCA2 dysfunction sensitised cells to PARP inhibition (Farmer et al.), BRCA2-deficient cells and tumours were acutely sensitive (Bryant et al.), and PARP inhibitors trap PARP1 and PARP2 on damaged DNA, with trapping potency (niraparib above olaparib, far above veliparib) not tracking catalytic inhibition (Murai et al.). Normal tissue can share the vulnerability: normal Brca2-deficient mouse intestinal epithelium showed very high apoptosis within hours of PARP inhibition (Hay et al.). None of this establishes clinical benefit.

evidence.explanation: Two tolerated impairments form a lethal interaction in a tested system; genetic labels, oncogene dependence, synergy and clinical response remain distinct.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: What has to be shown. Compare matched cells with neither impairment, each alone and both, and check that the intended functions changed. Measure death separately from slower growth, because a viability signal can fall when cells divide less or change metabolism; pair a suitable death assay with long-term survival or colony formation, and record concentration, time and denominator, remembering that colony formation measures reproductive survival and not the way cells die. Synthetic lethality is not oncogene addiction, which is dependence on an active driver: in Src-, BCR-ABL- and EGF receptor-dependent cells, unequal attenuation of survival and pro-apoptotic signals after the driver is inactivated contributes to death (Sharma et al.). It is also not synergy, since a score above a reference model does not identify which losses interact. In the BRCA/PARP example, homologous recombination is a DNA repair process and HRD means deficiency of that process. Trapping PARP on DNA and inhibiting its catalytic activity are different perturbations, while repair restoration or changes in replication stress can change sensitivity. The first impairment can pre-exist, so a two-loss interaction does not require two drugs.

points.requirement: Define cancer-vaccine strategies and retain recognition teaching without guaranteeing tumour access, natural recognition or control.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Cancer-vaccine strategies seek useful recognition of cancer-associated targets. Their purpose is different from vaccination against an infection that can cause cancer: HPV and hepatitis B vaccines reduce infection-related cancer risk, rather than treat an established tumour. Teaching recognition is an aim, not a guarantee that responding cells will reach and control the cancer.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Follow a proposed vaccine response through separate questions. Is the antigen supplied or available with suitable supporting signals? evidence.supportingExcerpt: Checkpoint antibodies interrupt specified inhibitory contacts. These target-specific descriptions are more precise than treating all checkpoint drugs as one switch.

Hui's 2017 biochemical reconstitution and intact-cell experiments found that PD-1-recruited Shp2 preferentially dephosphorylated CD28 over the T-cell receptor, not that CD28 was the only possible affected signal. CTLA-4 and CD28 share CD80 and CD86. Qureshi's human and mouse cell experiments showed CTLA-4 capture and removal of these ligands from an opposing cell, reducing available costimulation. Contact and capture cartoons show these distinct receptor jobs; their molecule counts and positions are schematic, not a complete mechanism or a clinical comparison of blocking antibodies.

points.requirement: Read both complete partner/blockade diagrams: PD-1 has PD-L1 and PD-L2 partners, direct PD-L1 blockade does not directly block the PD-1/PD-L2 contact, and CD28/CTLA-4 share CD80/CD86.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Checkpoint antibodies interrupt specified inhibitory contacts. PD-1 is a receptor with two partners, PD-L1 and PD-L2; PD-L1 is a distinct molecule found on cancer and non-cancer cells. The pembrolizumab label describes blockade of PD-1 binding to both ligands. Atezolizumab instead binds PD-L1 and blocks its PD-1 and B7.1 interactions; directly blocking PD-L1 does not directly block the separate PD-1/PD-L2 contact. These target-specific descriptions are more precise than treating all checkpoint drugs as one switch.

points.requirement: Verify KEYNOTE-522: stage II/III early TNBC, 1174 randomised, pembrolizumab/placebo with preoperative chemotherapy and continuation after surgery, and 60-month overall survival 86.6 versus 81.7 per cent.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: KEYNOTE-522 randomised 1,174 people with previously untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer to pembrolizumab or placebo with chemotherapy before surgery, followed by continuation of the assigned antibody or placebo after surgery. At a median follow-up of 75.1 months, estimated 60-month overall survival was 86.6 per cent versus 81.7 per cent. Enrolment did not require PD-L1 positivity. The trial compared the whole perioperative regimen and was not designed to isolate the contribution of each treatment phase. These group results do not predict one person's outcome.

points.requirement: Verify KEYNOTE-355: 847 advanced first-line participants, pembrolizumab/placebo with chemotherapy, and the CPS-at-least-10 subgroup overall survival 23.0 versus 16.1 months with HR0.73.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: KEYNOTE-355 studied 847 people with previously untreated locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. In the PD-L1 combined-positive-score-at-least-10 subgroup, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy gave median overall survival of 23.0 months versus 16.1 with placebo plus chemotherapy, with a death hazard ratio of 0.73. A median divides a study group in half; it is not an individual forecast. The October 2026 U.S. pembrolizumab label has no PD-L1 qualifier for its high-risk early-stage TNBC regimen, while its advanced TNBC indications with chemotherapy or sacituzumab govitecan specify CPS at least 10 and an FDA-authorised test. The sacituzumab combination is a separate labelled regimen, not the KEYNOTE-355 comparison. Population, regimen, scoring context and evidence must stay together.

points.requirement: Define androgen-receptor antagonism and distinguish receptor expression from drug sensitivity.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An androgen receptor pathway inhibitor can act on hormone production or on the receptor itself. These are different interventions. Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone are androgen hormones; the full-length androgen receptor is a hormone-responsive transcription factor that helps regulate which DNA instructions are read into RNA. Bicalutamide and enzalutamide act at its ligand-binding region rather than removing the hormone supply. Blocking this receptor is also different from blocking the estrogen receptor. A receptor can be present while its partners, sequence, abundance or cellular setting change what an antagonist does.
evidence.explanation: Antagonism is defined at the receptor and distinguished from staining-defined presence and sensitivity. 19359544: primary research publication, complete abstract and targeted body paragraphs; NCI-enzalutamide: official technical dictionary, complete raw definition, not linked trial or drug-summary pages; NCI-targeted: official patient education, targeted type and hormone-mechanism paragraphs; universal safety language not adopted

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Traina and colleagues studied enzalutamide in a single-arm phase II trial of locally advanced or metastatic androgen-receptor-positive triple-negative breast cancer. The breast-optimised immunohistochemistry assay allowed enrolment with more than 0% nuclear staining. The evaluable subgroup additionally required at least 10% nuclear staining and a postbaseline assessment: 78 of 118 enrolled patients met that definition. The abstract reported clinical benefit at 16 weeks in 25% of all enrolled patients and 33% of that subgroup. The trial registry defines this endpoint as complete or partial response, or stable disease for at least 16 weeks. It is not the percentage with tumour shrinkage, and a single treatment arm does not measure a survival advantage over another treatment.

review.auditor: Coordinator full source-first reading and unit-by-unit field/source assessment; not independent expert, learner or language approval
review.rationale: All five unique bodies were read end to end before owner inspection. The original/later file pairs are byte-identical, so this assessment is reused by identity while both 55-section inventories remain separate. The frozen 123-row inventory contains 103 substantive obligations and 20 non-credit rows. Thirty-five connected notes, selected retained BRD4 passages, the explicit competitive-pocket refinement and six named source qualifications carry the definitions, model and clinical examples, measurement cards and all practice answers. Six actual registered readers and static exports verify exact passages. Sixteen complete abstracts, 40 targeted body paragraphs, official definitions/annotations and the joined Traina trial registry retain their reading depths. A listed funding erratum was read in full. No whole-paper, universal drug-response, main/live or named review credit is claimed.

points.requirement: Define BET pocket inhibition as interference with acetyl-mark recognition without assuming removal of every BET-protein function.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: BET proteins contain two recognition domains, BD1 and BD2, alongside other interaction regions. JQ1 competes with acetylated binding partners at these pockets. It was developed as an experimental chemical probe, with binding measured across bromodomains. The original work found binding to both BRD4 bromodomains and other BET-family members; a drawing of one occupied pocket does not make the compound specific to BD1. Compare the actual protein and domain profile of each compound. A preference for BD2, or for one family member, is not comparative evidence of human safety or anticancer benefit. Pocket occupation also leaves protein regions that a separately verified depletion experiment removes.
evidence.explanation: Pocket recognition and remaining protein functions are separated; occupation is not whole-protein depletion. 20871596: primary research publication, complete abstract and targeted body paragraphs; 26735014: primary research publication, complete abstract and targeted body paragraphs

points.requirement: Define selected cyclin-dependent kinase inhibition while separating cell-cycle and transcription roles.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Cyclin-dependent kinases are enzymes that transfer phosphate groups to proteins. Cyclins are regulatory protein partners; different kinase-partner combinations help control cell division or transcription, the reading of DNA into RNA. Naming a drug a CDK inhibitor does not identify the job it changes, and the same kinase can participate in connected processes.

points.requirement: Interpret the selected-role diagram without treating it as an exhaustive job map: CDK4/6 and CDK2 around G1/DNA copying, CDK7 at initiation and activation of other CDKs, and CDK9 at elongation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: DNA is the cell's genetic material. During copying, a replication fork can slow or stall; that stress is not itself a diagnosis of a double-strand break. points.requirement: Define EGFR-directed signalling inhibition with receptor-alteration and cellular-context dependence.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: EGFR, also called HER1 or ERBB1, is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Ligand binding outside the cell can change receptor arrangement and the activity of phosphate-transfer machinery inside. Cetuximab binds the extracellular region, whereas an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor acts at the intracellular kinase. An antibody conjugate instead adds a cargo-delivery job to target recognition. Its mechanism and evidence need separate assessment, including any antibody-mediated immune effects. A schematic contact or cargo arrow is not a molecular map of receptor processing, and delivery to a recognised target does not by itself establish dependence on the receptor kinase.

points.requirement: Define catalytic inhibition and PARP-DNA trapping as related but different actions, with obstacles that cells must tolerate or resolve.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: PARP means poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, a protein family involved in cellular signalling and repair. PARP1 is one representative. At damaged DNA it can build signals on proteins from chains of the chemical unit ADP-ribose, called poly(ADP-ribose), or PAR. Catalytic inhibition reduces this output. Some inhibitors can also stabilise DNA-associated PARP complexes, often called trapping. A repair-worker analogy separates a reduced call for help from a worker remaining in a doorway; proteins and medicines have no purpose, and the cell has more than one response route.
evidence.explanation: Catalytic output and stabilised DNA complexes are distinguished from the resulting cell-response hypotheses. Source scope: Source-backed teaching with explicitly marked reading inferences Point P-001: Catalytic output and stabilised DNA complexes are distinguished from the resulting cell-response hypotheses.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA-associated protein obstacle can challenge copying without every encounter becoming a measured collision, double-strand break or cell death. Farmer 2005 demonstrated increased sensitivity to PARP inhibition in experimental BRCA-deficient systems. Cong 2021 studied single-stranded replication gaps in cellular models: gap suppression tracked resistance or resensitisation, while restoring fork protection did not always restore resistance in the tested models. Obstacle and gap explanations can coexist, but their relative contribution in a patient's tumour is not established by these experiments. A repair-gene variant alone does not reproduce the functional losses tested in a synthetic-lethal experiment.

points.requirement: PARP1 is a representative protein, not a claim that every PARP family member is trapped identically; no figure-derived drug or patient-benefit ranking.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: PARP means poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase, a protein family involved in cellular signalling and repair. PARP1 is one representative. At damaged DNA it can build signals on proteins from chains of the chemical unit ADP-ribose, called poly(ADP-ribose), or PAR. Catalytic inhibition reduces this output. Some inhibitors can also stabilise DNA-associated PARP complexes, often called trapping. A repair-worker analogy separates a reduced call for help from a worker remaining in a doorway; proteins and medicines have no purpose, and the cell has more than one response route.

items.title: PI3K and AKT inhibitors: choose the actual signaling step

review.auditor: Coordinator full source-first reading and unit-by-unit field/source assessment; not independent expert, learner or language approval
review.rationale: All five unique bodies were read end to end before owner inspection. The original/later file pairs are byte-identical, so this assessment is reused by identity while both 55-section inventories remain separate. The frozen 123-row inventory contains 103 substantive obligations and 20 non-credit rows. Thirty-five connected notes, selected retained BRD4 passages, the explicit competitive-pocket refinement and six named source qualifications carry the definitions, model and clinical examples, measurement cards and all practice answers. Six actual registered readers and static exports verify exact passages. Sixteen complete abstracts, 40 targeted body paragraphs, official definitions/annotations and the joined Traina trial registry retain their reading depths. A listed funding erratum was read in full. No whole-paper, universal drug-response, main/live or named review credit is claimed.

points.requirement: Separate PI3K, AKT and mTOR nodes, target profiles and clinical evidence.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: PI3K, AKT and mTOR name different parts of a signalling network. In the selected membrane route, PI3K adds a phosphate to the lipid PIP2 to make PIP3; PTEN removes the relevant phosphate and opposes that lipid signal. PIP3 helps recruit proteins including AKT to the membrane. AKT, also called protein kinase B, phosphorylates proteins, and its connection to mTORC1 includes intermediate regulators. mTOR participates in the distinct mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. A diagram showing this route leaves other branches out.
evidence.explanation: PI3K, AKT and mTOR are named as different intervention nodes with distinct profiles and clinical evidence. UniProt-PIK3CA: reviewed protein annotation, complete function comment; CDK2 subunit comment also read, underlying linked papers not independently read; UniProt-PTEN: reviewed protein annotation, complete function comment; CDK2 subunit comment also read, underlying linked papers not independently read; UniProt-MTOR: reviewed protein annotation, complete function comment; CDK2 subunit comment also read, underlying linked papers not independently read; NCI-capivasertib: official technical dictionary, complete raw definition, not linked trial or drug-summary pages

points.requirement: Carry the network analogy's feedback and compensation limits rather than treating it as a straight wire of isolated boxes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: O'Reilly and colleagues found that mTOR inhibition relieved feedback inhibition and increased AKT activation in studied cancer cell lines and patient tumour samples. The indirect return path in a network sketch represents a feedback brake, not a direct physical wire or every branch. In a fictional experiment, reduced downstream output with a higher AKT phosphosite signal is compatible with network compensation. Those two measurements alone do not prove that this loop caused the change, that every tumour rebounds or that the drug missed its target; they also do not measure net survival benefit.

In the selected membrane route, PI3K adds a phosphate to the lipid PIP2 to make PIP3; PTEN removes the relevant phosphate and opposes that lipid signal. PIP3 helps recruit proteins including AKT to the membrane. AKT, also called protein kinase B, phosphorylates proteins, and its connection to mTORC1 includes intermediate regulators. mTOR participates in the distinct mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes. A diagram showing this route leaves other branches out.
evidence.explanation: PTEN phosphatase action is sourced and DNA, RNA, protein and enzyme-function measurements remain distinct. points.requirement: Verify the historical 2023 FDA capivasertib/fulvestrant population: adults with HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced disease, specified PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alterations and prior endocrine-treatment conditions, without deriving a TNBC indication.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The FDA's November 2023 capivasertib approval is a defined historical example: capivasertib with fulvestrant for adults with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer carrying a PIK3CA, AKT1 or PTEN alteration detected by an FDA-approved test. These disease, test, combination and prior-treatment conditions do not become a triple-negative breast-cancer indication from a pathway alteration alone.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: CAPItello-290 tested capivasertib plus paclitaxel against placebo plus paclitaxel as first-line treatment for metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. points.requirement: ADC toxicity follows the payload more than the antibody target; three routes: early linker release, target-independent uptake by healthy cells, target on healthy tissue (on-target off-tumour).

evidence.explanation: Payload-associated patterns and proposed exposure routes are separated from product-specific incidence, susceptibility and unsettled mechanisms.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Why ADC side effects follow the payload more than the target. Payload can reach healthy cells by early release from an unstable linker, by antigen-independent uptake (pinocytosis), or by the target sitting on healthy tissue; the Drago review concludes that off-target, off-tumour adverse events appear to dominate the toxicity profiles of most existing ADCs, while giving true on-target examples. A pooled analysis of ADC trials (Masters et al.; 43 studies with grade 3 to 4 data) found anaemia, neutropenia and peripheral neuropathy consistently reported with MMAE ADCs, thrombocytopenia and liver toxicity with DM1, and ocular toxicity with MMAF, and concluded the key toxicities are likely off-target and related to the payload. Those are patterns within published data with non-uniform reporting, and each product's own label governs its figures.

evidence.explanation: Payload-associated patterns and proposed exposure routes are separated from product-specific incidence, susceptibility and unsettled mechanisms.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: What the current labels report for the breast cancer products. Sacituzumab govitecan (SN-38 payload): neutropenia 64 per cent (grade 3 to 4, 48 per cent; febrile 6 per cent) and diarrhoea 62 per cent (grade 3 to 4, 10 per cent), with higher risk of neutropenia, febrile neutropenia and anaemia in people homozygous for UGT1A1*28. Trastuzumab deruxtecan: interstitial lung disease 12 per cent at 5.4 mg/kg, fatal 0.9 per cent. Datopotamab deruxtecan: interstitial lung disease 3.0 per cent (fatal 0.2 per cent) among 841 people with breast cancer, and 7 per cent in a pool of 484 with non-small-cell lung cancer. Trastuzumab emtansine: thrombocytopenia in 494 of 1,624 treated patients, grade 3 or higher in 145. These come from different trials and populations and cannot be compared head to head, a payload class does not make products equivalent, and a label rate is not a personal risk.

evidence.explanation: Event-specific grading, adjudicated lung disease and distinct payload/antibody measurements answer different safety questions.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: The general CTCAE descriptions run from grade 1, mild, through grade 2, moderate, grade 3, severe or medically significant, grade 4, life-threatening, and grade 5, death related to the event. Not every grade is defined for every event. Seriousness is a separate reporting concept: a grade is not an attribution to the drug or a substitute for the event's specific criteria. Immune-effector syndromes can use ASTCT scales instead, so do not apply a generic five-grade ladder to every syndrome.

evidence.explanation: Event-specific grading, adjudicated lung disease and distinct payload/antibody measurements answer different safety questions.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Label and trial figures differ by product, disease pool and definition. The trastuzumab deruxtecan label (5.4 mg/kg monotherapy pool) reports ILD in 12 per cent, fatal in 0.9 per cent, and DESTINY-Breast04 adjudicated 12.1 per cent with 0.8 per cent grade 5. The datopotamab deruxtecan label reports 3.0 per cent (0.2 per cent fatal) in 841 people with breast cancer and 7 per cent (1.7 per cent fatal) in 484 with non-small-cell lung cancer. The separate 15.4 per cent pooled-analysis figure below has another denominator and should not be compared directly. The datopotamab deruxtecan trials excluded people with a history of ILD or pneumonitis that needed steroids, so prior lung injury can bear on eligibility for later treatment.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: For an antibody-drug conjugate, specify whether an assay follows conjugated antibody, total antibody, unconjugated payload or an active breakdown product. The 2024 FDA guidance defines total antibody as antibody with or without attached payload and discusses relevant constituent parts, metabolites and catabolites. Their concentration histories can differ: persistent antibody signal does not establish active payload in every cancer cell. Living cell products can expand or persist, and a radioligand combines radioactive decay with biological removal, so a freely circulating drug's half-life gives no universal clock for them.

points.requirement: Three panels: gut-brain nerve signalling plus blood-borne and learned inputs; reporting windows 0-24 h and beyond 24 h with overlap; nausea and vomiting as separate outcomes; no vomiting does not establish no nausea.

evidence.explanation: Separate gut/brain and learned pathways support overlapping timing categories; nausea and vomiting remain distinct outcomes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Nausea and vomiting are different outcomes. Nausea is the sensation and vomiting the expulsion; they often occur together but one can occur without the other. Serotonin acting at 5-HT3 receptors and substance P acting at NK1 receptors contribute with other transmitters, and in two phase II cisplatin studies serotonin appeared to dominate early vomiting and substance P the later phase, with overlap (Hesketh et al.), so acute and delayed are reporting windows and not sealed pathways. The NCI PDQ classes are acute (the first 24 hours after chemotherapy), delayed, anticipatory, breakthrough, refractory and chronic; anticipatory nausea was reported in about 29 per cent of patients and anticipatory vomiting in 11 per cent, with prevalence varying with definitions and methods. It lists other causes too, such as fluid and electrolyte imbalance including hypercalcaemia or volume depletion, and tells clinicians to consider all potential causes when people receive several treatments, so new nausea needs a cause assessment.

evidence.explanation: Separate gut/brain and learned pathways support overlapping timing categories; nausea and vomiting remain distinct outcomes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Gut-to-brain nerve signalling, blood-borne inputs and learned associations can contribute, so one blocked route does not account for every symptom. The timing terms organise observations. Acute commonly refers to the first 24 hours, delayed to symptoms beyond 24 hours, anticipatory to symptoms before treatment associated with previous experiences, and breakthrough to symptoms despite prevention. Learned symptoms are real; delayed does not mean mild, and early and later responses can overlap with multiday treatment. Prevention and treatment of symptoms that have appeared are different questions. In a fictional trial, no vomiting and no rescue medicine can meet its complete-response endpoint while the participant still reports nausea. Relief of either symptom does not measure tumour response.

Serotonin acting at 5-HT3 receptors and substance P acting at NK1 receptors contribute with other transmitters, and in two phase II cisplatin studies serotonin appeared to dominate early vomiting and substance P the later phase, with overlap (Hesketh et al.), so acute and delayed are reporting windows and not sealed pathways. The NCI PDQ classes are acute (the first 24 hours after chemotherapy), delayed, anticipatory, breakthrough, refractory and chronic; anticipatory nausea was reported in about 29 per cent of patients and anticipatory vomiting in 11 per cent, with prevalence varying with definitions and methods. It lists other causes too, such as fluid and electrolyte imbalance including hypercalcaemia or volume depletion, and tells clinicians to consider all potential causes when people receive several treatments, so new nausea needs a cause assessment.

evidence.explanation: The named Navari regimen and endpoint definitions show why no vomiting/no rescue does not mean no nausea; patient reporting and alternative causes remain visible.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Reading antiemetic trials. In Navari et al. (380 evaluable chemotherapy-naive adults given cisplatin at 70 mg per square metre or more, or cyclophosphamide-doxorubicin, all with dexamethasone, an NK1 antagonist and a 5-HT3 antagonist), nausea prevention was the primary endpoint and complete response (no emesis and no rescue medication) a secondary one. No nausea in the first 24 hours was 74 per cent with olanzapine against 45 per cent with placebo, while complete response was 86 per cent against 65 per cent, so a complete response does not mean no nausea, and a person with no vomiting can still have persistent nausea. MASCC and ESMO updated their regimen-specific guideline in 2023 (Herrstedt et al., published 2024). Read patient-reported nausea severity, vomiting episodes, rescue-medication use and the observation window together with the preventive regimen and adherence; symptoms that limit drinking or eating warrant prompt contact with the care team. This describes how to read endpoints, not a medicine schedule.

evidence.explanation: Multicellular inflammatory signalling is interpreted through clinical attribution, competing causes, treated denominator and product-specific observation, not a cytokine curve.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Reading CRS without over-reading a cytokine level. CRS is a clinical syndrome, graded from attributed findings and not from a cytokine concentration. In a mouse model of CD19 CAR T-cell CRS, severity was mediated not by CAR T-cell-derived cytokines but by IL-6, IL-1 and nitric oxide from the recipient's macrophages, and IL-1 blockade abated it (Giavridis et al.); that supports a multicell amplification mechanism and does not show the same sources or shares in every human product. Infection and other conditions can cause or accompany the same findings, so the cause of a fever cannot be read from timing alone. A comparable report gives its grading version, observation window and treated denominator, with onset, maximum grade, interventions and resolution. Safety belongs to the product, disease, tumour burden and preparation, so experience with one blood-cancer product does not supply a solid-tumour product's rate, and no severe CRS in a small early study does not rule out uncommon events. CRS is a different problem from injury to healthy tissue that carries the target (on-target, off-tumour) and from neurotoxicity (ICANS). The treatment need not carry a cytokine payload to trigger endogenous inflammatory signalling. Tumour response does not establish acceptable inflammatory risk, and mild CRS does not establish lack of anticancer activity. Stopping a treatment input does not guarantee immediate removal of released signals or established injury. In a fictional early study, no severe CRS and a modest cytokine rise would not make every fever harmless CRS: attribution, clinical findings, a named grading framework, treated denominator and observation window are still needed.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: How CRS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. The definition requires a fever of 38 degrees Celsius or higher that cannot be attributed to another cause. Severity is then the more severe of two findings, again not attributable to another cause. Grade 1 has neither. Grade 2 is low blood pressure that does not need vasopressors and/or oxygen by low-flow nasal cannula (up to 6 litres a minute) or blow-by. Grade 3 is one vasopressor, with or without vasopressin, and/or high-flow cannula, face mask, non-rebreather mask or Venturi mask. Grade 4 is multiple vasopressors, excluding vasopressin, and/or positive pressure such as CPAP, BiPAP or intubation. Once someone has had a fever-lowering or anti-cytokine treatment such as tocilizumab or steroids, fever is no longer needed to grade later severity: the grade then follows blood pressure and oxygen, and the person still counts as having CRS until the signs resolve. Organ toxicities linked to CRS are graded separately and do not change the CRS grade, and neurotoxicity during or after CRS is scored on the neurotoxicity scale, not added here. The 2026 ASTCT update (Perales et al.) convened experts to consider updating CRS, ICANS and haemophagocytic-lymphohistiocytosis-like grading, but only its abstract could be read, so whether it keeps, changes or relaxes any of these 2019 rules is not stated here; a report should say which version graded it.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, or ICANS, is a neurologic syndrome associated with immune-effector-cell therapy. Changes in language, attention, handwriting or awareness and more severe findings such as seizures need assessment against baseline and alternative explanations. An immune-marker plot does not establish the syndrome.

evidence.explanation: Neurologic findings and their timing are assessed separately from CRS, with vascular associations scoped to the Gust cohort and competing causes retained.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: What is known about mechanism, timing and attribution. In 133 adults given CD19 CAR T cells, Gust et al. found that those with severe neurotoxicity had endothelial activation (disseminated intravascular coagulation, capillary leak) and increased blood-brain barrier permeability, and that the permeable barrier failed to protect the cerebrospinal fluid from high systemic cytokine concentrations including interferon-gamma. Higher risk went with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, high marrow CD19-positive burden, high CAR T-cell dose, CRS and pre-existing neurological disease, and markers of endothelial activation before lymphodepletion were higher in people who later had grade 4 or worse neurotoxicity. That is an association in one product class and population, not a complete mechanism for every treatment. ICANS can accompany CRS or follow its own timetable, and neurotoxicity after CRS is scored separately, so recovery of blood pressure and oxygen does not show neurological recovery. If a person is confused while taking a sedating medicine and the ICE score falls, the grading rule requires that sedation be excluded, so the fall calls for clinical assessment, neither ignored nor diagnosed from the score alone. Clinical assessment also considers infection, metabolic disturbances, medicines and pre-existing neurologic disease. A safety report should retain onset, severity, attributed cause, interventions, duration, recovery and how many people were adequately observed. Separate fictional CRS and neurologic timelines can end at different times; they do not specify a typical order or duration. Stopping an engineered input does not guarantee immediate reversal of established neurologic injury.

points.requirement: ICE tasks: orientation, naming, commands, writing, attention; not whole neuro exam or stand-alone diagnosis; ASTCT 2026 separates monitoring tool from diagnosing ICANS; baseline matters; grading also considers consciousness, seizures, motor findings, brain swelling. Unresolved against primary text: ICE item scoring, grade thresholds, ASTCT 2019 vs 2026 grade criteria and the 2026 definition of other neurologic syndromes.
remaining: Detailed ASTCT 2026 full text is access-blocked; 2019 criteria are explicitly attributed and supported.

evidence.explanation: The adult 2019 ICE bands and other domains are explicit; a 2026 revision of detailed criteria or diagnostic use of ICE remains unverified.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: How ICANS is graded, from the ASTCT 2019 consensus. For adults, the grade is the most severe of five findings, none attributable to another cause. The 10-point ICE screen of orientation, naming, command-following, writing and attention scores 7 to 9 for grade 1, 3 to 6 for grade 2, 0 to 2 for grade 3, and 0 because the person is unarousable and cannot be tested for grade 4; an ICE of 0 in someone who is awake with global aphasia can still be grade 3. Level of consciousness counts only if no other cause such as a sedating medicine explains it: awakens spontaneously, awakens to voice, only to touch, or unarousable or requiring vigorous or repeated tactile stimulation. Any seizure that resolves rapidly, or EEG-only seizures that resolve with treatment, is grade 3, and prolonged (over 5 minutes) or repeated seizures without return to baseline are grade 4. Deep focal motor weakness is grade 4, while tremor and myoclonus may be graded on CTCAE but do not change the ICANS grade. Focal oedema on imaging is grade 3; diffuse oedema, posturing, cranial nerve VI palsy, papilloedema or Cushing's triad is grade 4; intracranial haemorrhage is excluded from ICANS grading. So ICE is a screen for encephalopathy and one input, not the whole examination: a person with an ICE of 3 who has a generalised seizure is grade 3, and headache alone is not a useful marker. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract adds categories such as non-ICANS neurological toxicities (parkinsonism, cranial nerve palsies, polyneuropathies) and tumour inflammation-associated neurotoxicity; their criteria, and any change to how ICE is used, were not readable here.

points.requirement: irAE = harm to healthy tissue attributed to treatment-related immune activity; the label names suspected mechanism, not organ, severity or treatment.

evidence.explanation: Immune attribution is separated from occurrence, organ inflammation, severity, general checkpoint restraint and neighbouring effector-cell syndromes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immune-related adverse events are injuries attributed to treatment-related immune activity, commonly discussed with checkpoint inhibitors. They can affect the bowel, lung, skin, liver, hormone-producing glands and other organs. A symptom or laboratory change during treatment does not by itself establish an immune cause.

evidence.explanation: Immune attribution is separated from occurrence, organ inflammation, severity, general checkpoint restraint and neighbouring effector-cell syndromes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: What the label does and does not say. An adverse event is any unfavourable and unintended sign, symptom or abnormal laboratory finding that occurs during treatment, whether or not the treatment caused it; grading records that it occurred and how severe it was, and the clinical team assigns attribution to the drug, the intervention or something else (NCI Cancer Therapy Evaluation Program). An irAE is the narrower attribution of harm to treatment-related immune activity, so a symptom during immunotherapy is not automatically an irAE, and the abbreviation names a suspected mechanism, not an organ, a severity or a treatment. The SITC 2021 guideline uses the same wording, grades events including irAEs on a scale such as CTCAE version 5, and says that some irAEs need organ-specific management while overarching principles apply to all checkpoint-inhibitor toxicity. Checkpoint regulation helps limit responses against healthy tissue, part of peripheral tolerance; disrupting that protection can contribute to immune injury, but no single mechanism explains every event. Colitis names bowel inflammation and pneumonitis lung inflammation. A symptom or the suffix "-itis" does not establish its cause.

evidence.explanation: Immune attribution is separated from occurrence, organ inflammation, severity, general checkpoint restraint and neighbouring effector-cell syndromes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Timing and neighbouring syndromes. Immune-mediated reactions to PD-1 or PD-L1 antibodies can occur in any organ system at any time after starting and can also appear after treatment stops (pembrolizumab prescribing information), so the infusion calendar does not define the observation window; onset differs by organ, with a SITC median of 5 to 10 weeks for diarrhoea or colitis and rash typically presenting 2 to 5 weeks after the first treatment. Cytokine release syndrome and ICANS after immune effector cell therapy are separate syndromes with their own ASTCT definitions and grading, not substitute labels for checkpoint-related organ injury, and stopping a treatment does not guarantee the immune effect has stopped.

points.requirement: Patient task: use care-team reporting plan; tell clinicians about current and previous immunotherapy; new/worsening breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion warrants urgent assessment; do not wait for next infusion or self-start immunosuppressants.

evidence.explanation: A new cough after treatment needs assessment rather than automatic dismissal or diagnosis; symptoms and a suspected irAE do not establish efficacy.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Report symptoms using the care team's plan and tell evaluating clinicians about current and previous immunotherapy. points.requirement: Insertional mutagenesis = integration that disrupts a gene or its regulation with consequence; integration is the event; most insertions do not cause cancer; clonal expansion != malignancy (useful responses expand clones).

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Three primary reports show why the setting matters. After retrovirus-mediated gamma-c gene transfer into autologous CD34-positive bone marrow cells for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, 9 of 10 patients were corrected, but almost three years later the two youngest developed uncontrolled clonal proliferation of mature T cells; both clones carried vector integration near the LMO2 proto-oncogene promoter with abnormal LMO2 expression, which the authors attributed most likely to retrovirus enhancer activity (Hacein-Bey-Abina et al., 2003). In a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia given CD19 CAR T cells, 94 per cent of CAR T cells at the peak of response came from one clone in which lentiviral insertion had disrupted TET2, the patient's second TET2 allele carried a hypomorphic mutation, and the clone showed a central memory phenotype alongside complete remission: an expanded clone linked to benefit, not a new cancer (Fraietta et al., 2018). In 724 patients treated with T-cell therapies at one centre, a lethal T-cell lymphoma followed axicabtagene ciloleucel for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; the tumour, the CAR T cells and the patient's normal blood cells were profiled in depth, both lymphomas were Epstein-Barr virus positive and linked to DNMT3A and TET2 mutant clonal haematopoiesis, and no evidence of oncogenic retroviral integration was found with multiple techniques (Hamilton et al., 2024). The first is a specific stem-cell regimen and the others are single-centre or single-patient observations, so none is an incidence estimate for a vector or product.

points.requirement: Lymphodepletion reduces existing lymphocytes (T, B, NK) before some cell therapies; chemo agents/intensity/timing protocol-set; not one regimen.

evidence.explanation: Preparation changes immune competition and regulation, with mouse cytokine-sink evidence and melanoma regimen outcomes separated from transferable product claims.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Why preparing the body can help transferred cells, and what it costs. In mouse adoptive-transfer experiments, a nonmyeloablative regimen enhanced antitumour effect even without regulatory T cells, through greater function of tumour-reactive CD8-positive T cells rather than greater numbers; interleukin-7 and interleukin-15 were required, and removing endogenous cells that respond to those cytokines reproduced the effect, which points to lymphodepletion removing cells that act as cytokine sinks (Gattinoni et al.). That is a mouse mechanism and it does not describe an empty physical space. When a trial tests conditioning, transferred cells and cytokine support together, the outcomes belong to the whole package: in the phase 3 tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte trial in advanced melanoma (Rohaan et al.; 168 patients, 86 per cent with disease refractory to anti-PD-1 treatment), cells were infused after nonmyeloablative cyclophosphamide plus fludarabine and followed by high-dose interleukin-2, and grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in all patients given TILs, mainly chemotherapy-related myelosuppression. Nonmyeloablative therefore does not mean harmless.

evidence.explanation: Preparation changes immune competition and regulation, with mouse cytokine-sink evidence and melanoma regimen outcomes separated from transferable product claims.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Lymphocytes include T cells, B cells and natural killer cells. Preparation can affect competition, regulation and, for donor products, host rejection; it can also act on cancer directly. It does not create a missing tumour antigen or guarantee that transferred cells enter a solid tumour. The need for preparation and its recovery criteria belong to the named protocol, rather than to every cell therapy. Serial blood counts consume blood samples rather than tumour tissue. Report absolute lymphocytes and neutrophils with units, sampling time and reference ranges, and measure transferred-cell number, location and function separately from the counts. More depletion is not automatically more benefit. Nonmyeloablative describes a regimen not intended to eliminate marrow blood production completely, rather than a promise of mild count suppression. Report severity, duration, recovery, infections, organ harms and relevant support with the regimen. More transferred cells, more depletion and more tumour killing are separate propositions.

points.requirement: On-target off-tumour = recognition of the intended target on healthy tissue; distinct from off-target cross-reactivity (unintended molecule) and from CRS; categories can co-occur.

evidence.explanation: Intended-target recognition in healthy tissue differs from unintended peptide recognition, CRS and binding specificity; the two cases and complementary tests retain their limits.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: On-target, off-tumour toxicity is injury from recognition of the intended target on healthy tissue. It differs from recognition of an unintended molecular target. The predictable, lymphoma-specific consequences of aiming at lineage antigens (B-cell aplasia, low immunoglobulin, and the effects of CD52, CCR4 and CD47 targeting) are described in the record on the cost of aiming at a lineage antigen, which this record does not repeat.

evidence.explanation: Intended-target recognition in healthy tissue differs from unintended peptide recognition, CRS and binding specificity; the two cases and complementary tests retain their limits.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Many candidate cancer targets are normal proteins found at different levels or places in the body, so tumour-associated does not mean tumour-exclusive. A treatment that recognises its intended target wherever it is accessible, such as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell, can harm any healthy tissue that displays it, and tissue location, target density, receptor properties and exposure all shape the outcome. This differs from off-target cross-reactivity, in which the receptor recognises an unintended molecule, and from cytokine release syndrome, which is systemic inflammatory activation; the three can occur together. It also differs from payload toxicity in an antibody-drug conjugate: a pooled analysis of ADC trials found the key grade 3 to 4 toxicities grouped by payload and concluded they were likely off-target and related to the payload (Masters et al., 2018). Binding specificity is not tissue selectivity, and experience with an antibody against a target does not automatically carry over to a living cell with a different recognition and signalling system.

evidence.explanation: Intended-target recognition in healthy tissue differs from unintended peptide recognition, CRS and binding specificity; the two cases and complementary tests retain their limits.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Two primary reports show the contrast. A patient with colon cancer metastatic to the lungs and liver received 10 billion autologous T cells expressing a trastuzumab-based CAR against ERBB2 (HER2), the largest number permitted in the first dose-escalation cohort, the day after a lymphodepleting regimen of cyclophosphamide (60 mg/kg daily for 2 days) and fludarabine (25 mg/m2 for 5 days). Within 15 minutes the patient had respiratory distress, chest imaging showed pulmonary oedema, and the patient died 5 days after treatment, with marked rises in interferon-gamma, GM-CSF, tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10. At autopsy multiple organs showed systemic ischaemia and haemorrhagic microangiopathic injury and the lungs diffuse alveolar damage; histological examination of autopsy tissue found ERBB2 at 3+ in liver metastases and 2+ in lung metastases and much lower levels in normal lung parenchyma, normal liver and normal breast. evidence.supportingExcerpt: How the question is asked before and during trials. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance says to assess both undesired targeting of healthy tissue that expresses the intended antigen (on-target/off-tumour) and unintended targeting of other antigens, using examples such as tissue cross-reactivity studies with an antibody carrying the same recognition domain, protein arrays, cytotoxicity and cytokine-release testing on panels of primary cells, cell lines or stem-cell-derived organ systems, and relevant animal models, and encourages a combination of methods; antigen recognition domains can differ in affinity or avidity or recognise a different site, which should be evaluated, and CAR T cells can carry added components such as suicide genes. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract lists on-target, off-tumour toxicity among the toxicities for which it considered definitions and grading; its criteria were not readable.

points.requirement: GnRH agonist during chemotherapy quiets ovaries and lowers chance of chemotherapy-induced early menopause; mechanism of protection not settled; quiet != eggs preserved for pregnancy.

evidence.explanation: Physiologic pulses, product-specific transient rise and chronic suppression are separated from chemotherapy injury, endocrine treatment and future fertility.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Temporary ovarian suppression during chemotherapy aims to reduce chemotherapy-induced ovarian insufficiency. It is a different use from ovarian suppression as endocrine treatment of hormone-receptor-positive cancer. Pulsatile hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone normally signals to the pituitary to release follicle-stimulating and luteinising hormones. The goserelin label describes a transient initial rise in oestrogen in women with breast cancer, followed by pituitary down-regulation with continued agonist exposure and suppression of ovarian hormone production. The 3.6 mg formulation uses a 28-day schedule in its label; this is a product description, not a schedule for every agonist or indication. It usually stops ovulation and menstruation during use, but does not ensure contraception. Hormone levels generally return after stopping, while chemotherapy-related ovarian injury can still prevent recovery. The classical Belchetz experiments compared continuous and intermittent GnRH delivery in rhesus monkeys; they established a pattern-dependent pituitary response rather than a breast-cancer treatment effect. The mechanism of ovarian protection during chemotherapy remains unsettled, so quieter ovaries do not guarantee preserved eggs or future pregnancy.

points.requirement: Chemotherapy depletes immature egg pool; highest risk with alkylators (cyclophosphamide), rises with age; premature ovarian insufficiency (amenorrhoea, FSH postmenopausal range, early fertility end).

evidence.explanation: Follicular injury, treatment and age dependence are retained while permanent sterility is not inferred from POI or amenorrhoea alone.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Chemotherapy can damage ovarian follicles containing immature eggs. NCI identifies alkylating agents as a high-risk group and describes risk as depending on age, baseline fertility, treatment type, dose and duration. Primary ovarian insufficiency can include intermittent ovulation or occasional periods; it should not be equated automatically with permanent sterility. Arecco and colleagues' 2021 review describes reduced recruitment of follicles and reduced ovarian perfusion as proposed explanations for protection by GnRH agonists, while noting that the mechanism is not fully clear. The clinical comparisons do not establish which mechanism caused the observed difference.

points.requirement: PROMISE-GIM6 started agonist >= 1 week before first dose through end of chemo; proposed mechanisms (fewer follicles recruited, ovarian blood flow); clinical effect better established than mechanism.

evidence.explanation: The PROMISE timing is trial-specific; reduced recruitment and perfusion are attributed review hypotheses rather than demonstrated causes of benefit.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: PROMISE-GIM6 randomised 281 premenopausal women with stage I to III breast cancer. Triptorelin began at least one week before chemotherapy and was given every four weeks for its duration in that trial. Early menopause, defined by absent menstrual recovery and postmenopausal FSH and oestradiol one year after chemotherapy, occurred in 8.9% versus 25.9%, odds ratio 0.28 (95% confidence interval 0.14 to 0.59). Lambertini and colleagues' individual-patient meta-analysis included 873 participants from five trials: premature ovarian insufficiency was 14.1% versus 30.9%, adjusted odds ratio 0.38 (95% confidence interval 0.26 to 0.57); at least one later pregnancy was reported by 10.3% versus 5.5%. The adjusted disease-free-survival hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% confidence interval 0.72 to 1.42). Those pooled results are not specific to triple-negative disease and do not prove absence of harm.

points.requirement: Pneumonitis = lung inflammation, cause and severity need assessment; multiple causes (radiation, drugs, inhaled substances, infection); in cancer reports often noninfectious injury, check definition.

evidence.explanation: Lung inflammation needs cause, timing, competing explanations and severity assessment; Naidoo is a scoped cohort, and improvement alone does not prove cause or safe restart.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: In cancer-treatment reporting, pneumonitis often refers to non-infectious inflammation of lung tissue; the report's diagnostic definition matters. In cancer care it can occur with immune checkpoint inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates or chest radiotherapy. New or worsening respiratory symptoms require prompt assessment. The medicine, severity and suspected cause matter when interpreting a scan and deciding how treatment is modified.

evidence.explanation: Lung inflammation needs cause, timing, competing explanations and severity assessment; Naidoo is a scoped cohort, and improvement alone does not prove cause or safe restart.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: In the two-institution cohort reported by Naidoo and colleagues in 2017, investigators diagnosed pneumonitis in 43 of 915 recipients of anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 antibodies, about 5% (95% confidence interval 3% to 6%). It occurred in 24 of 716 receiving one antibody (about 3%) and 19 of 199 receiving an anti-CTLA-4 combination (about 10%). Cases with confirmed infection or malignant lung infiltration were excluded. These are cohort-specific observational estimates, not a randomised comparison or universal class rates. One institution included advanced solid cancers and the other melanoma only, which further limits transfer to other populations.

evidence.explanation: Lung inflammation needs cause, timing, competing explanations and severity assessment; Naidoo is a scoped cohort, and improvement alone does not prove cause or safe restart.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: An abnormal CT pattern is evidence of a lung problem, not a unique fingerprint of its cause. CT uses X-rays to form cross-sectional images. Infection, malignant lung involvement, fluid and other treatment effects enter the differential assessment and can coexist. Symptoms, oxygen needs, imaging and lung function may improve on different timetables. Conte and colleagues' 2022 multidisciplinary expert opinion includes spirometry and carbon-monoxide diffusing capacity alongside imaging and tests for infection; those tests measure functional impact rather than identifying the cause alone.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Timing and neighbouring syndromes. Immune-mediated reactions to PD-1 or PD-L1 antibodies can occur in any organ system at any time after starting and can also appear after treatment stops (pembrolizumab prescribing information), so the infusion calendar does not define the observation window; onset differs by organ, with a SITC median of 5 to 10 weeks for diarrhoea or colitis and rash typically presenting 2 to 5 weeks after the first treatment. Cytokine release syndrome and ICANS after immune effector cell therapy are separate syndromes with their own ASTCT definitions and grading, not substitute labels for checkpoint-related organ injury, and stopping a treatment does not guarantee the immune effect has stopped.

points.requirement: DESTINY-Breast04 (previously treated HER2-low): independent committee attributed ILD/pneumonitis to T-DXd in 12.1%, fatal 0.8%; T-DXd label boxed warning with grade-based interruption/discontinuation; Dato-DXd label 841 breast pts ILD 3.0% fatal 0.2%; mechanism unsettled; rates differ by product.

evidence.explanation: Product-specific populations and label interruption rules are preserved; a generic severity ladder cannot replace them.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: There is no single grade-based interruption rule for all of these treatments. The October 2026 US pembrolizumab label withholds treatment for grade 2 pneumonitis and permanently discontinues it for grade 3 or 4. The May 2026 trastuzumab deruxtecan label specifies permanent discontinuation for symptomatic grade 2 or higher interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis. The May 2026 datopotamab deruxtecan label requires withholding while suspected disease is investigated and permanent discontinuation for confirmed grade 2 or higher disease. The trastuzumab deruxtecan label separately addresses suspected radiotherapy-only pneumonitis in the adjuvant setting. Those distinctions, including the footnotes and conditions for resumption, belong with the named product.

evidence.explanation: Product-specific populations and label interruption rules are preserved; a generic severity ladder cannot replace them.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: The May 2026 US trastuzumab deruxtecan label, Table 3, interrupts treatment for asymptomatic grade 1 interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis until resolution to grade 0. It retains the dose if resolution occurs within 28 days of onset and reduces it one level if longer. Symptomatic grade 2 or higher calls for permanent discontinuation. For asymptomatic grade 1, the table also says to consider corticosteroids as soon as interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis is suspected. review.auditor: GPT-6.1 Sol coordinator; semantic and source assessment at stated primary/inference scope, not blind, expert, learner or language acceptance
review.rationale: Full later lessons and complete original teaching differences assessed. The earlier 197 parent rows are retained: 176 teaching obligations, 19 bibliographic rows and 2 personal-case pointers excluded; 11 subclauses refine parents without extra points. Exact reader paragraphs carry definitions, controls, measurement limits and fictional examples. Two detailed ASTCT 2026 clauses remain source-open. No point is earned from citation presence, a source hash or an unapplied proposal.

points.requirement: PFT measures airflow, lung volume and gas transfer (spirometry, lung volumes, DLCO); low DLCO is a pattern, not a cause.

evidence.explanation: Airflow, total volume and gas transfer have distinct manoeuvres, units and interpretation; low FVC alone does not establish restriction.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: A full set has three parts. Spirometry has the person breathe in fully and blow out as hard and as long as possible, measuring the forced vital capacity (FVC) and how fast air leaves; the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and its ratio to FVC are the usual numbers. The ATS/ERS 2019 spirometry standard describes the test as the maximal volume of air a person can inspire and expire with maximal effort, reports FEV1/FVC as a decimal fraction, and sets acceptability and repeatability criteria for each manoeuvre, so a poor-effort test is a quality problem before it is a finding. Spirometry is used to look for obstructive conditions, in which the airways narrow so air flows out with difficulty, as in asthma, bronchitis and emphysema (MedlinePlus). A lung volume test, often done by body plethysmography in a sealed booth, measures the total lung capacity (TLC), the amount of air the lungs can hold; restrictive conditions, in which the lungs cannot fill fully, such as pulmonary fibrosis and interstitial lung disease, lower it. The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) has the person breathe in a gas mixture with a trace of carbon monoxide and a tracer gas, hold the breath for about 10 seconds and breathe out; it shows how well gas crosses into the blood. The ERS/ATS 2022 interpretation standard explains that a low DLCO with normal alveolar volume can be consistent with pulmonary vascular impairment, emphysema with preserved volume or anaemia. Low alveolar volume with low or normal transfer coefficient can accompany interstitial lung disease or emphysema with loss of lung volume. These are patterns to interpret, not diagnoses from one value. The 2017 ERS/ATS standard asks for no smoking or other carbon-monoxide exposure on the day of the test, recording the last cigarette and accounting for recent or heavy exposure. Its preparation instructions are technical test conditions, not an individual treatment plan.

evidence.explanation: Airflow, total volume and gas transfer have distinct manoeuvres, units and interpretation; low FVC alone does not establish restriction.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Spirometry measures forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC) and their ratio. A ratio below its appropriate lower limit supports an obstructive pattern. Restriction is defined by low total lung capacity (TLC); reduced FVC alone does not establish it. A single-breath DLCO test estimates carbon-monoxide uptake after inhaling test gas with a tracer, holding the breath for about ten seconds and exhaling. Conventional units include mL per minute per mmHg. Poor effort, technique and repeatability are quality issues to assess before interpreting an apparent impairment.

points.requirement: Results are compared with suitable reference values; LLN and uncertainty differ from fixed percent-predicted rules, haemoglobin affects DLCO interpretation, and preparation and serial variability need stated conditions.

evidence.explanation: LLN, reference variability, haemoglobin-aware interpretation and day-of-test smoking conditions are supported; no universal adult DLCO change threshold or unwritten adjustment equation is supplied.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: How a result is judged. A value is compared with a healthy reference population for the person's age, sex and height. The ERS/ATS 2022 technical standard defines the lower limit of normal as the 5th percentile, a z-score of minus 1.645, so 5 per cent of a healthy reference population lie below that limit by definition. It strongly discourages the fixed cut-offs of 80 per cent of predicted for FEV1 and 0.70 for the FEV1/FVC ratio, because percent of predicted ignores how measurement variability changes with age, and it adds the qualifier that neither simple cut-offs nor the 5th percentile should be used as absolute diagnostic criteria, since healthy and diseased values overlap in a zone of uncertainty. Ideally the comparison is with the person's own earlier baseline. Serial results need their test quality, measurement variability and clinical context. A threshold developed for another test or population should not be turned into a universal DLCO monitoring rule. For DLCO the standard says the importance of haemoglobin cannot be overemphasised and all interpretations must have the reference values adjusted for haemoglobin, with particular care when people are monitored for drug toxicity and haemoglobin shifts, as in chemotherapy. A 2024 transplant cohort report likewise states that DLCO is affected by haemoglobin and that two adjustment equations (Cotes, recommended by ATS/ERS, and Dinakara) gave different results, so the method should be named.
