This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Lymph drains fluid from tissues back to the blood, passing through nodes where T and B cells inspect it for infection; cancer cells that enter lymph vessels lodge in the nearest nodes first, so node involvement (the N in TNM) is a central marker of a cancer's tendency to spread and raises the stage. Sentinel-node biopsy identifies and removes only the first node or two that drain a tumour, sparing patients the arm swelling (lymphoedema) that removing all nodes causes. Lymph nodes are also where immune responses against a tumour are launched, and where immunotherapy needs functioning T cells to be primed. Afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and efferent vessels carry it out, and a draining node names a route and not a finding of cancer. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). A node has a cortex, a paracortex and a medulla, and B cells and T cells home to separate areas within them (Willard-Mack, 2006); in the mouse, a venous population in the medulla was predicted to recruit myeloid cells rather than lymphocytes, which videomicroscopy confirmed (Brulois et al., 2020). In gene-targeted mice, loss of the chemokine receptor CCR7 altered the organisation of lymphoid organs and stopped skin dendritic cells reaching draining nodes (Förster et al., 1999). Arrival of material in a node does not show that priming succeeded. Pathological involvement means cancer was identified in examined tissue, which differs from a drainage route, enlargement or an imaging observation, and a negative sampled node does not certify the unsampled nodes (the National Cancer Institute notes that a false-negative biopsy gives a false sense of security about the extent of cancer).

points.requirement: The best-established outcome link is simpler than TLS: in early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), a higher stromal lymphocyte (sTIL) score goes with better survival after chemotherapy. In 2,148 patients, each 10% increase was associated with an overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 ([Loi et al., 2019](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30650045/)). That is **prognostic**. It does not show who gains more from a checkpoint inhibitor. The [TIL concept](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/tumor-infiltrating-lymphocytes#why-it-matters-in-cancer) gives the populations, and [prognostic vs predictive](/wiki/education/concepts/evidence-and-statistics/biomarkers/prognostic-vs-predictive) explains the difference.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In the pooled analysis of 2,148 early-stage TNBC patients given anthracycline-based chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in pretreatment stromal TILs corresponded to an adjusted invasive disease-free survival hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.91) and overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89). These associations do not establish an added pembrolizumab benefit by TIL level.

points.requirement: **To understand a T-cell response, ask which cells are present, what they recognize and what they can do. A count answers only the first question.**

points.requirement: A **naive** T cell has not undergone its initial antigen-driven activation. An **effector** cell has acquired response functions. **Memory** describes persistence and potential for a renewed response. These are starting categories rather than promises about one cell’s future.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Naive describes absence of initial antigen-driven activation, not recent thymic birth. Effector denotes developed response functions, including help or killing; memory can support renewed responses but promises neither permanent protection nor cancer specificity. State categories are not one mandatory developmental trajectory. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression and regulatory role remain distinct.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Priming is a naive cell's initial activation in a supporting context. Signal one is TCR recognition of peptide-HLA, signal two includes CD80/CD86-CD28 costimulation and inhibitory context, and signal three includes differentiation-supporting cytokines. The receptor pre-exists the encounter. These signals interact over time; the model is not a three-button checklist and antigen-experienced or engineered cells can have different requirements.

points.requirement: Quiet cells need an explanation before an intervention. In a fictional test, a viable population responds poorly to one peptide. The matching receptor may be absent; the stimulus may be unsuitable; or a responsive population may be restrained. A weak test result alone cannot choose among these explanations. An anergy experiment needs a defined response history and a controlled later response test.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Anergy is antigen-related reduced responsiveness that persists into a later controlled response test. In Jenkins and Schwartz's mouse and T-cell-clone experiments, chemically altered presenting cells induced reduced responsiveness to subsequent antigen stimulation with normal presenting cells. Macian and colleagues identified an NFAT-associated anergy gene programme in mechanistic experiments. These findings are model evidence, not a universal tumour-cell classifier.

Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression, absent antigen-specific cells and assay failure are different possible explanations for a low response. Low interleukin-2 alone leaves the mechanism unresolved. Check specificity, viable-cell recovery, stimulus controls, responsive comparators and response history; measure division and cytokine responses under matched conditions. Laboratory rescue does not establish tumour recognition, safe killing or clinical benefit.
evidence.explanation: Anergy requires response history and a controlled later challenge. Absent specificity, unsuitable stimulus, suppression and exhaustion are different explanations for a weak response; they are not interchangeable stages. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Anergy is persistent reduced antigen-driven responsiveness after a defined antigen encounter, assessed with a suitable later challenge. It is not simply resting, a naive identity, missing support at one encounter or failure to divide now. Altered-presenting-cell induction followed by normal-presenting-cell retesting in mouse clones supports this distinction.

Report dividing-cell fractions or cytokine concentration with assay units and conditions. Missing recognition, damaged preparations, suppression or exhaustion remain alternatives.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation, altered function, multiple inhibitory receptors and transcriptional and chromatin changes. Mouse TOX experiments identified a central regulator of this programme. It is neither brief tiredness, every weak assay, anergy nor a DNA sequence change. Deficits can be graded and subsets retain different capacities.

points.requirement: Not dividing is a separate observation from weak antigen responsiveness. [Cell-cycle state](/wiki/education/concepts/biology-basics/cells/cell-cycle), [senescence](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/cell-death-and-survival/senescence) and exhaustion answer different biological questions. An alive, non-dividing cell is not automatically senescent or exhausted. Assign the state using appropriate evidence rather than treating these labels as synonyms for an inactive cell.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: G1 prepares the cell, S copies DNA, and G2 precedes the mitotic phase. Mitosis separates nuclear chromosomes; cytokinesis separates cytoplasm into daughter cells. G0 describes a noncycling state, which need not mean death or loss of function. Cyclins, CDKs and checkpoints regulate transitions, and their alteration can contribute to cancer without making every checkpoint absent or guaranteeing error-free division. Cell-cycle checkpoints and immune checkpoints describe different biological processes.
evidence.explanation: Alive/nondividing, senescence, quiescence/cycle state and exhaustion retain their distinct evidence requirements; one weak division result assigns none of them. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Senescence is a stress-associated cell state with durable cell-cycle arrest and other context-dependent features. Identifying it requires combined measurements rather than one marker. In genetically switchable blood-cancer models, release from senescence allowed renewed division with enhanced clonogenic potential. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human studies support continued thymic output into adulthood, with age-related decline rather than a fixed birthday shutdown. Existing naive cells can also survive and divide outside the thymus. Human and mouse kinetic studies found different contributions of thymic output and peripheral division; mouse dependence on new output cannot be transferred directly to adult humans.

T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) are rearrangement by-products that do not replicate with chromosomes. Peripheral division can dilute measured TREC content. In a fictional closed ledger, 2 cells carrying 4 total circles divide into 4 cells retaining 4 circles: average copies per cell fall from 2 to 1. Allocation can be uneven. This isolates division and does not count new arrivals or daily thymic export. Copies per cell and copies per blood volume have different denominators. Interpret output with survival, division, movement, compartment and timing; naive phenotype, thymic imaging or TREC content alone cannot provide a complete immune-age or cancer-benefit forecast.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Beta match, alpha hidden, fictional: three cells carry beta chains B, B and C, so a bulk beta-chain view lists B, B, C and loses the alpha chains. The paired view keeps alpha X with beta B, alpha Y with beta B and alpha Z with beta C, so the shared beta B does not make alpha X and alpha Y equal. Single-cell methods that sequence the alpha and beta genes of individual T cells retain each pair and can be combined with function-related gene expression, and the same TCR sequence can sit in functionally different cells (Han 2014). A bulk method profiles a mixed sample, often one chain, whereas TIRTL-seq generates paired alpha and beta repertoire data at cohort scale and is distinguished from bulk single-chain data and from single-cell throughput limits (Pogorelyy 2026). Paired identity plus an expression program is more context and is still not evidence of the receptor's antigen.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Beta match, alpha hidden, fictional: three cells carry beta chains B, B and C, so a bulk beta-chain view lists B, B, C and loses the alpha chains. The paired view keeps alpha X with beta B, alpha Y with beta B and alpha Z with beta C, so the shared beta B does not make alpha X and alpha Y equal. Single-cell methods that sequence the alpha and beta genes of individual T cells retain each pair and can be combined with function-related gene expression, and the same TCR sequence can sit in functionally different cells (Han 2014). A bulk method profiles a mixed sample, often one chain, whereas TIRTL-seq generates paired alpha and beta repertoire data at cohort scale and is distinguished from bulk single-chain data and from single-cell throughput limits (Pogorelyy 2026). Paired identity plus an expression program is more context and is still not evidence of the receptor's antigen.

points.requirement: [Human leukocyte antigen (HLA)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/antigen-presentation/hla) holds displayed fragments. A [peptide–HLA multimer assay](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/immune-monitoring/peptide-hla-multimer-staining) tests binding to a defined display complex. An [enzyme-linked immunospot (ELISpot) assay](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/immune-monitoring/elispot) measures a secreted response under defined stimulation. Neither alone proves killing of naturally presenting cancer cells.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Method card, what it measures: binding of cells to a specified peptide held by a specified HLA allele, under the staining conditions. How: HLA molecules are assembled with the selected peptide and several copies are attached to a labelled scaffold (a tetramer is one format), cells are exposed and analysed, usually by flow cytometry, with viable-cell and gate selection. Input: blood or tissue cells, where staining uses a defined aliquot and compatibility with later living-cell assays depends on the preparation, and the reagent must match both peptide and allele. Thresholds: gate and positivity rules need background and reagent controls, and no universal percentage shows efficacy. Failure modes: nonspecific binding, weak binding, dead cells, a wrong or poorly formed reagent, chain differences or sampling loss. It cannot tell cytokine response, tumour-cell killing, healthy-tissue specificity or benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Method card, what it measures: cells that secrete a chosen molecule, most often interferon gamma, under defined stimulation, counted as spots on an antibody-coated membrane. How: capture antibodies hold the released molecule near the cell, the cells are removed and detection reagents make localised spots visible. Input: viable cells, often PBMCs, allocated to the test. Prior culture expansion changes the measured population, and the cells are removed before the membrane spots are read. Output: spot-forming units per stated number of input cells, with background handling stated. Thresholds: response and quality rules fixed in advance for that assay and study, so one paper's positivity rule is not imported into another laboratory's report. Failure modes: high background, dead cells, weak stimulation, merged spots, inconsistent counting or failed controls. It cannot tell each receptor's target, natural tumour recognition, safety in healthy tissue or clinical benefit.

points.requirement: Labels can outrun their measurements. An expression program may be described as cytotoxic without directly testing killing. A nearby cell may be described as tumor-reactive without testing its target. A blood clone may be described as an intratumoral clone without a tissue comparator.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: T cells develop through the thymus. Conventional alpha-beta T cells recognise peptide-HLA displays through a paired receptor; CD4 and CD8 identify major co-receptor populations, rather than fixed helper and killer jobs. Some human bladder-tumour CD4 cells showed class-II-dependent cytotoxicity in controlled experiments, while regulatory populations restrain responses. Identity, receptor specificity, state and measured function need separate evidence. A CD3 or CD8 stain establishes a sampled population under a defined panel, not tumour recognition or killing. Report compartment, viable-cell denominator, marker panel and timing. Controlled recognition and target-cell-death assays address different claims; cytokine production, division and treatment benefit are also separate outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

points.requirement: Engineering recognition does not eliminate state constraints. A [chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/cell-therapies/car-anatomy) can change what a cell responds to, but engineered cells still encounter local suppression, metabolic limits and chronic stimulation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional population of 100 cancer cells, 80 display target X and 20 do not. Killing the X-positive 80 leaves 20 survivors; ten times as many effector cells does not create X on them. For two targets, suppose 20 cells carry both X and Y, 60 carry X only, ten Y only and ten neither. An idealised either-target rule covers 90 cells, whereas a both-target rule covers 20. These are recognition-coverage calculations, not measured killing or healthy-tissue selectivity. Expression thresholds, tissue access and cell function still matter.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Kawalekar’s defined human-CAR experiments linked 4-1BB signalling to outgrowth of CD8 central-memory cells with greater respiratory capacity, fatty-acid oxidation and mitochondrial biogenesis. These are construct-and-system observations, not a ranking of clinical speed, persistence or safety by domain name. Other receptor parts, preparation, starting-cell state, target and disease setting remain relevant. Ramos simultaneously infused separately tracked second- and third-generation products. Their different expansion and persistence did not let a shared tumour response isolate either product’s clinical contribution.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: T-cell exhaustion is a distinct programme associated with persistent stimulation, multiple inhibitory receptors and altered transcription and chromatin. It is distinct from anergy and ordinary memory. Mouse experiments identified TOX as a central regulator. In chronic-infection and tumour models, progenitor exhausted populations retained response capacity and supplied descendants with different functions; terminally exhausted cells responded differently to anti-PD-1. A related melanoma association does not establish a universal treatment-selection test. PD-L1 blockade in mice re-engaged effector transcription with limited chromatin remodelling, and continued high antigen could lead to renewed exhaustion. Human skin-cancer studies also supported clonal replacement by clonotypes not previously detected in the sampled tumour. One marker, subset count or laboratory rescue does not establish tumour specificity, safe killing or individual clinical benefit.

points.requirement: Two other labels need care. [**Anergy**](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/anergy) describes reduced antigen-driven responsiveness in a defined context. **Exhaustion** is a differentiation program associated with persistent stimulation and altered function. They are different mechanisms; [anergy versus exhaustion](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/anergy-vs-exhaustion) compares the evidence that separates them. An exhausted population can include cells with different capacities to divide and respond.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Anergy is antigen-related reduced responsiveness that persists into a later controlled response test. In Jenkins and Schwartz's mouse and T-cell-clone experiments, chemically altered presenting cells induced reduced responsiveness to subsequent antigen stimulation with normal presenting cells. Macian and colleagues identified an NFAT-associated anergy gene programme in mechanistic experiments. These findings are model evidence, not a universal tumour-cell classifier.

Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation. Anergy, exhaustion, external suppression, absent antigen-specific cells and assay failure are different possible explanations for a low response. Low interleukin-2 alone leaves the mechanism unresolved. Check specificity, viable-cell recovery, stimulus controls, responsive comparators and response history; measure division and cytokine responses under matched conditions. Laboratory rescue does not establish tumour recognition, safe killing or clinical benefit.

points.requirement: **Regulatory T cells**, often shortened to **Tregs**, help protect tolerance and limit excessive responses. They are one of several programs a CD4 T cell can learn during priming; [CD4 T-cell subsets](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/cd4-t-cell-subsets) compares Tregs with the helper programs that support killing. Some can also restrain useful immunity near a tumor. They are not simply worn-out effector cells. Their regulatory role and an effector cell's exhaustion program describe different things. [Peripheral tolerance](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/peripheral-tolerance) includes several ways to restrain mature cells, including reduced responsiveness, deletion and regulatory suppression. Those mechanisms protect normal tissue as well as creating constraints near tumors.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Regulatory T cells help maintain self-tolerance and can restrain antitumour responses. Mouse experiments established a regulatory role for CD4/CD25 populations and linked Foxp3 to the regulatory programme. CTLA-4 can remove CD80/CD86 from antigen-presenting cells, reducing support available to other T cells. This is one mechanism, rather than a complete account of every regulatory population.

In defined human cultures, induced FOXP3 expression did not confer suppressive function. Human colorectal cancers also contained functionally distinct FOXP3-positive populations. FOXP3 staining alone therefore does not establish suppression or a universal prognosis; CD25 also needs identity and activation context. Use a defined marker panel, tissue location and controlled suppression assays. Mixed RNA signatures do not locate every contributing cell. Regulatory cells are not exhausted effectors, and removing restraint does not automatically provide safe clinical benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Central and peripheral tolerance include distinct mechanisms. Higher receptor affinity is not automatically more selective. Receptors can cross-react with peptides from unrelated proteins, as in the titin peptide recognised by the MAGE-A3-directed receptor (Cameron et al., 2013, PMID 23926201; Linette et al., 2013, PMID 23770775). evidence.supportingExcerpt:
CD4 T-cell subsets are differentiation programmes shaped by antigen recognition, cytokines and gene regulation. Conventional naive CD4 cells recognize peptide-HLA class II during priming, often on dendritic cells. Th1, Th2, Th17, follicular helper and regulatory programmes have characteristic signals, transcription factors and outputs, but these are not permanent job titles or mutually exclusive functional tests. The original Th1/Th2 distinction came from mouse clones in 1986; human tissue can contain mixed programmes.

CD4 help can improve the magnitude and quality of a CD8 response. Bennett’s experiments showed that CD40 signalling on antigen-presenting cells could replace CD4 help in a defined cross-priming system. Cella found that CD40 ligation increased dendritic-cell IL-12, ICAM-1, CD80 and CD86 and their T-cell-stimulating capacity. These support one licensing mechanism, not a requirement that every response follows an identical route.

Alspach’s mouse-tumour work required tumour-antigen-specific CD4 and CD8 responses even when the cancer cells lacked class-II molecules; tumour expression of class-II-restricted antigens was needed at the successful rejection site. In Ott’s phase-I melanoma vaccine trial, six people received personal neoantigens. CD4 responses targeted 58 of 97 neoantigens (60%) and CD8 responses 15 (16%). Four of six had no recurrence at 25 months, but the small uncontrolled study did not isolate clinical efficacy.

In untreated human breast tumours, Gu-Trantien found CXCL13-producing Tfh cells mainly in tertiary-lymphoid-structure germinal centres and an eight-gene signature associated with survival or preoperative-chemotherapy response. That is a prognostic association. DeNardo’s mouse mammary-cancer experiments showed a different possibility: IL-4-producing CD4 cells shaped macrophages that promoted invasion and lung metastasis. Subset identity therefore needs tissue, timing and measured-function context.

points.requirement: **An immune response can lose its target, its display route, its access or its ability to act. Name the failed step before proposing a way around it.**

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

A common antibody-derived CAR joins an external binding region, a hinge or spacer, a membrane anchor and intracellular signaling domains. The receptor is a protein; its encoding instructions and the living cell carrying it are different objects. Approved products and experimental constructs differ in cell source, receptor, manufacturing and clinical setting. Product labels and trial records define their actual uses; a platform name does not establish eligibility or benefit.

In early work, Gross, Waks and Eshhar joined antibody-variable regions to T-cell receptor components in 1989. Eshhar and colleagues subsequently tested single-chain antibody-binding regions joined to gamma or zeta signaling chains in 1993. These experimental designs helped separate recognition from the signaling machinery attached to it.

FDA-approved examples include tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, obecabtagene autoleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel and ciltacabtagene autoleucel. Their labeled diseases, treatment settings and eligibility differ; the individual product records retain those distinctions.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

points.requirement: An immune checkpoint inhibitor blocks one inhibitory interaction, such as [programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/immune-checkpoint), or cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4). [Lesson 7](/wiki/education/guides/how-the-immune-system-fights-cancer/07-what-checkpoint-inhibitors-change) covers what that changes, and the [checkpoint sites-of-action comparison](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/immune-regulation/immune-checkpoint#checkpoint-sites-of-action) compares the checkpoints. Measuring one receptor does not establish that its pathway causes the functional limitation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: PD-1 on a T cell, when it meets PD-L1 on another cell, tells the T cell to stand down; CTLA-4 is often emphasised earlier, during priming, and PD-1 during ongoing responses in tissues, but these are overlapping emphases and not separate addresses. Reviews describe CTLA-4 as acting early in lymph nodes and PD-1 later in peripheral tissues, while CTLA-4 is also expressed on activated effector CD8 T cells (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016; Pardoll, 2012), and LAG-3, TIM-3 and TIGIT as co-inhibitory receptors with their own specialised functions (Anderson et al., 2016), so the early or late shorthand for CTLA-4 and PD-1 should not be stretched to them. Tumours coat themselves in PD-L1 and exploit this, and antibodies that block PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab), PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab) or CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) restore the attack, producing durable remissions in melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder and many other cancers since 2011. The price is autoimmune side effects when the brakes come off everywhere, and only a minority of patients respond, which drives the search for newer checkpoints (LAG-3, TIGIT) and combinations. The 'checkpoint' in 'cell-cycle checkpoint' is an unrelated concept. The checkpoints work through different contacts and are not interchangeable versions of PD-1. In reconstitution and cell experiments, PD-1 engaged by PD-L1 recruited the phosphatase Shp2, which dephosphorylated the co-receptor CD28 in preference to the T-cell receptor (Hui et al., 2017). PD-1 has two ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, and PD-L1 is found on leukocytes and on non-haematopoietic cells in non-lymphoid tissues as well as on cancer cells, and can be induced by interferon gamma (Buchbinder and Desai, 2016). In the current US prescribing information for pembrolizumab, the indication for high-risk early-stage triple-negative breast cancer (chemotherapy before surgery, then pembrolizumab alone afterwards) carries no PD-L1 qualifier, whereas the indications for locally recurrent unresectable or metastatic disease (with chemotherapy) and for unresectable locally advanced or metastatic disease (with sacituzumab govitecan) name a PD-L1 combined positive score of 10 or more as determined by an FDA-authorized test. That describes how the approved uses are worded and is not a trial finding about who benefits. CTLA-4 shares the ligands CD80 and CD86 with CD28 and can capture them from opposing cells by trans-endocytosis, so the neighbouring cell has fewer costimulatory ligands to offer (Qureshi et al., 2011). These descriptions concern the receptors' own contacts and are not a model of what a blocking antibody does or a prediction of clinical benefit. LAG-3 selectively recognised stable complexes of peptide and MHC class II and suppressed T cells responding to them, without recognising every class II complex or blocking CD4 binding (Maruhashi et al., 2018). Bat3 bound to and repressed TIM-3 function and protected helper T cells from galectin-9-mediated death, and in cell-line co-expression experiments galectin-9 abolished Bat3 binding to TIM-3 (Rangachari et al., 2012). TIGIT disrupted dimerisation of the costimulatory receptor CD226 on the same cell, and in mouse tumour and chronic-infection models combined TIGIT and PD-L1 antibody blockade enhanced CD8 T-cell function in a CD226-dependent way (Johnston et al., 2014). Staining for a checkpoint measures a component in sampled cells and not ligand contact or causal inhibition: PD-1-positive cells need not all be exhausted or cancer-reactive, more staining does not prove more inhibition or greater drug benefit, and TIM-3-positive cells do not select TIM-3 over PD-1 blockade. A checkpoint inhibitor interrupts one pathway: it does not teach T cells a new target, build a route into the tumour or repair every dysfunctional cell, and changing normal regulation can also harm healthy organs.

PD-1 is a receptor with two partners, PD-L1 and PD-L2; PD-L1 is a distinct molecule found on cancer and non-cancer cells. The pembrolizumab label describes blockade of PD-1 binding to both ligands. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The adenosine route works outside cells. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
The sequence proposed by Taube and colleagues and mapped in more detail since is a loop. A T cell recognises a tumour peptide on HLA and releases interferon gamma; the interferon acts through the Janus kinases JAK1 and JAK2 in nearby tumour and immune cells; PD-L1 rises; PD-L1 binds PD-1 on the T cell and damps it. In melanoma cell lines, Garcia-Diaz and colleagues found that the interferon gamma, JAK1 and JAK2, STAT1, STAT2 and STAT3, IRF1 axis primarily regulates PD-L1, with IRF1 binding the PD-L1 promoter, and biopsies from patients with melanoma showed enrichment of that interferon signature and of STAT and IRF1 target genes in tumours that responded to anti-PD-1 treatment.

PD-L1 is not the only brake that follows the attack. Spranger and colleagues found in human melanoma that the T-cell-inflamed tumours were the ones with high indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), PD-L1 and regulatory T cells, and in mice that all three depended on CD8 T cells being present: IDO and PD-L1 through interferon gamma, and regulatory T cells through CCR4-binding chemokines with some induced proliferation. Their reading was that these pathways are driven by the immune response rather than orchestrated by the cancer cells.

Evidence from tissue. In human melanocytic lesions, 98% of PD-L1-positive (B7-H1-positive) tumours had tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes compared with 28% of PD-L1-negative tumours; positive melanocytes sat almost always immediately next to lymphocytes, and interferon gamma was detected at the interface but not in PD-L1-negative tumours (Taube and colleagues). The same colocalisation appeared in inflamed benign naevi, which fits PD-L1 as a response to tissue inflammation. In triple-negative breast cancer, Gruosso and colleagues described an immunoreactive group whose tumours had granzyme B-positive CD8 T cells inside cancer-cell regions, a type 1 interferon signature and elevated IDO and PD-L1, the pattern adaptive resistance predicts; that is an association in tissue and not a direct test of the loop. The alternative, called innate or constitutive resistance, is PD-L1 driven by the cancer cell's own signalling regardless of T cells.

A functionally important loss of JAK1 or JAK2 can impair the tumour cell response to interferon gamma. In four people with metastatic melanoma that relapsed on anti-PD-1 treatment, two relapse samples carried loss-of-function JAK1 or JAK2 mutations with deletion of the remaining normal allele, and truncating JAK1 or JAK2 mutations left the cells unresponsive to interferon gamma (Zaretsky and colleagues). The JAK2-deficient relapse cells lost interferon-gamma-induced PD-L1 and class-I increases but retained responses to interferon alfa and beta. In engineered melanoma cells, JAK1 or JAK2 loss did not abolish recognition by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Loss of inducibility is therefore different from absence of all baseline recognition. This selected series does not estimate a frequency for all cancers.

points.requirement: The tempting shortcut is a rescue story: “This system failed, so the other system will work.” Losing one HLA allele does not guarantee NK killing. Missing-self recognition depends on the balance of activating and inhibitory [NK-cell receptors](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/innate-and-unconventional-cells/nk-cell-receptors), the NK population and its environment. A bypass aimed at a protein that healthy tissue also carries adds its own safety question.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.
evidence.explanation: Reduced class I can remove an NK inhibitory input but does not guarantee missing-self killing; activation, population and tissue context still matter. Surface-target bypass adds its own safety question. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Many tumour-associated antigens come from unmutated proteins, so their usefulness depends on higher expression, an unusual expression pattern or accessibility in the cancer. A neoantigen, by contrast, arises from a tumour-specific sequence alteration. For an antibody or a chimeric antigen receptor, the question is accessible surface antigen on tumour and on healthy cells. For a peptide-directed T-cell receptor it is the particular peptide displayed by a particular HLA allele. RNA for the source gene establishes neither recognition surface, and a gene-expression result does not specify accessibility or peptide display.

Two hazards need different controls. On-target, off-tumour recognition means the receptor recognises its intended target in the wrong tissue. Off-target cross-reactivity means the receptor also recognises a different molecular target, so screening the intended antigen alone cannot rule it out. A published example of the second is an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor directed at HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3: in a clinical study the first two treated patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days, no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and the T cells recognised an unrelated peptide from the striated-muscle protein titin (Linette et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2013, who describe the preclinical analysis as having found no off-target concern). That illustrates the hazard for one engineered receptor and is not a toxicity rate for tumour-associated targets. Immune tolerance also shapes the available response to self antigens, and a stronger receptor does not remove the need to test healthy tissues and alternative targets.

A shared antigen can support a treatment intended for more than one person's cancer, with a trade-off between tumour coverage and healthy-tissue exposure; expression prevalence in a cohort is not a safe recognition threshold for a product. For vaccine-elicited peptide-specific T cells, a shared antigen offers another candidate when credible private targets are few, which is a coverage hypothesis, not demonstrated benefit. A peptide from a shared antigen and one from a neoantigen may depend on the same HLA allele, so changing the antigen does not restore a missing display route: Tran et al. (2016) documented escape after loss of the restricting HLA allele in one colorectal cancer patient. Antibodies and CARs have different recognition requirements, and epitope spreading is a separate widening of recognition that adding a shared antigen does not guarantee.

points.requirement: **A checkpoint inhibitor removes one brake from T cells that already recognize the cancer. In early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), adding pembrolizumab to chemotherapy raised the complete-response rate and improved survival, whether or not the tumor stained for PD-L1.**

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Checkpoint antibodies interrupt specified inhibitory contacts. PD-1 is a receptor with two partners, PD-L1 and PD-L2; PD-L1 is a distinct molecule found on cancer and non-cancer cells. The pembrolizumab label describes blockade of PD-1 binding to both ligands. Atezolizumab instead binds PD-L1 and blocks its PD-1 and B7.1 interactions; directly blocking PD-L1 does not directly block the separate PD-1/PD-L2 contact. These target-specific descriptions are more precise than treating all checkpoint drugs as one switch.

PD-1 is a receptor with two partners, PD-L1 and PD-L2; PD-L1 is a distinct molecule found on cancer and non-cancer cells. The pembrolizumab label describes blockade of PD-1 binding to both ligands. Atezolizumab instead binds PD-L1 and blocks its PD-1 and B7.1 interactions; directly blocking PD-L1 does not directly block the separate PD-1/PD-L2 contact. These target-specific descriptions are more precise than treating all checkpoint drugs as one switch.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The pathways also differ inside and between cells. points.requirement: - [T-cell exhaustion](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell-exhaustion): the restrained program T cells enter under persistent antigen.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Exhaustion is a distinct differentiation programme associated with persistent stimulation, altered function, multiple inhibitory receptors and transcriptional and chromatin changes. Deficits can be graded and subsets retain different capacities.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In chronic LCMV infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor exhausted cells self-renewed and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-L1 blockade.
