points.requirement: Tumors often display PD-L1 *because* T cells are attacking them. T cells that recognize a tumor release interferon gamma, and interferon gamma induces PD-L1 on nearby tumor and immune cells. This is called **[adaptive immune resistance](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/adaptive-immune-resistance)**: the brake is pulled in response to the attack ([Taube et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22461641/)). That is why PD-L1 staining and a [lymphocyte-rich "hot" pattern](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/hot-excluded-cold-tumor) often travel together.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
The sequence proposed by Taube and colleagues and mapped in more detail since is a loop. A T cell recognises a tumour peptide on HLA and releases interferon gamma; the interferon acts through the Janus kinases JAK1 and JAK2 in nearby tumour and immune cells; PD-L1 rises; PD-L1 binds PD-1 on the T cell and damps it. In melanoma cell lines, Garcia-Diaz and colleagues found that the interferon gamma, JAK1 and JAK2, STAT1, STAT2 and STAT3, IRF1 axis primarily regulates PD-L1, with IRF1 binding the PD-L1 promoter, and biopsies from patients with melanoma showed enrichment of that interferon signature and of STAT and IRF1 target genes in tumours that responded to anti-PD-1 treatment.

PD-L1 is not the only brake that follows the attack. Spranger and colleagues found in human melanoma that the T-cell-inflamed tumours were the ones with high indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), PD-L1 and regulatory T cells, and in mice that all three depended on CD8 T cells being present: IDO and PD-L1 through interferon gamma, and regulatory T cells through CCR4-binding chemokines with some induced proliferation. Their reading was that these pathways are driven by the immune response rather than orchestrated by the cancer cells.

Evidence from tissue. In human melanocytic lesions, 98% of PD-L1-positive (B7-H1-positive) tumours had tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes compared with 28% of PD-L1-negative tumours; positive melanocytes sat almost always immediately next to lymphocytes, and interferon gamma was detected at the interface but not in PD-L1-negative tumours (Taube and colleagues). The same colocalisation appeared in inflamed benign naevi, which fits PD-L1 as a response to tissue inflammation. In triple-negative breast cancer, Gruosso and colleagues described an immunoreactive group whose tumours had granzyme B-positive CD8 T cells inside cancer-cell regions, a type 1 interferon signature and elevated IDO and PD-L1, the pattern adaptive resistance predicts; that is an association in tissue and not a direct test of the loop. The alternative, called innate or constitutive resistance, is PD-L1 driven by the cancer cell's own signalling regardless of T cells.

A functionally important loss of JAK1 or JAK2 can impair the tumour cell response to interferon gamma. In four people with metastatic melanoma that relapsed on anti-PD-1 treatment, two relapse samples carried loss-of-function JAK1 or JAK2 mutations with deletion of the remaining normal allele, and truncating JAK1 or JAK2 mutations left the cells unresponsive to interferon gamma (Zaretsky and colleagues). The JAK2-deficient relapse cells lost interferon-gamma-induced PD-L1 and class-I increases but retained responses to interferon alfa and beta. In engineered melanoma cells, JAK1 or JAK2 loss did not abolish recognition by the tested NY-ESO-1-specific T cells. Loss of inducibility is therefore different from absence of all baseline recognition. This selected series does not estimate a frequency for all cancers.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A PD-L1 stain measures protein on defined tumour and immune cells, not why it is present. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. First, the 64.8% pCR figure comes from the first interim analysis; across all 1,174 patients the US label reports 63.0% vs 55.6% ([FDA label, section 14.20](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/125514s194lbl.pdf)). points.requirement: **Location, receptor identity, function and tumor response are different measurements. A useful immune story connects them without treating one as proof of all the others.**

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An immune observation suggests a question ladder: identify the cells and their location; ask whether a proposed peptide is produced and displayed; test recognition against appropriate target and background controls; distinguish tissue entry from useful target-specific function; then seek clinical comparisons for benefit and harm. Poor display, few matching cells, failed tissue access and impaired local function are different proposed failures. A count, supplied-peptide response or plausible pathway alone cannot complete that chain. These are task-dependent interpretation questions, not a mandatory clinical test menu.
evidence.explanation: Cell location, receptor identity, measured stimulation/function and a comparative clinical result address different claims. The interpretation ladder preserves target controls, model limits and no attribution of benefit to one clone. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

points.requirement: **Before you start:** [T cells](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell) establishes cell identity. A [T-cell receptor (TCR)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell-receptor) is the reader. [TCR sequencing (TCR-seq)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/immune-monitoring/tcr-sequencing) explains sequence identities. [T-cell states](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell-states) separates markers from function. [Hot, excluded and cold patterns](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/hot-excluded-cold-tumor) explains tissue location. [Flow cytometry](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/immune-monitoring/flow-cytometry) groups prepared cells by measured features; [cell segmentation](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/proteins-and-spatial/cell-segmentation) estimates cell regions in images.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

points.requirement: A tissue sample preserves a local view. A blood sample allows repeated views of circulating populations. Neither is the universal first step. The right sample depends on the question, available material and assay requirements.

Sampling, damage, mixed compartments, unsuitable markers and culture selection are different failure modes, and descriptive pathology, research function and clinical treatment selection require different validation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: What the fraction is: peripheral blood mononuclear cells are circulating white blood cells with a single unsegmented nucleus, mainly lymphocytes and monocytes, with T, B and natural killer cells among them, isolated by layering anticoagulated blood over a density-separation medium and collecting the interface. The classic density-gradient method dates from 1968 (Boyum 1968). Isolation selects a recoverable blood fraction and does not sample tumour or give a complete immune census.

points.requirement: [Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/proteins-and-spatial/multiplex-immunofluorescence) and [imaging mass cytometry (IMC)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/proteins-and-spatial/imaging-mass-cytometry) preserve a section's geography through different marker-detection methods. Their per-cell interpretations depend on segmentation. A merged boundary can falsely assign an immune marker and a cancer-cell marker to one cell. Inspecting the original image and boundary overlay comes before interpreting that combination.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. A cell phenotype is a rule-based call from the measured panel, a density needs a stated denominator, and a distance needs a stated definition (cell centre or cell boundary).

points.requirement: In a fictional vaccine study, clonotype A becomes more frequent after dosing. The same sequence is found in a tumor sample. An intended-peptide stimulation test is positive.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In an invented vaccine report, one blood clonotype becomes more frequent, its sequence also appears in sampled tumour, a separately tested cell mixture responds to added peptide, and ctDNA becomes undetectable. These are four observations, not proof that this clone killed the cancer. Link the responding cells to a compatible paired receptor, test natural tumour recognition and target death, and preserve each assay's denominator and detection limit. Surgery, chemotherapy, shedding and sampling can also affect ctDNA. Conversely, an unchanged blood repertoire does not exclude a response in unsampled tissue. Temporal coincidence does not establish the causal contribution of one clone.
evidence.explanation: The fictional frequency/overlap/separate-mixture response/ctDNA observations do not assign a clone-mediated effect. Responding cells, compatible paired receptor, natural display/killing, timing and clinical comparisons are separate links, and unsampled tissue responses remain possible. Author-labelled inference from stipulated premises or distinct assay/clinical endpoints. Fictional arithmetic was recomputed; no empirical result or clinical threshold is inferred.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional report, A rises from 0.1% to 2.0% of sampled blood receptors and is 0.5% in sampled tumour; its blood share rose twentyfold. points.requirement: A compatible single-cell method can pair receptor identity with gene-expression features. Paired alpha-beta sequences supply a more complete identity than a beta-chain junction alone; a match under one chain definition does not establish the same complete receptor. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Beta match, alpha hidden, fictional: three cells carry beta chains B, B and C, so a bulk beta-chain view lists B, B, C and loses the alpha chains. The paired view keeps alpha X with beta B, alpha Y with beta B and alpha Z with beta C, so the shared beta B does not make alpha X and alpha Y equal. Single-cell methods that sequence the alpha and beta genes of individual T cells retain each pair and can be combined with function-related gene expression, and the same TCR sequence can sit in functionally different cells (Han 2014). A bulk method profiles a mixed sample, often one chain, whereas TIRTL-seq generates paired alpha and beta repertoire data at cohort scale and is distinguished from bulk single-chain data and from single-cell throughput limits (Pogorelyy 2026). Paired identity plus an expression program is more context and is still not evidence of the receptor's antigen.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Naive, effector, memory and exhausted populations describe response histories and differentiation programmes, not one mandatory sequence for every T cell. Anergy and exhaustion are distinct mechanisms. Regulatory function is a separate role. Identity, location, receptor specificity, state and measured function are complementary observations.

In chronic viral infection in mice, TCF1-associated progenitor populations sustained responses and supplied the proliferative burst after PD-1 blockade. In tumour models, progenitor exhausted cells differed from terminally exhausted cells; the related melanoma observations were associations rather than a universal treatment-selection rule. Progenitor-like exhaustion is not ordinary memory. A shared receptor does not require a shared functional phenotype, and PD-1 or TCF1 alone does not establish state or tumour specificity.

Paired human skin-cancer biopsies after PD-1 blockade showed expanded clonotypes not previously observed in the same tumour, supporting clonal replacement as another response model. Absence from an earlier sample does not establish absence throughout the body. A fictional PD-1-positive population near cancer can include viral-reactive and tumour-peptide-reactive cells. Neither proximity nor peptide response proves natural tumour recognition or killing. Preserve response history, sampling site, time, multiple markers and controlled function; neither division nor a favourable pattern predicts individual benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is made up of DNA fragments shed by tumour cells into the bloodstream, where they form only a small fraction of all cell-free DNA and are detected with sensitive sequencing. Its uses span genotyping for companion diagnostics, tracking resistance mutations such as EGFR T790M and ESR1, molecular residual disease, early detection and response monitoring. Shedding varies with tumour type and burden, and clonal haematopoiesis can confound results. The term underpins the Liquid biopsy (ctDNA), MRD / molecular residual disease testing and Multi-cancer early detection (MCED) technologies, and it appears in the SERENA-6, CIRCULATE-Japan and IMvigor011 trials and in ideas on molecular-progression switching beyond ESR1 and HPV ctDNA to guide cervical cancer therapy.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) can be reported as a concentration, as a fraction, or as a yes or no call, and the three are not interchangeable. A concentration counts tumour-attributed molecules in a stated volume of plasma. One example is mean tumour molecules per millilitre (MTM/mL), which the I-SPY 2 breast-cancer study of Magbanua and colleagues used for ctDNA across tracked variants. A fraction divides tumour-attributed molecules by a stated total, such as all evaluated alleles at one position (variant allele fraction, VAF) or all evaluated DNA (an estimated tumour fraction). Parts per million (PPM) is a fraction multiplied by one million, so the number is only as meaningful as the fraction it scales: 0.01% is 100 PPM, and 0.00024% is 2.4 PPM, the lowest allele fraction Santonja and colleagues reported for ctDNA detection in breast cancer.

Concentration and fraction can move apart. If two equal one-millilitre aliquots each hold the same number of tumour molecules but one holds more background cell-free DNA, the concentration is unchanged and the fraction falls. A detection call and a reliable amount are also different claims, because the detection limit and the quantitation range are validated separately. Nothing here gives a conversion between assays: MTM/mL cannot be turned into PPM from the printed result, and a VAF of 100 PPM at one variant is not a tumour fraction of 100 PPM.
evidence.explanation: Tumour-attributed circulating DNA, concentration/fraction/detection-call units and sampling rules are separate from T-cell function. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In an invented vaccine report, one blood clonotype becomes more frequent, its sequence also appears in sampled tumour, a separately tested cell mixture responds to added peptide, and ctDNA becomes undetectable. These are four observations, not proof that this clone killed the cancer. Link the responding cells to a compatible paired receptor, test natural tumour recognition and target death, and preserve each assay's denominator and detection limit. Surgery, chemotherapy, shedding and sampling can also affect ctDNA. Conversely, an unchanged blood repertoire does not exclude a response in unsampled tissue. Temporal coincidence does not establish the causal contribution of one clone.

points.requirement: Samples can differ in handling, timing, quality and depth. A relative frequency is easily mistaken for an absolute cell count. A tissue section or selected field can miss another region's biology. An antigen assay can use conditions that differ from natural tumor presentation. A negative blood result can miss a tissue-localized response.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Assay card: measures receptor identities, usually by the complementarity-determining region 3 of the variable region, and their measured representation in the sampled population. How: extract nucleic acid, amplify or capture receptor regions, sequence, then group and count under stated rules, which may use nucleotide or amino-acid sequence, gene segments, one chain or paired chains. Input: blood cells or tissue nucleic acid for bulk methods and compatible cell preparations for single-cell methods, and preparation consumes material. A high-resolution human repertoire method reported chain diversity without sequence-associated or quantitative restrictions (Ruggiero 2015). Failure modes: poor material, shallow sampling, amplification bias, chain mismatch, inconsistent definitions and batch effects. It cannot tell every receptor's target, tissue position, killing or benefit, and a research method is not automatically a treatment-selection test.

This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Handling is evidence: in HIV vaccine assay studies, the time from venipuncture to cryopreservation was the most important parameter, and blood processed at 24 hours compared with within 8 hours lost on average about 8% of PBMC viability, about 32% of cell recovery and 36% to 56% of interferon gamma T-cell frequencies by ELISpot, which led the authors to recommend cryopreservation within 8 hours (Bull 2007). A rapidly processed baseline and a delayed follow-up can therefore confound a biological comparison, and a high viability percentage alone does not show that every population or function was preserved.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

points.requirement: The remedy is to write the claim beside the readout and name its limit. This keeps a promising signal useful while making the next experiment clear.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An immune observation suggests a question ladder: identify the cells and their location; ask whether a proposed peptide is produced and displayed; test recognition against appropriate target and background controls; distinguish tissue entry from useful target-specific function; then seek clinical comparisons for benefit and harm. Poor display, few matching cells, failed tissue access and impaired local function are different proposed failures. A count, supplied-peptide response or plausible pathway alone cannot complete that chain. These are task-dependent interpretation questions, not a mandatory clinical test menu.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Method card, what it measures: whether specified effector cells cause death of specified target cells under controlled laboratory conditions, at a stated effector-to-target ratio and time. Readouts: flow cytometry that separates labelled targets from effectors and uses death-associated staining, release assays, or imaging over time. A fall in a metabolic or growth signal can reflect slowed growth and not death, so it needs validation as evidence of killing. Controls: target-only survival wells, effector identification and viability, a positive-control response, irrelevant or antigen-negative targets and suitable antigen or presentation perturbations, plus maximum release where relevant. Failure modes: high spontaneous death, mistaken target identity, aggregates, dye transfer, artificial loading, mismatched ratios or a readout that mainly measures growth.

points.requirement: **A [T-cell receptor (TCR)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell-receptor) sequencing report is an inventory: it lists which receptor sequences were found in a sample and how common each was. It tells you who was sampled and how often, not what any receptor recognizes.**

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An original sequencing study quantified rearranged T-cell receptor beta-chain sequences to examine repertoire diversity. A beta-chain repertoire is a sampled molecular measurement, not a complete map of paired receptors or the antigens they recognize. The specimen, sequencing method and definition of a clonotype belong with the result. Following a sequence over time is distinct from demonstrating its antigen specificity or the function of the cells that carry it.
evidence.explanation: A repertoire is a sample-defined collection/distribution, not a complete paired-target inventory. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. evidence.supportingExcerpt: The repertoire is a distribution of receptor identities and abundances in a stated population and time. A clone is a cellular lineage; a clonotype is an operational sequence grouping. Single-chain labels and paired identities have different resolution. V(D)J assembly and thymic selection contribute diversity, while expansion changes abundance; diversity and total T-cell count are different quantities.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

HLA alleles are shared across people, and a person inherits a combination that is not necessarily unique. Each person inherits two copies each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C, so a cell can display up to six classical class I variants at once. The IPD-IMGT/HLA statistics page read on 9 November 2026 listed 46,146 HLA alleles, 31,311 class I and 14,835 class II (9,457 HLA-A, 11,328 HLA-B and 9,580 HLA-C alleles). Binding predictors estimate whether a peptide can fit a specified allele's groove, but processing, transport, loading and surface expression decide whether it is displayed. Sarkizova et al. (2020) profiled more than 185,000 peptides eluted from 95 mono-allelic cell lines to learn allele-specific motifs and build prediction models; that is allele-level data, not proof of any cell's display. Kaur et al. (2017) showed that HLA-C surface expression varies across individuals in an allele-specific manner, influenced by the structure of the peptide-binding cleft and peptide diversity; Apps and colleagues found lower HLA-C than HLA-A/B in the analysed healthy-donor peripheral blood lymphocytes with the A*02:01/B*44:02/C*05:01 haplotype; the magnitude differed between flow cytometry and mass spectrometry. This is a defined comparison, not a universal hierarchy. The small HLA-C peptide share observed by Schellens and colleagues in four B lymphoblastoid cell lines was also affected by their assignment method, which gave HLA-A/B precedence; it is not a universal biological fraction.

In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

B2M is the light chain of classical class I and does not span the membrane; class II contains no B2M, so CD4 T-cell recognition can remain when B2M is lost. B2M also partners other class I-like molecules: UniProt records heterotrimers with HLA-E, HLA-G, HLA-F and MR1 and lists CD1 interactions, and a B2M mutation caused deficiency of the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn in two siblings (Wani et al., 2006), so complete B2M loss can remove more than classical class I. Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

items.title: Why the immune system doesn't just kill a tumor, and what checkpoint inhibitors change

review.auditor: Coordinator source-first manual field assessment at specified source depth; not independent expert or learner acceptance
review.rationale: All ten later bodies were read end to end; four originals were read in full and five through complete diffs against fully read later counterparts. Original nine pages/102 sections and later ten pages/114 sections remain separate. The source-first frozen inventory has 358 candidate blocks, 342 represented at stated scope, five source-open and eleven explicit navigation/framing exclusions; all 192 initially noncredit blocks also have dispositions. Twenty new or rewritten root note paragraphs, three unapplied peer notes, one narrowed summary paragraph and one canonical TLDR correction have exact field proofs; fourteen root owners change without a new record/schema. Fifty-five complete abstracts, 107 selected body passages in twenty bodies including three short corrections, a fourth one-page correction PDF and selected official text retain their actual depth. No original paper was read end to end. Eight native whole source-art views and ten unique Mermaid theme renders were freshly inspected. Sixty actual root SSR readers plus thirteen labelled proposed/frozen peer overlays pass 538 field and 199 anchor checks; sixty JSON and 410 Markdown passage checks pass. Thirty-six existing short summaries are corrected without native-language approval. Source/peer/root/main/live and acceptance boundaries remain explicit; no source artwork is imported.

points.requirement: **T cells can recognize cancer, but tumors survive by hiding the target, keeping T cells out or switching them down. Checkpoint inhibitors release one of those brakes; in early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), adding one to chemotherapy improved survival.**

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Chen and Mellman’s 2013 framework describes seven linked steps: release of cancer antigens; their collection and presentation; T-cell priming and activation; trafficking; entry into tumour tissue; recognition of cancer cells; and killing. Further antigen release may support another round. In conventional T-cell recognition, a displayed peptide-HLA complex and a suitable T-cell receptor are separate dependencies.

This is a T-cell-centred organizing model, not a universal route, assay result or treatment-selection algorithm. Steps overlap, priming may occur away from the tumour, and other immune mechanisms require their own account. Checkpoints and local tissue conditions affect several steps. Vaccines aim to generate or expand reactive responses, checkpoint drugs interrupt selected inhibitory signals, and engineered cells provide a recognition system and effectors. Each still needs appropriate targets, access, function and safety evidence.
evidence.explanation: Cancer-directed recognition, several escape dependencies and the tested early-TNBC chemotherapy-plus-checkpoint survival comparison retain population and mechanism scope. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immune escape can involve loss of a targeted antigen, altered HLA alleles or processing, defective inducible signalling, inhibition after entry or impaired access. Anagnostou found loss of putative neoantigens in checkpoint-resistant lung tumours with accompanying T-cell evidence. McGranahan described allele-specific HLA loss in lung cancer evolution. Montesion’s commercial pan-cancer genomic series contained 83,644 samples with HLA-I loss of heterozygosity in 17%; this assay-defined pan-cancer observation is not a breast-specific prevalence. Allele loss differs from reversible expression change or a B2M defect affecting class-I surface display.
evidence.explanation: Cancer-directed recognition, several escape dependencies and the tested early-TNBC chemotherapy-plus-checkpoint survival comparison retain population and mechanism scope. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: KEYNOTE-522 randomised 1,174 people with previously untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer to pembrolizumab or placebo with chemotherapy before surgery, followed by continuation of the assigned antibody or placebo after surgery. At a median follow-up of 75.1 months, estimated 60-month overall survival was 86.6 per cent versus 81.7 per cent. Enrolment did not require PD-L1 positivity. The trial compared the whole perioperative regimen and was not designed to isolate the contribution of each treatment phase. These group results do not predict one person's outcome.

points.requirement: 1. **A T cell sees a fragment, not a whole cell.** It recognizes a short protein piece displayed on [human leukocyte antigen (HLA)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/antigen-presentation/hla). No display, no recognition.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: T cells develop through the thymus. Conventional alpha-beta T cells recognise peptide-HLA displays through a paired receptor; CD4 and CD8 identify major co-receptor populations, rather than fixed helper and killer jobs. Some human bladder-tumour CD4 cells showed class-II-dependent cytotoxicity in controlled experiments, while regulatory populations restrain responses. Identity, receptor specificity, state and measured function need separate evidence. A CD3 or CD8 stain establishes a sampled population under a defined panel, not tumour recognition or killing. Report compartment, viable-cell denominator, marker panel and timing. Controlled recognition and target-cell-death assays address different claims; cytokine production, division and treatment benefit are also separate outcomes.

points.requirement: 3. **Tumors are shaped by the attack.** Immune pressure removes visible cancer cells; survivors hide targets, exclude T cells or exhaust them. This is [immunoediting](/wiki/education/concepts/cancer-biology/what-cancer-is/immunoediting).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immune surveillance concerns immune control of transformed cells. Immunoediting adds that immune pressure can alter which cancer populations persist. Elimination, equilibrium and escape describe processes that can coexist or occur independently, not a mandatory three-stage calendar. Shankaran’s genetically defined mouse experiments support lymphocyte and interferon-gamma contributions to control and selection. They do not measure what fraction of all human cancers immunity prevents.
evidence.explanation: Immune control and selection are model-supported processes rather than a compulsory phase assignment or claim that immunity generated every later change. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An editing claim combines longitudinal populations or antigens, recognition or functional assays and relevant comparisons. Apparent antigen loss can instead reflect sampling, detection limits, expression change or another treatment. Neither sequencing alone nor a killing experiment reconstructs the whole history. One immune-rich sample, negative blood test or model cannot assign an individual postoperative phase, explain every recurrence or forecast personal risk; different lesions can face different pressures.

points.requirement: 5. **Markers do different jobs.** Stromal tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (sTILs) predict outcome after chemotherapy; programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) picks who gains from a checkpoint inhibitor only in advanced TNBC.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In the pooled analysis of 2,148 early-stage TNBC patients given anthracycline-based chemotherapy with or without taxanes, each 10 percentage-point increase in pretreatment stromal TILs corresponded to an adjusted invasive disease-free survival hazard ratio of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.91) and overall survival hazard ratio of 0.84 (0.79 to 0.89). These associations do not establish an added pembrolizumab benefit by TIL level.
evidence.explanation: The early chemotherapy-treated prognostic TIL association and advanced-setting CPS selection remain distinct from the unselected high-risk early-TNBC label and individual comparative benefit. Named current field passage inspected for its assigned teaching; primary evidence keeps the earlier recorded depth unless separately listed as a fresh read. This does not re-certify all older assertions in the owner.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: KEYNOTE-355 studied 847 people with previously untreated locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. In the PD-L1 combined-positive-score-at-least-10 subgroup, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy gave median overall survival of 23.0 months versus 16.1 with placebo plus chemotherapy, with a death hazard ratio of 0.73. A median divides a study group in half; it is not an individual forecast. The October 2026 U.S. pembrolizumab label has no PD-L1 qualifier for its high-risk early-stage TNBC regimen, while its advanced TNBC indications with chemotherapy or sacituzumab govitecan specify CPS at least 10 and an FDA-authorised test. The sacituzumab combination is a separate labelled regimen, not the KEYNOTE-355 comparison. Population, regimen, scoring context and evidence must stay together.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The study question concerns the whole assigned sequence in previously untreated, non-metastatic stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer: T1c with N1 or N2, or T2 to T4 with N0 to N2, and performance status 0 or 1. The registry excludes prior checkpoint therapy and active autoimmune disease requiring systemic treatment in the preceding two years, among other criteria. There was one assignment of 784 people to pembrolizumab and 390 to placebo across preoperative chemotherapy, surgery and postoperative treatment, without a separate postoperative randomisation. Immune material and cells reach a node by different routes: soluble antigen can reach resident dendritic cells through conduits in the node before migrating dendritic cells arrive (Sixt et al., 2005, mouse), while lymphocytes are recruited from the blood through high endothelial venules (Brulois et al., 2020, mouse). Lymph is interstitial fluid collected by lymph capillaries and returned to the venous blood (National Cancer Institute SEER training), so lymph and blood are different fluids and a sample of one does not stand in for the other. A tertiary lymphoid structure is an ectopic lymphoid aggregate that forms in tissue such as a tumour, and it is not a lymph node (Schumacher and Thommen, 2022). Size on imaging is a measurement in millimetres and not a finding of cancer or priming, and a report should say which node was measured, by what method and when (OnCo reporting advice). Loss of one HLA allele can leave other presenting alleles usable, whereas loss of functional B2M impairs many class I targets at once, so several peptides on different alleles are not independent protection. A B2M variant, low RNA, absent surface class I and a blood B2M concentration are different observations: one variant does not show complete functional loss, and blood B2M does not count tumour peptide-HLA complexes. Zaretsky et al. (2016) linked a truncating B2M mutation to lost surface class I in one melanoma relapse after PD-1 blockade, which is a mechanism in that setting, not a frequency. Reduced class I display does not guarantee NK-cell killing, because activating signals are still needed.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Chen and Mellman’s 2013 framework describes seven linked steps: release of cancer antigens; their collection and presentation; T-cell priming and activation; trafficking; entry into tumour tissue; recognition of cancer cells; and killing. Further antigen release may support another round. In conventional T-cell recognition, a displayed peptide-HLA complex and a suitable T-cell receptor are separate dependencies.

This is a T-cell-centred organizing model, not a universal route, assay result or treatment-selection algorithm. Steps overlap, priming may occur away from the tumour, and other immune mechanisms require their own account. Checkpoints and local tissue conditions affect several steps. Vaccines aim to generate or expand reactive responses, checkpoint drugs interrupt selected inhibitory signals, and engineered cells provide a recognition system and effectors. Each still needs appropriate targets, access, function and safety evidence.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

points.requirement: [Ablation](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/ablation) destroys tissue at a selected site, for example through freezing or heating. [Radiation therapy](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/radiation-therapy-basics) deposits energy that can damage cells and impair their ability to reproduce. These physical effects can act without a T cell recognizing a cancer antigen. Antigen-specific T-cell killing has additional requirements.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.
evidence.explanation: Physical injury and loss of reproductive ability do not require conventional antigen-specific T-cell recognition. The proposed immune addition is a separate mechanism. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Radiation transfers energy to tissue and can damage DNA directly or through reactive molecules. Cells can repair damage or lose their ability to keep dividing, and death can occur later. One treatment session is an exposure, rather than an immediate count of dead cells. Oxygen, cell state and repair affect the response.

External beams, brachytherapy sources and systemically distributed radiopharmaceuticals have different exposure patterns. An external-beam target can include tissue at risk of microscopic disease after surgery, even when no mass is visible. Planning and verification consider geometry, motion, normal organs and previous overlapping exposure. Precision does not eliminate normal-tissue dose or injury.

Absorbed dose in gray is energy per mass: one gray is one joule per kilogram. Total dose, fraction size, timing and exposed volume influence biological effects. Physical-dose arithmetic alone does not establish equivalence of schedules. Local or regional control, symptom relief, distant disease and survival remain distinct clinical outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Delivery can be compared without ranking treatments. A fictional probe card controls a selected liver site, a beam card specifies a lung volume and motion assessment, and a radioactive-drug card requires distribution, retention and organ dosimetry. They are different routes, not a ladder from one lesion to invisible disease. A systemically distributed radioactive product still does not guarantee exposure of every microscopic deposit. Radiation injury does not require a conventional T cell to recognise peptide-HLA; proposed antigen-specific immune effects still need presentation, access, recognition and function. In another invented study, people receiving the same systemic strategy are randomised to a local addition or no local addition. With the same defined progression endpoint, starting time and follow-up, treated sites are controlled but new lesions occur in both arms and the progression-free-survival interval spans effects in both directions. That supports local control while leaving the added progression effect uncertain; survival, quality of life, pain and harms remain separate outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

Steps overlap, priming may occur away from the tumour, and other immune mechanisms require their own account. Checkpoints and local tissue conditions affect several steps. Vaccines aim to generate or expand reactive responses, checkpoint drugs interrupt selected inhibitory signals, and engineered cells provide a recognition system and effectors. review.rationale: Eight later lessons were read end to end. Of ten originals, three were read in full, six through complete counterpart diffs and one reused by exact byte identity. The separate inventories retain 107 original and 84 later section signatures. All 412 frozen blocks were dispositioned: 286 substantive units, 285 represented at stated scope and one unsupported surgery-frequency clause, plus 126 explicit noncredit blocks. Of the represented units, 234 use registered draft-root fields and 51 depend on two unapplied PR-373 proposals. Twelve existing root owners change, with no new record or schema field. Twenty-one cited abstracts, one context-only abstract, 72 selected body passages in eight articles and selected official text retain their actual reading depths; no original paper was read end to end. Four whole native source images and six standalone Mermaid theme renders were viewed. Thirty-five actual root readers and two labelled in-memory peer proposals pass 263 field and 101 anchor checks. Actual JSON/Markdown/OpenAPI exports and 87 root Markdown anchors pass. Twenty-two existing short summaries are corrected without native-language approval; no missing entry is created. Full gates pass, with separately verified post-gate line-end-whitespace cleanup. No main, live, graph-integration, independent, expert or learner acceptance is created.

points.requirement: **You will learn to describe the job of a local treatment before discussing its timing.** Start with [the mechanism lesson](/wiki/education/local-treatment-modalities/01-mechanism) and [neoadjuvant versus adjuvant therapy](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/treatment-setting/neoadjuvant-vs-adjuvant) if treatment-setting language is new.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Start with the goal and history before choosing a clock. A smaller lesion is a response observation at assessment; local control concerns keeping that site from progressing during follow-up. Postoperative local-recurrence prevention, relief of pain from a bone metastasis and a growing lesion during otherwise controlled metastatic disease are different questions. A meaningful pain improvement need not wait for an untreated tumour to shrink. A positive blood molecular test does not identify a lesion's position, boundary or safe access. An earlier scan date alone does not demonstrate improved outcomes. These distinctions organise evidence review rather than select a dose, procedure or treatment date. Nonmetastatic disease means no established distant metastases; a stage and subtype still need their own comparison of local and systemic care. Recovery, healing, previous exposure, overlapping toxicities and protocol assessment times supply other clocks. They are reasons to examine the studied sequence rather than invent a universal interval or repeat a procedure whenever a blood marker rises.
evidence.explanation: Goals, postoperative prevention, pain relief and progression during otherwise controlled disease require different settings and clocks. Healing, prior exposure, overlap toxicity and protocol timing support reviewing the studied strategy, not an invented dose/date or marker-triggered repeat procedure. evidence.supportingExcerpt: A local-treatment proposal needs five connected answers: the local and hoped-for wider outcomes with their measurements; evidence matching the cancer, disease history, complete strategy and comparator; access, intended coverage, margins, motion and nearby structures; actual exposure and normal-tissue risk; and alternatives, burdens and remaining uncertainty. In a fictional pair of equally sized lesions, proximity to a sensitive airway and a different approach can change feasibility. Depth alone is also insufficient: some deep lesions can be accessed, while a superficial lesion can have a difficult margin. Small diameter and a positive tracer scan settle none of the wider immune or outcome claims. Comparators can include systemic treatment alone, another local strategy, observation where appropriate or a study; include visits, recovery and additional sampling among the burdens. For a tracer and therapeutic product, establish the relationship between them rather than treating target uptake as a measured therapeutic dose. This review identifies missing facts and does not authorise treatment.

points.requirement: “Before or after immunotherapy?” sounds like one question. It can hide several different ones. Are we trying to relieve pain, prevent growth at a vulnerable site, lower local recurrence risk after surgery, or test whether local injury adds to a systemic response? Each goal has its own comparison, constraints and evidence.

points.requirement: [Ablation](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/ablation) and external [radiation therapy](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/radiation-therapy-basics) act at selected sites. They can have a useful local job even when an added immune effect is uncertain. Conversely, successful treatment of selected sites does not establish control of cancer elsewhere.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Surgery, ablation and external radiation address defined tissues, while systemically administered medicines and radiopharmaceuticals distribute more broadly. Regional delivery has an intermediate anatomical scope. Distribution, effective exposure and benefit are separate questions; neither local nor systemic is a guarantee of complete cellular coverage.

Local control, distant progression, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief should be measured separately. A null added-survival comparison does not make palliation irrelevant, and a controlled treated site does not establish control throughout the body. Compare the actual complete strategies rather than assuming that adding a local method always improves outcomes.
evidence.explanation: A useful site-directed effect and an uncertain wider immune effect can coexist; selected-site control is not whole-body control. Current field re-read and semantically compared. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Radiation transfers energy to tissue and can damage DNA directly or through reactive molecules. Cells can repair damage or lose their ability to keep dividing, and death can occur later. One treatment session is an exposure, rather than an immediate count of dead cells. Oxygen, cell state and repair affect the response.

External beams, brachytherapy sources and systemically distributed radiopharmaceuticals have different exposure patterns. An external-beam target can include tissue at risk of microscopic disease after surgery, even when no mass is visible. Planning and verification consider geometry, motion, normal organs and previous overlapping exposure. Precision does not eliminate normal-tissue dose or injury.

Absorbed dose in gray is energy per mass: one gray is one joule per kilogram. Total dose, fraction size, timing and exposed volume influence biological effects. Physical-dose arithmetic alone does not establish equivalence of schedules. Local or regional control, symptom relief, distant disease and survival remain distinct clinical outcomes.

points.requirement: These [oligometastatic and related setting labels](/wiki/education/concepts/breast-cancer/natural-history/oligometastatic-disease) describe patterns; each study supplies its own eligibility definition:

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Oligometastatic disease describes limited detected distant spread, under a specified clinical or study definition. It is a hypothesis that some limited patterns may be amenable to treatment directed at all visible sites; a few visible lesions do not prove a distinct biology or the absence of microscopic disease. Regional lymph nodes alone are not distant metastases.

The ESTRO-ASTRO consensus describes one to five lesions, with every site safely treatable, while acknowledging that there is no universally established maximum. A consensus definition is not proof of added benefit. Treatment decisions require the cancer setting, prior burden and treatment, comparator, endpoint, safety and the person's goals.
evidence.explanation: Limited detected spread, induced/residual disease after response and progressive subsets are different historical classifications, with study-specific eligibility and no benefit inferred from the count. Current field re-read and semantically compared. Retains inherited source assessment and its depth; no claim that every sentence in this field was freshly primary-verified. Current named teaching field was reread and compared semantically. Earlier source assessments retain their documented depth; citations and field presence alone do not re-certify every old assertion.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A few lit windows show what is detectable, not a census of every room. This analogy does not mean that every limited pattern conceals widespread disease. Synchronous metastases are detected near the initial diagnosis; metachronous metastases are detected later, with the interval defined by the author or protocol. Induced limited disease follows previously widespread disease and systemic treatment. Oligoprogression means a growing subset while other disease remains controlled during treatment. Limited residual or persistent disease means limited visible disease remains after treatment; specify whether it is stable or progressing. These labels are not universal synonyms.

points.requirement:
| Setting | What the label describes | What it leaves unanswered |
| Oligoprogressive disease | A limited set of sites grows while other disease remains controlled | Whether treating the growing sites improves outcomes or safely extends a systemic strategy |

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Oligoprogression describes limited progression within otherwise controlled metastatic disease during treatment. It is not restricted to one or two lesions or to targeted pills: the number, imaging rules and prior treatment depend on the definition being used. Oligometastatic disease describes limited detected distant spread, while limited residual disease describes what remains after treatment; retain the earlier burden and whether the remaining lesions are growing.

Treating progressing sites while continuing systemic therapy is a strategy to evaluate, rather than an automatic instruction. CURB tested adding stereotactic body radiation to standard care in lung and breast cohorts with different results. A current lesion count cannot establish benefit, safety or which systemic treatment should continue.
evidence.explanation: Limited progression with other disease controlled is retained without a fixed one-or-two rule or blanket instruction to continue a pill. evidence.supportingExcerpt: CURB was an open-label randomised phase 2 study after at least first-line systemic treatment, defining oligoprogression as at most five progressive lesions on CT or PET-CT. The prespecified lung cohort had median progression-free survival of 10.0 months with SBRT plus standard care versus 2.2 with standard care, hazard ratio 0.41, 95% confidence interval 0.22 to 0.75. The breast cohort had 4.4 versus 4.2 months, hazard ratio 0.78, interval 0.43 to 1.43. Failure to show a breast-cohort improvement does not establish an exact zero effect or a precise effect in every breast subtype. The intervention, comparator and harms must stay with the population.

points.requirement: External radiation is often divided into fractions, or treatment sessions. [Hypofractionation](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/hypofractionation) uses larger doses per fraction than a specified conventional comparator. Fewer sessions do not automatically make a course [stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT)](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/sbrt). Treatment volume, planning, normal-tissue constraints and the clinical evidence all matter.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Hypofractionation uses larger doses per fraction relative to a stated conventional comparison, commonly with fewer treatments. Keep total gray, dose per fraction, count, spacing, overall duration and treatment volume together. For equal fractions, total physical dose is the fraction count multiplied by dose per fraction; this arithmetic does not establish biological equivalence. Acceleration changes overall timing; a boost changes the dose to a selected region. Hypofractionation does not by itself identify stereotactic delivery.

Biological response depends on tissue, repair and timing, rather than total physical dose alone. Alpha/beta is a model parameter in gray describing fraction-size sensitivity. Under the linear-quadratic model and its assumptions, a lower ratio predicts greater sensitivity to fraction size at the same total physical dose. Historical teaching values near 10 gray for early effects and 3 for late effects are conventions, not universal constants. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for tumour control, with confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, with interval 2.3 to 4.5. Keep the model, endpoint and uncertainty.

START-B compared 50 gray in 25 fractions over five weeks with 40 in 15 over three weeks after surgery for early breast cancer, assessing local-regional relapse and late effects. FAST-Forward tested 40 gray in 15 fractions over three weeks against 27 or 26 in five over one week to the whole breast or chest wall. Its five-year report supported non-inferiority of 26 gray for breast relapse under the trial margin; 27 gray produced more normal-tissue effects. These results do not validate every five-visit course, nodal field, reirradiation plan or immune-priming schedule.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:

A biologically effective dose calculation compares modelled effects under assumptions; it does not document stereotactic localisation, motion management or verification. Modern non-stereotactic radiotherapy can also use imaging, conformal beams and motion assessment.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Surgery, ablation and external radiation address defined tissues, while systemically administered medicines and radiopharmaceuticals distribute more broadly. Regional delivery has an intermediate anatomical scope. Distribution, effective exposure and benefit are separate questions; neither local nor systemic is a guarantee of complete cellular coverage.

Local control, distant progression, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief should be measured separately. A null added-survival comparison does not make palliation irrelevant, and a controlled treated site does not establish control throughout the body. Compare the actual complete strategies rather than assuming that adding a local method always improves outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: NRG-BR002 tested adding ablation to first-line systemic therapy in breast cancer with at most four metastases, controlled primary disease, at most 12 months of first-line therapy without progression, and all visible sites amenable to SBRT or resection. Of 129 enrolled patients, 125 were eligible for analysis and 79% had HR-positive/HER2-negative disease. In the protocol-specified phase 2 go/no-go analysis with a December 20, 2021 data cutoff, median progression-free survival was 23.0 months without ablation and 19.5 months with it; the hazard ratio was 0.92, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.57 to 1.47 and stratified P = .42. Overall survival did not differ significantly and the study did not proceed to phase 3. This does not supply a definitive effect for every subtype or erase a separate symptom-relief goal.
