review.rationale: Eight later lessons were read end to end. Of ten originals, three were read in full, six through complete counterpart diffs and one reused by exact byte identity. The separate inventories retain 107 original and 84 later section signatures. All 412 frozen blocks were dispositioned: 286 substantive units, 285 represented at stated scope and one unsupported surgery-frequency clause, plus 126 explicit noncredit blocks. Of the represented units, 234 use registered draft-root fields and 51 depend on two unapplied PR-373 proposals. Twelve existing root owners change, with no new record or schema field. Twenty-one cited abstracts, one context-only abstract, 72 selected body passages in eight articles and selected official text retain their actual reading depths; no original paper was read end to end. Four whole native source images and six standalone Mermaid theme renders were viewed. Thirty-five actual root readers and two labelled in-memory peer proposals pass 263 field and 101 anchor checks. Actual JSON/Markdown/OpenAPI exports and 87 root Markdown anchors pass. Twenty-two existing short summaries are corrected without native-language approval; no missing entry is created. Full gates pass, with separately verified post-gate line-end-whitespace cleanup. No main, live, graph-integration, independent, expert or learner acceptance is created.

points.requirement: **You will learn to unpack a local-treatment proposal without turning a reading framework into a treatment recipe.** Start with [the evidence lesson](/wiki/education/local-treatment-modalities/03-overlap-and-sequencing), [ablation](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/ablation) and [radiation therapy](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/radiation-therapy-basics).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A local-treatment proposal needs five connected answers: the local and hoped-for wider outcomes with their measurements; evidence matching the cancer, disease history, complete strategy and comparator; access, intended coverage, margins, motion and nearby structures; actual exposure and normal-tissue risk; and alternatives, burdens and remaining uncertainty. In a fictional pair of equally sized lesions, proximity to a sensitive airway and a different approach can change feasibility. Depth alone is also insufficient: some deep lesions can be accessed, while a superficial lesion can have a difficult margin. Small diameter and a positive tracer scan settle none of the wider immune or outcome claims. Comparators can include systemic treatment alone, another local strategy, observation where appropriate or a study; include visits, recovery and additional sampling among the burdens. For a tracer and therapeutic product, establish the relationship between them rather than treating target uptake as a measured therapeutic dose. This review identifies missing facts and does not authorise treatment.
evidence.explanation: The five connected questions carry goal/measurement, matched evidence, access/coverage, exposure and alternatives/burden/uncertainty. A small lesion and positive tracer do not complete them or authorise treatment. points.requirement: A proposal may sound complete because it names a technology: “Freeze the lesion,” “use focused radiation,” or “send radiation to the target.” The name leaves out the goal, anatomy, comparison and risk. Good questions bring those missing pieces into view.

In a fictional pair of equally sized lesions, proximity to a sensitive airway and a different approach can change feasibility. Depth alone is also insufficient: some deep lesions can be accessed, while a superficial lesion can have a difficult margin. Small diameter and a positive tracer scan settle none of the wider immune or outcome claims. Comparators can include systemic treatment alone, another local strategy, observation where appropriate or a study; include visits, recovery and additional sampling among the burdens. For a tracer and therapeutic product, establish the relationship between them rather than treating target uptake as a measured therapeutic dose. This review identifies missing facts and does not authorise treatment.

points.requirement: A smaller treated lesion measures local activity. A response at untreated sites is a distant response. For radiation, response outside the irradiated field concerns a possible [abscopal effect](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/tumor-immunology/abscopal-effect); for ablation, name the procedure when describing a distant or abscopal-like response. Time without progression, survival, quality of life and harms are additional outcomes. A claim about one cannot silently stand in for the others.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Stereotactic body radiotherapy, also called SABR, uses specialised localisation, planning, positioning, image guidance and delivery to give a high dose per fraction to a body target outside the brain. A small number of visits does not establish that this delivery package was used. A biologically effective dose calculation compares modelled effects under assumptions; it does not document stereotactic localisation, motion management or verification. Modern non-stereotactic radiotherapy can also use imaging, conformal beams and motion assessment.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Planned exposure, verified delivery, local control and toxicity need their own measurements.

A 2010 prospective study concerned medically inoperable peripheral early-stage lung cancer and measured local control, distant failure and toxicity. That setting does not validate treatment of every central lesion or organ. CURB and NRG-BR002 tested different metastatic settings and comparisons. Local control, added progression-free or overall survival, symptom relief and an immune response are separate outcomes.

points.requirement: Size matters, but a single size cutoff is not universal across organs, devices, goals or protocols. An imageable lesion deep in the body can sometimes be accessible; a superficially located lesion can still have a difficult margin. “Only one lesion” and “under a certain diameter” are descriptions, not enough information to choose a tool. points.requirement: A visible treatment boundary is not necessarily the full lethal boundary. A probe's operating temperature is not the temperature throughout the tumor margin. Precise beam placement does not eliminate normal-tissue dose. A targeted radioactive drug does not eliminate normal-organ exposure. These shortcuts can make a proposal look more certain than its plan.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Freezing and thawing can injure cells through ice formation, osmotic changes and vascular injury. The historical mechanistic literature emphasises temperature, time, thawing and repetition; a probe setpoint is not exposure everywhere in the tissue. The visible frozen region and the lethal boundary need separate assessment.

Georgiades and colleagues studied normal renal tissue in swine. Measurements from six test animals found a mean nonlethal rim of 0.75 millimetres, with variation and widening near large vessels. Their proposed six-millimetre visible-ice margin for renal cancer was an extrapolation under stated assumptions, rather than a measured universal human margin.

Site, geometry, applicators and nearby structures affect feasibility and harm. Freezing, preserved material or local tissue destruction alone does not establish antigen presentation, useful immune priming or distant tumour control.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Stereotactic body radiotherapy, also called SABR, uses specialised localisation, planning, positioning, image guidance and delivery to give a high dose per fraction to a body target outside the brain. A small number of visits does not establish that this delivery package was used. A biologically effective dose calculation compares modelled effects under assumptions; it does not document stereotactic localisation, motion management or verification. Modern non-stereotactic radiotherapy can also use imaging, conformal beams and motion assessment.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Planned exposure, verified delivery, local control and toxicity need their own measurements.

A 2010 prospective study concerned medically inoperable peripheral early-stage lung cancer and measured local control, distant failure and toxicity. That setting does not validate treatment of every central lesion or organ. CURB and NRG-BR002 tested different metastatic settings and comparisons. Local control, added progression-free or overall survival, symptom relief and an immune response are separate outcomes.

points.requirement: **You will learn to ask what an imaging or tissue result actually measured before using it to explain a treatment response.** Start with [immunohistochemistry](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/pathology-readouts/immunohistochemistry), which stains selected proteins in tissue, and [bulk RNA sequencing](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/transcriptomics/bulk-rna-seq), which measures a sample's combined ribonucleic acid messages.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Measurement layers ask different questions. Anatomical imaging describes structure; tracer imaging depends on the stated product and its distribution; immunohistochemistry localises a protein in sampled tissue; bulk RNA pools captured messages; receptor sequencing describes recovered sequences and their sampled abundances; and controlled recognition or killing assays test a specified function under their conditions. RNA abundance is not accessible surface protein. Formenti's lung-cancer radiation-plus-ipilimumab study used clinical, blood-repertoire and selected functional readouts together; none is a universal immune-success marker or a substitute for the other measurements.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibody binding and signal development to show a selected protein in a prepared tissue section. Interpretation retains which cells and compartments stain, the intensity and distribution, and the named marker-specific method. A percentage, intensity category or composite score can describe different aspects of the result. Fixation, retrieval, controls, sampling and observer variation affect interpretation. Automated quantification also needs validation for its marker, specimens and intended use. A research stain or generic score does not replace a validated clinical selection assay.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Immuno-PET uses radiolabelled antibodies or antibody-derived binders. Full immunoglobulin G (IgG), antigen-binding fragments (Fab), minibodies and single-domain nanobodies differ in size and pharmacokinetics. The format can affect penetration, clearance, retention and normal-organ background; there is no universal best format. A label makes the binder traceable, not a perfect detector of every target site.

The radionuclide must suit the product's imaging time course. Dijkers' 89Zr-trastuzumab study examined a full antibody over several days; Keyaerts' 68Ga-HER2 nanobody study imaged at earlier times. These are product-specific examples. Antibody imaging can concern a tumour-associated target or immune cells. CD8 binder imaging belongs here; granzyme-B peptide or peptidomimetic imaging is a different tracer class and has its own record.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A tumour specimen can contain malignant, immune, stromal and normal cells. A difference in an aggregate molecular signal can reflect a changed mixture, changed expression within cells or both. That is different from a directly counted cell fraction or a density per sampled area, each of which also needs its denominator and sampled region.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Surgery, ablation and external radiation address defined tissues, while systemically administered medicines and radiopharmaceuticals distribute more broadly. Regional delivery has an intermediate anatomical scope. Distribution, effective exposure and benefit are separate questions; neither local nor systemic is a guarantee of complete cellular coverage.

Local control, distant progression, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief should be measured separately. A null added-survival comparison does not make palliation irrelevant, and a controlled treated site does not establish control throughout the body. Compare the actual complete strategies rather than assuming that adding a local method always improves outcomes.

| Approach | How exposure reaches tissue | What limits its reach | Main distinction |
| [Probe-based ablation](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/local-therapies/ablation), such as freezing or heating | Image-guided placement of one or more probes | Access, treatment-zone coverage, margins and nearby structures | Treats selected tissue; it does not physically treat every distant site |

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Image-guided thermal ablation includes radiofrequency current, microwave fields and cryoablation. The applicator changes tissue temperature; injury depends on exposure through space and time. Chemical ablation and membrane-disrupting electrical approaches belong to a broader ablation category and should be named separately. These methods differ from ionising radiation.

Planning considers access, the target and intended margin, blood flow and nearby structures. Neither a central reading nor a visible treatment zone proves lethal exposure throughout the target. A study’s lesion-size rule is not a universal physical ceiling. Treatment can injure normal tissue and may require further procedures; outpatient treatment, preserved function and unlimited repeatability are not guaranteed.

The reporting consensus separates technical coverage, technique efficacy at a defined follow-up and later local progression. The method, assessment, retreatments and complications belong with each result. Local control or symptom relief does not establish eradication of disease elsewhere or a systemic immune benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Radiation transfers energy to tissue and can damage DNA directly or through reactive molecules. Cells can repair damage or lose their ability to keep dividing, and death can occur later. One treatment session is an exposure, rather than an immediate count of dead cells. Oxygen, cell state and repair affect the response.

External beams, brachytherapy sources and systemically distributed radiopharmaceuticals have different exposure patterns. points.requirement: A fraction is a radiation treatment session. Hypofractionation describes dose per session relative to a specified conventional schedule. SBRT adds a particular approach to precise, high-dose treatment of a defined body target; session count alone cannot identify it.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Hypofractionation uses larger doses per fraction relative to a stated conventional comparison, commonly with fewer treatments. Keep total gray, dose per fraction, count, spacing, overall duration and treatment volume together. For equal fractions, total physical dose is the fraction count multiplied by dose per fraction; this arithmetic does not establish biological equivalence. Acceleration changes overall timing; a boost changes the dose to a selected region. Hypofractionation does not by itself identify stereotactic delivery.

Biological response depends on tissue, repair and timing, rather than total physical dose alone. Alpha/beta is a model parameter in gray describing fraction-size sensitivity. Under the linear-quadratic model and its assumptions, a lower ratio predicts greater sensitivity to fraction size at the same total physical dose. Historical teaching values near 10 gray for early effects and 3 for late effects are conventions, not universal constants. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for tumour control, with confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, with interval 2.3 to 4.5. Keep the model, endpoint and uncertainty.

START-B compared 50 gray in 25 fractions over five weeks with 40 in 15 over three weeks after surgery for early breast cancer, assessing local-regional relapse and late effects. FAST-Forward tested 40 gray in 15 fractions over three weeks against 27 or 26 in five over one week to the whole breast or chest wall. Its five-year report supported non-inferiority of 26 gray for breast relapse under the trial margin; 27 gray produced more normal-tissue effects. These results do not validate every five-visit course, nodal field, reirradiation plan or immune-priming schedule.

The linear-quadratic model expresses the surviving cell fraction after dose d as exp(-alpha × d - beta × d squared). The alpha/beta ratio is a parameter in gray for a specified tissue and endpoint. At fixed total physical dose, a lower ratio gives fraction size greater weight. Historical teaching values near ten gray for many tumours and early-responding tissues such as skin and mucosa, and three for late normal-tissue effects, are conventions rather than constants for every tumour or organ. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for breast tumour control, with 95% confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, interval 2.3 to 4.5. The trialists interpreted these estimates as similar fraction-size sensitivity for breast cancer and its dose-limiting normal tissues.

The basic equal-fraction calculation assumes equal effects per fraction and complete repair between fractions and does not include overall treatment time. Extrapolation to a large fraction size or prolonged irradiation needs assessment; a model calculation alone validates neither the pattern nor clinical equivalence.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
The linear-quadratic model expresses the surviving cell fraction after dose d as exp(-alpha × d - beta × d squared). The alpha/beta ratio is a parameter in gray for a specified tissue and endpoint. At fixed total physical dose, a lower ratio gives fraction size greater weight. Historical teaching values near ten gray for many tumours and early-responding tissues such as skin and mucosa, and three for late normal-tissue effects, are conventions rather than constants for every tumour or organ. A planned START-A/pilot meta-analysis estimated 4.6 gray for breast tumour control, with 95% confidence interval 1.1 to 8.1, and 3.4 for late photographic breast change, interval 2.3 to 4.5. The trialists interpreted these estimates as similar fraction-size sensitivity for breast cancer and its dose-limiting normal tissues.

The basic equal-fraction calculation assumes equal effects per fraction and complete repair between fractions and does not include overall treatment time. Too short an interval or slow repair can violate that assumption. Extrapolation to a large fraction size or prolonged irradiation needs assessment; a model calculation alone validates neither the pattern nor clinical equivalence.

The target, motion, dose distribution, positioning uncertainty, prior overlapping radiation and normal-organ constraints determine the coverage problem. Dose falls through space rather than stopping at a drawn line. There is no universal one-centimetre safe boundary, lesion-size ceiling or prescription that applies to every organ. Planned exposure, verified delivery, local control and toxicity need their own measurements.

A 2010 prospective study concerned medically inoperable peripheral early-stage lung cancer and measured local control, distant failure and toxicity. Local control, added progression-free or overall survival, symptom relief and an immune response are separate outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Antigen-processing machinery (APM) is the set of proteins that generate, transport and load peptides onto HLA. A common class I route has five steps. (1) The proteasome cuts intracellular proteins into fragments, which can create a useful peptide or destroy it. (2) The transporter associated with antigen processing, TAP1 with TAP2, moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum; Shepherd et al. (1993) showed in a cell-free system that TAP1 is part of an ATP-dependent, sequence-selective peptide translocator. (3) ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim amino acids from the front end. York et al. (2002) found that ERAP1 can enhance or limit presentation by trimming epitopes to 8 to 9 residues, and Saveanu et al. (2005) found complementary human ERAP1 and ERAP2 activity, so more expression does not universally improve display. A class I HLA heavy chain assembles with beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a peptide, with helpers such as tapasin. (4) Stable peptide-HLA complexes reach the surface; the peptide stays held by HLA. (5) A compatible T-cell receptor on a conventional CD8 T cell may recognise the pair; recognition is a separate gate and display alone does not show killing.

Class II HLA commonly loads peptides in vesicles that process acquired proteins. An invariant chain protects the new groove and directs it there; after cutting, a remaining fragment is exchanged for other peptides with help from HLA-DM, and conventional CD4 T cells inspect these displays. Cross-presentation lets externally acquired material reach class I. The scheme is a common route, not a rule for every peptide.

A cancer cell may keep an altered protein and still show little of its peptide, and a shared processing defect can affect several targets at once, so adding candidate peptides does not bypass the bottleneck. Low expression, gene loss and a functional defect are different findings: a weak RNA signal does not prove deletion. Interferon gamma can increase presentation machinery when its signalling pathway and the required genes are intact, and cannot replace a deleted B2M or HLA gene. Sucker et al. (2017) described melanoma lesions in which JAK1 or JAK2 defects gave interferon-gamma resistance and evolved into HLA class I negative, T-cell-resistant lesions with antigen-presentation genes silenced and no longer inducible. Zaretsky et al. (2016) found, in biopsies from patients with acquired resistance to PD-1 blockade, JAK1 or JAK2 loss of function in two of four patients and a truncating B2M mutation with lost surface class I in a third. These are melanoma observations, not treatment-benefit evidence.

Evidence layers differ. DNA sequence and copy number show gene retention or alteration but not expression or function; RNA shows sampled gene activity but not protein, assembly or display; protein staining or flow cytometry detects protein but not which peptide is shown; HLA-associated peptide recovery shows a peptide was recovered with HLA in that preparation but not its cell of origin or recognition; controlled T-cell recognition shows function against tested targets. Peptide loading can bypass processing, so rescue by supplied peptide supports a bottleneck under those conditions only. Binding prediction is not presentation, and CD4 help is not proof of CD8 tumour recognition.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:

points.requirement: Do not infer universal superiority of freezing over heating from antigen-preservation arguments. The BOOSTER lung-cancer report claims, from a subgroup analysis, that cryoablation (13 patients) gave longer progression-free survival than thermal ablation (31 patients). Its randomization compared ablation with no ablation, so the freeze-versus-heat comparison is nonrandomized and small; it generates a hypothesis rather than a ranking. Do not equate higher dose with greater immune learning. Do not assume an [immune-checkpoint inhibitor](/wiki/education/concepts/therapeutics/immunotherapy/immune-checkpoint-inhibitor) repairs every missing recognition step. Compare complete strategies in matching populations rather than ranking tools by a single mechanism.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: BOOSTER randomised 65 selected patients with residual advanced lung cancer after checkpoint treatment, rather than the planned 137; its primary analysis included 42 with ablation and twenty without. The report separately gives a randomisation-clock analysis of 17.1 versus 4.4 months. These clocks cannot be exchanged when comparing headlines. The physician selected freezing or heating: the abstract says thirteen cryoablation and 31 thermal-ablation patients, whereas Figure 3 and the discussion say thirteen and 29 among the 42 analysed. The discussion also notes larger lesions in the thermal group and no correction for multiple comparisons. This internally discrepant, exploratory comparison does not establish universal superiority of freezing or an immune-optimal modality.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Clinical-trial phases describe development purposes rather than a fixed sample size, assignment method or promise of benefit. Phase 1 studies administration, exposure, safety and dosage, sometimes with early activity measures. Phase 2 asks whether activity and safety support further study in a specified population. Phase 3 compares with a defined alternative and can provide evidence for an approval decision; a phase 3 label is not itself approval. FDA's patient overview illustrates phase 3 with hundreds to thousands of participants, while the actual size follows the protocol's question and information requirements. Phase 4 studies an approved treatment in broader use. Read the protocol because phases can overlap or be combined.

review.rationale: Eight later lessons were read end to end. Of ten originals, three were read in full, six through complete counterpart diffs and one reused by exact byte identity. The separate inventories retain 107 original and 84 later section signatures. All 412 frozen blocks were dispositioned: 286 substantive units, 285 represented at stated scope and one unsupported surgery-frequency clause, plus 126 explicit noncredit blocks. Of the represented units, 234 use registered draft-root fields and 51 depend on two unapplied PR-373 proposals. Twelve existing root owners change, with no new record or schema field. Twenty-one cited abstracts, one context-only abstract, 72 selected body passages in eight articles and selected official text retain their actual reading depths; no original paper was read end to end. Four whole native source images and six standalone Mermaid theme renders were viewed. Thirty-five actual root readers and two labelled in-memory peer proposals pass 263 field and 101 anchor checks. Actual JSON/Markdown/OpenAPI exports and 87 root Markdown anchors pass. Twenty-two existing short summaries are corrected without native-language approval; no missing entry is created. Full gates pass, with separately verified post-gate line-end-whitespace cleanup. No main, live, graph-integration, independent, expert or learner acceptance is created.

points.requirement: **Explain what local treatment can control, how immune learning might follow and what evidence supports an added clinical benefit.**

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Surgery, ablation and external radiation address defined tissues, while systemically administered medicines and radiopharmaceuticals distribute more broadly. Regional delivery has an intermediate anatomical scope. Distribution, effective exposure and benefit are separate questions; neither local nor systemic is a guarantee of complete cellular coverage.

Local control, distant progression, progression-free survival, overall survival and symptom relief should be measured separately. A null added-survival comparison does not make palliation irrelevant, and a controlled treated site does not establish control throughout the body. Compare the actual complete strategies rather than assuming that adding a local method always improves outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The strategy uses relevant tumour antigens in place while supporting presenting cells and immune activation. points.requirement: 4. Delivery matters. A probe, externally aimed beams and a radioactive drug distributed through the blood do not provide the same exposure or risks.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Delivery can be compared without ranking treatments. A fictional probe card controls a selected liver site, a beam card specifies a lung volume and motion assessment, and a radioactive-drug card requires distribution, retention and organ dosimetry. points.requirement: A finite blood tube is not a survey of every tumour cell; retain specimen and input qualifications.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.
evidence.explanation: Finite evaluated plasma and sample/input qualifications explicitly prevent an all-body cell census. Source scope: Complete Moss abstract and targeted workflow guidance; definitions and finite-sample scope, without certifying older product or collection claims.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Method card: measures selected features of plasma DNA by a stated sequencing or molecular method, from a finite plasma aliquot that testing consumes. Output is detected or not detected, variant fractions, molecule concentrations or model estimates, each with its own unit. It cannot give an all-body cell count, lesion location, viability or treatment benefit, and validity belongs to the exact specimen, assay version and intended use.
evidence.explanation: Finite evaluated plasma and sample/input qualifications explicitly prevent an all-body cell census. Source scope: Re-read existing method card against targeted workflow and intended-use requirements, not a new measured sensitivity.

points.requirement: Define post-treatment molecular residual disease as an assay-defined signal; detection alone neither locates disease nor selects an effective intervention.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Residual-disease testing asks whether a qualifying disease signal is present after treatment in a specified sample. For solid tumours, plasma assays can look for selected tumour-associated DNA features, with results interpreted under their specimen, input, target and calling rules. Analytical detection, clinical detection in a population and recurrence association are different performance questions. A valid negative does not establish absence of every cancer cell.

Clinical usefulness belongs to a defined strategy: the cancer setting, assay, timing, triggering result, action and comparator. Evidence for genotyping, an approved indication or a strategy in another cancer does not automatically settle an early-breast-cancer question. The dated trial examples below retain their studied populations. More frequent detection, molecular clearance or favourable prognosis in treated negative groups does not by itself show improved patient outcomes or safe treatment omission.
evidence.explanation: The signal is assay-defined after treatment; neither its location nor a useful action follows from detection alone. Source scope: Assay-defined residual signal, evidence stages and context-specific utility; complete ESMO abstract and targeted FDA text, not every older trial statement.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A tumour-informed test uses a sampled tumour reference to select features for later tracking in plasma. The reference can come from a suitable biopsy or resection; it is not necessarily a surgically removed whole tumour or a complete inventory of tumour clones. Reference quality, selected targets, plasma input, background and the calling rule affect performance. A fixed list can miss features outside it, including variants that emerge after the reference was sampled.

A tumour-naive or tumour-agnostic method uses predefined features without first building that person's tumour reference. It still needs suitable input and a validated detector, and it does not promise a complete mutation profile. FDA's November 2024 drug-development guidance describes strengths and limits of both approaches rather than a universal ranking. Santonja's same-sample breast-cancer comparison supports its particular assays at low signal, not every branded product. Magbanua's 2025 study also found retained assay variants in sampled resistant tumours from some patients with negative plasma; a negative draw does not by itself prove that the reference targets disappeared.
evidence.explanation: The specimen approach is separated from three test jobs; combined methods remain possible. Source scope: Reference design, targeted comparative-assay findings and resistant-tumour observations at their named study scope.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Separate three test jobs. Tumour-informed monitoring asks whether selected known tumour features reached the plasma sample; it need not discover new variants outside that list. Reference-free monitoring asks whether a qualifying cancer-associated signal is present without prior tumour sequencing; it need not return a complete genomic profile. Plasma genomic profiling asks which covered alterations are detectable; it does not automatically have a dedicated low-signal monitoring assay's sensitivity. Real methods can combine features. Methylation and fragment-pattern analysis need not produce a mutation list, and a captured circulating tumour cell is a cell, a different object from cell-free DNA fragments.
evidence.explanation: The specimen approach is separated from three test jobs; combined methods remain possible. Source scope: Method-scope comparison based on targeted FDA passages and the complete raw NCI cell definition. It makes no category-wide sensitivity ranking.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The blank, detection and quantitation limits answer different questions. The blank limit is the highest apparent analyte concentration expected from replicate samples with no analyte; the detection limit is the lowest concentration reliably distinguished from that background; the quantitation limit is the lowest concentration meeting predefined bias and imprecision goals (Armbruster and Pry, 2008). Quantitation and detection limits may coincide or differ. A qualifying detection below a validated quantitative range supports presence more strongly than an exact fold change. For a read-based variant allele fraction, the denominator is informative reads covering that locus, not cancer cells or plasma volume; keep a molecule-based method's own definition instead.
evidence.explanation: Applicable analytical criteria remain beside the number, with their different questions explained. Source scope: Complete Armbruster/Pry abstract and the already assessed read-based VAF definition; molecule-based methods retain their own denominator.

points.requirement: Acquired clonal blood-cell mutations can contribute plasma DNA; check tumour-versus-blood origin with method-specific white-cell sensitivity and coverage, without calling it a perfect certificate.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Source attribution in plasma, interpretation rule: TP53 is a tumour gene and also a therapy-selected blood-cell gene, so a TP53 variant in plasma after chemotherapy can come from either compartment. Matched white-blood-cell DNA and the tumour's variant list, where available, help assess its origin; some variants remain ambiguous. In Razavi's paired sequencing 53.2% of cfDNA mutations in 124 people with metastatic cancer and 81.6% in 47 controls without cancer had features of clonal haematopoiesis, and variants that could not be separated from white-blood-cell DNA kept an explicit ambiguous category, so subtracting every blood match is not a complete attribution method.

Source scope: Complete primary abstract confirms 124/47 and 53.2%/81.6%; earlier explicit ambiguous-category assessment is retained, not a perfect subtraction rule.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Fictional example: a plasma assay detects a variant that sensitive matched blood-cell sequencing finds at 0.8% VAF. The blood result supports a blood-cell contribution even below the 2% cut-off, but it does not make the variant CHIP or exclude a tumour contribution, because tumour evidence, shared variants and each method's limits still apply. Matched sequencing has its own gene coverage, depth and detection rules, so a clone below its sensitivity can stay unseen, and a clone finding is not a leukaemia diagnosis or a solid-tumour treatment instruction.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A gene name does not settle a plasma variant's source. Shah and colleagues found TP53 to be the most frequently mutated gene in their 2012 primary triple-negative breast-cancer cohort; Bolton's 2020 study found that radiation, platinum and topoisomerase II inhibitor exposure selected blood-cell clones with TP53 and other DNA-damage-response mutations. Those are different populations and compartments. A tumour reference and a matched blood-cell comparison help answer different questions, each within its own coverage and sensitivity. A newly confirmed tumour alteration can also reflect evolution rather than a blood-cell clone or technical noise.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A tumour-informed test uses a sampled tumour reference to select features for later tracking in plasma. The reference can come from a suitable biopsy or resection; it is not necessarily a surgically removed whole tumour or a complete inventory of tumour clones. Reference quality, selected targets, plasma input, background and the calling rule affect performance. A fixed list can miss features outside it, including variants that emerge after the reference was sampled.

A tumour-naive or tumour-agnostic method uses predefined features without first building that person's tumour reference. It still needs suitable input and a validated detector, and it does not promise a complete mutation profile. FDA's November 2024 drug-development guidance describes strengths and limits of both approaches rather than a universal ranking. Santonja's same-sample breast-cancer comparison supports its particular assays at low signal, not every branded product. Magbanua's 2025 study also found retained assay variants in sampled resistant tumours from some patients with negative plasma; a negative draw does not by itself prove that the reference targets disappeared.
evidence.explanation: Evolution is a possible tumour explanation, and a fixed old target list can miss newly emerged features. Source scope: Reference design, targeted comparative-assay findings and resistant-tumour observations at their named study scope.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) can be reported as a concentration, as a fraction, or as a yes or no call, and the three are not interchangeable. A concentration counts tumour-attributed molecules in a stated volume of plasma. One example is mean tumour molecules per millilitre (MTM/mL), which the I-SPY 2 breast-cancer study of Magbanua and colleagues used for ctDNA across tracked variants. A fraction divides tumour-attributed molecules by a stated total, such as all evaluated alleles at one position (variant allele fraction, VAF) or all evaluated DNA (an estimated tumour fraction). Parts per million (PPM) is a fraction multiplied by one million, so the number is only as meaningful as the fraction it scales: 0.01% is 100 PPM, and 0.00024% is 2.4 PPM, the lowest allele fraction Santonja and colleagues reported for ctDNA detection in breast cancer.

Concentration and fraction can move apart. If two equal one-millilitre aliquots each hold the same number of tumour molecules but one holds more background cell-free DNA, the concentration is unchanged and the fraction falls. A detection call and a reliable amount are also different claims, because the detection limit and the quantitation range are validated separately. Nothing here gives a conversion between assays: MTM/mL cannot be turned into PPM from the printed result, and a VAF of 100 PPM at one variant is not a tumour fraction of 100 PPM.
evidence.explanation: Fraction, shedding, background and tumour volume are kept separate; uncertainty remains attached. Source scope: Previously assessed quantity definitions re-read in full; no new primary verification of every retained assay example.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Residual-disease testing asks whether a qualifying disease signal is present after treatment in a specified sample. For solid tumours, plasma assays can look for selected tumour-associated DNA features, with results interpreted under their specimen, input, target and calling rules. Analytical detection, clinical detection in a population and recurrence association are different performance questions. A valid negative does not establish absence of every cancer cell.

Clinical usefulness belongs to a defined strategy: the cancer setting, assay, timing, triggering result, action and comparator. Evidence for genotyping, an approved indication or a strategy in another cancer does not automatically settle an early-breast-cancer question. The dated trial examples below retain their studied populations. More frequent detection, molecular clearance or favourable prognosis in treated negative groups does not by itself show improved patient outcomes or safe treatment omission.
evidence.explanation: A valid negative means no qualifying signal under evaluated conditions and does not establish absence of all cancer. Source scope: Assay-defined residual signal, evidence stages and context-specific utility; complete ESMO abstract and targeted FDA text, not every older trial statement.

evidence.explanation: The named 4,500/about-15-ng input and 0.01% conditional Poisson model are present; allele/genome assumptions and multi-target calling are explicit. Source scope: Exact named input rechecked in targeted primary text; not the whole retained fragment-size and genome-mass note.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional model, an evaluated aliquot supplies 4,500 independent amplifiable opportunities at one locus, each with a target-allele probability of 1 in 10,000. The expected target count is 0.45. If target counts follow a Poisson distribution, the chance of no target is exp(-0.45), 63.8%. Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.
evidence.explanation: The named 4,500/about-15-ng input and 0.01% conditional Poisson model are present; allele/genome assumptions and multi-target calling are explicit. Source scope: Conditional Poisson arithmetic: independent loci, retained-target calling, target-allele probability and copy-number assumptions are explicit, not a clinical false-negative rate.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A worked limit: for multiplex PCR across 21 to 47 patient-specific structural variants on 4,500 amplifiable copies, the theoretical limit is 1 / (4,500 x variants), which is 1 in 211,500, or 4.7 parts per million, at 47 variants. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Analytical detection and clinical sensitivity answer different questions. FDA diagnostic-test guidance dated March 2007 defines clinical sensitivity by the proportion testing positive among people who have the specified condition, judged against the reference standard in the intended-use population. In a residual-disease study, disease definition, follow-up, draw schedule, evaluable samples and recurrence sites shape that denominator. An analytical limit measured in prepared material does not supply that clinical proportion, and a negative test does not establish absence of cancer.
evidence.explanation: Analytical detection is distinguished from clinical sensitivity under a population, reference, sites and sampling schedule. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.
evidence.explanation: The complete equal-volume fictional extraction example shows why total cfDNA yield does not measure tumour burden. Source scope: Complete Moss abstract and targeted workflow guidance; definitions and finite-sample scope, without certifying older product or collection claims.

points.requirement: Selected blood features may pool more than one source but do not localise origin; low shedding and finite input can miss a tumour.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.
evidence.explanation: A pooled finite blood signal neither localises origin nor guarantees tumour sampling; shedding and input limits remain visible. Source scope: Complete Moss abstract and targeted workflow guidance; definitions and finite-sample scope, without certifying older product or collection claims.

points.requirement: Verify the 84-person high-risk neoadjuvant I-SPY2 pilot and serial blood/MRI functional tumour volume; define the protocol-specific contrast-based volume.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assay looks for tumour-associated features in a finite sample of cell-free DNA. How much tumour DNA reaches the sampled blood varies between lesions, and recovery, background DNA, the features tracked and the assay's detection limit all shape the call. Imaging measures a defined region through a physical signal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can report contrast enhancement or the volume of enhancing tissue, which is not a direct count of viable cancer cells. The two tests can therefore differ without either being wrong, and neither automatically replaces the other.

They can also share information. In Magbanua and colleagues' pilot of 84 women having neoadjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, ctDNA concentration was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at all four time points, with Spearman correlations of 0.42 to 0.49, and patients with detectable ctDNA had a higher median volume. Agreement was partial, and adding ctDNA early in treatment to volume-based prediction of pathological complete response gave only a numerical gain that was not statistically significant. ctDNA positivity after treatment added significantly to volume for predicting distant recurrence and death. A mismatch calls for checking dates, assay limits, the imaged region and the exact finding. It does not by itself show a false test or hidden metastatic disease.
evidence.explanation: The named 84-person high-risk pilot, serial measurements and its protocol-specific contrast-defined FTV are present; neither a general volume standard nor an independent strategy trial. Source scope: Complete primary abstract and targeted cohort/methods paragraphs; limited 84-person pilot and partial association, not clinical utility.

points.requirement: Correlated/complementary prognostic information is not a universal blood-to-volume conversion or evidence that using the pair changes survival.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) assay looks for tumour-associated features in a finite sample of cell-free DNA. How much tumour DNA reaches the sampled blood varies between lesions, and recovery, background DNA, the features tracked and the assay's detection limit all shape the call. Imaging measures a defined region through a physical signal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can report contrast enhancement or the volume of enhancing tissue, which is not a direct count of viable cancer cells. The two tests can therefore differ without either being wrong, and neither automatically replaces the other.

They can also share information. In Magbanua and colleagues' pilot of 84 women having neoadjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, ctDNA concentration was correlated with MRI functional tumour volume at all four time points, with Spearman correlations of 0.42 to 0.49, and patients with detectable ctDNA had a higher median volume. Agreement was partial, and adding ctDNA early in treatment to volume-based prediction of pathological complete response gave only a numerical gain that was not statistically significant. ctDNA positivity after treatment added significantly to volume for predicting distant recurrence and death. A mismatch calls for checking dates, assay limits, the imaged region and the exact finding. It does not by itself show a false test or hidden metastatic disease.
evidence.explanation: Partial correlation and prognostic improvement do not supply a universal conversion or evidence for changing a treatment strategy. Source scope: Complete primary abstract and targeted cohort/methods paragraphs; limited 84-person pilot and partial association, not clinical utility.

points.requirement: Negative blood does not establish a scan finding as dead tissue.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Four patterns illustrate the reading boundary. A smaller lesion and lower detected blood signal mean that both recorded measures fell in their own units, not that pCR or eradication of distant disease is proved. A residual scan finding with undetected blood leaves viability, treatment effects and other causes unresolved. Detected blood with no suspicious finding in the scanned region does not establish the signal's location, full extent or best intervention. If neither shows qualifying evidence, neither has proved zero microscopic disease or justified omitting indicated treatment. These are interpretation examples, not an action algorithm; disagreement alone does not establish pseudoprogression.
evidence.explanation: An abnormal region with undetected blood is explicitly not established as dead tissue. Source scope: Four premise-backed interpretation examples about different measurements. points.requirement: Verify c-TRAK TN population and denominators: 23 of 32 intervention-allocated people had metastases on staging, five began pembrolizumab and none achieved sustained clearance.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: c-TRAK TN (NCT03145961) registered 208 patients between January 2018 and December 2019 with early triple-negative breast cancer and residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy or stage II to III disease treated with adjuvant chemotherapy; 185 had tumour sequencing, 171 (92.4 percent) had trackable mutations and 161 entered digital PCR ctDNA surveillance every three months for 12 months (18 if samples were missed during the pandemic). ctDNA-positive patients were randomised 2 to 1 to intervention (staging scans, then pembrolizumab for a year if free of recurrence) or blinded observation; a September 2020 amendment closed the observation group. ctDNA was detected in 27.3 percent by 12 months (44 of 161; 95 percent confidence interval 20.6 to 34.9) and seven patients relapsed without prior ctDNA detection. Of 32 patients allocated to intervention, 72 percent (23) already had metastases on staging and four declined pembrolizumab; of the five who started it, none achieved sustained ctDNA clearance, so the second co-primary endpoint was not met. The authors emphasised earlier and more sensitive or frequent testing as implications for future study design. The trial did not demonstrate that those changes, or a ctDNA-triggered intervention, improve survival.
evidence.explanation: The 23/32 staging denominator, five treated people and absent sustained clearance remain tied to the early-TNBC design. Source scope: Complete raw primary abstract, preserving surveillance, intervention-allocated, staged and treated denominators and the design amendment.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a ctDNA monitoring study, lead time is the date of a defined later event, such as confirmed clinical recurrence, minus the date of the first qualifying positive blood sample. The definition needs rules: whether recurrence means imaging, pathology or symptoms, whether the blood date is collection or reporting, whether a positive result triggered an extra scan, and whether treatment began on the signal. Blood draws and scans are both intermittent, so the observed gap reflects both schedules. A negative draw at month 3 and a first positive at month 6 do not locate when the signal began.

points.requirement: Integrate specimen origin, target scope, quantities, imaging/tissue distinction and detection-versus-action evidence without extra independent science credit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.
evidence.explanation: Derived overview integrates chapter teaching on source, scope, quantity, tissue and evidence stages; no additional independent science credit. Source scope: Complete Moss abstract and targeted workflow guidance; definitions and finite-sample scope, without certifying older product or collection claims.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Separate three test jobs. Tumour-informed monitoring asks whether selected known tumour features reached the plasma sample; it need not discover new variants outside that list. Reference-free monitoring asks whether a qualifying cancer-associated signal is present without prior tumour sequencing; it need not return a complete genomic profile. Plasma genomic profiling asks which covered alterations are detectable; it does not automatically have a dedicated low-signal monitoring assay's sensitivity. Real methods can combine features. Methylation and fragment-pattern analysis need not produce a mutation list, and a captured circulating tumour cell is a cell, a different object from cell-free DNA fragments.
evidence.explanation: Derived overview integrates chapter teaching on source, scope, quantity, tissue and evidence stages; no additional independent science credit. Source scope: Method-scope comparison based on targeted FDA passages and the complete raw NCI cell definition. It makes no category-wide sensitivity ranking.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Consider a fictional assay estimating tumour fraction at 6 parts per million (PPM) and then 2 PPM. Both samples are called detected, but the second is below the assay's reliable quantitation range. The printed estimates fall by two-thirds; they do not establish that the cancer volume fell by two-thirds. Retain the qualifying calls and uncertainty, because shedding and background DNA can change the signal. A second method reporting molecules per millilitre cannot simply be placed on this fraction scale. Even a matching unit label does not establish matching calibration. Keeping serial methods and input comparable helps interpretation without removing biological variation.
evidence.explanation: Derived overview integrates chapter teaching on source, scope, quantity, tissue and evidence stages; no additional independent science credit. Source scope: Fictional 6-to-2 arithmetic with explicitly qualified quantitative range; interpretation of different quantities, not a measured tumour-volume result.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The two-window comparison is about scope. A finite plasma aliquot contains extracellular DNA, of which tumour-derived fragments may be one part; breast MRI observes regional, sequence-dependent features rather than individual cancer cells. Contrast enhancement reflects vascular and contrast-delivery behaviour as well as the acquisition protocol; it is not a one-to-one viable-cell count. In the 84-person I-SPY2 MRI pilot, functional tumour volume summed voxels meeting 70% enhancement about two and a half minutes after contrast, inside a manually drawn box around the lesion. A camera-and-stream analogy illustrates those two sampled views without promising that every tumour sheds DNA. Keep the imaging method visible: mammography uses X-rays, ultrasound uses sound, and PET/CT combines tracer-distribution images with anatomical CT images. A formal response category needs its framework, comparison timepoint and findings outside a selected lesion measurement. None of these measurements is an interchangeable all-body tumour-cell number.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional model, an evaluated aliquot supplies 4,500 independent amplifiable opportunities at one locus, each with a target-allele probability of 1 in 10,000. The expected target count is 0.45. If target counts follow a Poisson distribution, the chance of no target is exp(-0.45), 63.8%. Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.

points.requirement: Verify the Annals of Oncology 84-person high-risk mixed-subtype neoadjuvant study, serial sampling and up-to-16-mutation tumour-informed design; keep it distinct from the companion MRI paper.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
This retrospective analysis used samples collected prospectively in I-SPY2 from 84 high-risk early breast-cancer patients receiving standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without the AKT inhibitor MK-2206. The cohort included hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, HER2-positive and triple-negative disease. Personalised panels tracked up to 16 mutations from pretreatment tumour sequencing. Blood collection was planned before treatment, three weeks after starting paclitaxel, between chemotherapy blocks and after chemotherapy before surgery. The analysis used 291 of 336 potential plasma samples; availability differed by draw.

The authors reported ctDNA detection in 61 of 84 at baseline (73%), followed by 35%, 14% and 9% at successive draws. These are not four proportions with a common denominator of 84. In the joint post-treatment pathology and outcome analysis of 60 patients, all 17 with the specified pathological complete response were ctDNA-negative. Among 43 without that response, the six ctDNA-positive patients had greater distant-recurrence risk than the 37 negative patients: hazard ratio 10.4, 95% confidence interval 2.3 to 46.6. Comparing ctDNA-negative non-pCR patients with pCR patients gave hazard ratio 1.4, interval 0.15 to 13.5; that wide interval does not establish equivalence. Median survival follow-up was 4.8 years. This assay analysis did not randomise a blood-guided treatment strategy.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Complete abstract plus targeted methods, availability and 60-person joint-analysis paragraphs. The exact final-draw denominator for the reported 9% remains unverified.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The assay required at least two detected somatic variants for a positive call and selected 12 to 16 targets per person, with a median of 16. A fixed personalised panel is therefore neither a complete tumour genome nor a one-molecule guarantee. The four blood collection moments and the available specimens belong beside each reported percentage; the joint 60-person analysis is a separate denominator from the whole cohort of 84. The MRI companion report asks how blood and functional tumour volume relate, rather than supplying another independent treatment-strategy trial.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Targeted assay methods and joint-analysis passages plus complete abstracts. The 60-person joint analysis differs from the 84-person parent cohort; the MRI report is a companion analysis.

points.requirement: 2. [Human leukocyte antigen (HLA)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/antigen-presentation/hla) displays fragments; a [T-cell receptor (TCR)](/wiki/education/concepts/immunology/t-cells/t-cell-receptor) recognizes the fragment together with its holder.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.
evidence.explanation: HLA displays peptide and a conventional alpha-beta receptor recognises the combined surface. The qualification avoids extending this route to every T-cell family. Conventional alpha-beta peptide-HLA recognition is the scope; this is not asserted of every T-cell receptor family. Only the first paragraph is used; the allele census and later study figures are outside this proof. Exact named field passage reread and semantically compared. evidence.supportingExcerpt: A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. evidence.supportingExcerpt: RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

Its outputs and evaluation depend on the task, training data and model version. scGen combined variational autoencoders with latent-space vector arithmetic and was reported to model perturbation and infection responses across cell types, studies and species, having noted that generalisation to phenomena absent from training data had not previously been shown (Lotfollahi and colleagues, 2019). A 2025 benchmark found that none of five single-cell foundation models and two other deep-learning models predicted transcriptome changes after single or double gene perturbations better than deliberately simple baselines; for most genes the predictions of scGPT, UCE and scBERT did not vary across perturbations, and those of GEARS and scFoundation varied considerably less than the observed values (Ahlmann-Eltze and colleagues, 2025). An AI virtual cell is described as a multi-scale, multi-modal large neural network model in a perspective that sets priorities for accelerating discoveries and guiding experiments, not a validation (Bunne and colleagues, 2024).

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Reading guide (OnCo inference). The task defines what an output means: filling a missing RNA value from an image, estimating a drug response and predicting a gene-disruption response are different tasks, and success at one does not validate another. review.rationale: Four original and five later nonpersonal versions retain 46/55 actual section signatures. All five later bodies, two relocated original bodies and two complete original-to-later diffs were read. All 305 frozen source blocks have explicit clause dispositions, including 83 noncredit blocks. Two interval-level clauses remain source-open; 39 distinct complete units depend on one unapplied PR-371 proposal. Nineteen complete abstracts and 61 selected body passages in ten papers, eleven official/news paragraphs and one whole typeset page are the fresh source depth, not whole-source reads. A named recurrent-glioblastoma randomized trial corrects the broad no-solid-tumour-benefit claim; it does not validate another assay or breast/postoperative use. Six native theme views of three inline Mermaid codes were viewed. Eight existing root owners change without new IDs, aliases, relations, schema or artwork. Actual SSR, static exports and full gates pass. No main/live, independent, expert, learner or language approval is created. Targeted source-residual pass: exact source identities and all selected section signatures reproduce. Three delivery requirements per pin close through actual primary gate/time-course figures and appendix text. Frank's specified stem-cell model, Magbanua's final-draw denominator and Ladan's confidence-interval level/method remain explicitly open. Other assessments and their reading depth are retained; this is not a fresh whole-lesson or whole-paper acceptance.

points.requirement: **A model response earns a clinical prediction through independent, intended-use validation; improving care is a further question.**

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Analytical validity, clinical validity and clinical utility address different questions for a specified assay, specimen, population and intended use. MedlinePlus Genetics distinguishes detection of a genetic variant, its relationship to disease presence or risk, and whether the information helps diagnosis, treatment, management or prevention. Reliable measurement does not by itself establish clinical meaning, and an outcome association does not establish benefit from changing care. For a prediction model, reproducibility of fixed-input output, discrimination, calibrated probabilities and the consequences of model-guided decisions also require distinct evidence. These are related questions rather than a universal sequence that guarantees a useful test.
evidence.explanation: Independent intended-use prediction and improved care are distinct evidence questions; a measured model response alone does not establish either. points.requirement: Published agreement studies are small and setting-specific: a breast-slice chemotherapy assay matched magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) response in 15 of 20 evaluable patients but never called a tumor resistant ([Ladan 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/)). A pooled review of 17 organoid studies found no randomized trial of organoid-guided treatment ([Wensink 2021](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8042051/)). When colorectal patients were treated with organoid-selected drugs, none of 6 responded ([Ooft 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33887686/)). Agreement is not proof that choosing treatment by the model improves outcomes. A model may also omit a relevant population, change during establishment or use an exposure that does not translate to patients. Computation may fail in a new context. Even a strong clinical prediction may lack evidence that its use improves care. Keep those gaps beside the useful result.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Ladan's real study began with 41 consenting people: three did not undergo biopsy and eight biopsies lacked tumour cells, leaving 30 adequate tumour biopsies. Six assays failed the prespecified baseline-apoptosis criterion and one was lost to infection. Of 23 usable results, three people did not receive the chemotherapy, leaving 20 clinical comparisons. The main-text counts are used here; Table 2's footnote instead mentions two people not receiving chemotherapy. The reported interval for 15/20 agreement was 53 to 89 percent, and the pilot's prespecified target was at least 55 percent. Reaching that target supports further investigation, not a demonstration that using the assay to choose care improves outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Wensink's 2021 review included seventeen publications, five about colorectal cancer; seven used metastatic populations. Its pooled sensitivity was 81 percent and specificity 74 percent for the included response comparisons. The authors warned that these estimates were likely high because some studies lacked quantitative results needed for pooling and not all used a predefined index test; publication or outcome-reporting bias could not be excluded. The pooled establishment estimate was 68.0 percent at patient level and 68.5 percent at sample level, with heterogeneous studies and wide intervals. These are different quantities from response agreement and from clinical utility. The review also reports a 34-day median just to establish organoids from breast biopsies, distinct from a completed drug panel or an individual decision deadline.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Randomised outcome evidence must be assessed for the named assay and use rather than declared absent for all functional testing in solid tumours. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Read each omitted compartment. A tumour-only dish lacks required immune interactions unless those populations are added and shown functional. A fresh slice may retain resident neighbours while losing blood flow and recruitment from circulation. A conventional PDX adds mouse circulation, exposure and metabolism without reproducing an intact human immune system. A computational prediction depends on its data, assumptions and benchmark. Human-derived tissue can be used in both dish and animal models; do not claim that ex vivo is the only setting using human tissue. A living specimen can lose cells, adapt or undergo selection after removal; retaining a structure is not retaining complete physiology. In-vitro preparations can isolate direct effects, compare doses and drugs and support repeats, while omitting perfused blood supply, host metabolism and the original population mix unless specifically reconstructed. Latin labels such as in glass, out of the living and in the living are mnemonics for setting, not quality grades.
