evidence.supportingExcerpt: Functional drug testing exposes a defined living preparation to medicines and measures a specified response. Preparations may use dissociated cells, expanded organoids or short-term tissue cultures. Feasibility, outcome agreement and benefit from using a result to choose care are separate questions and must be tied to the actual assay version, cancer, treatment and setting.
evidence.explanation: A controlled laboratory response is useful within its conditions, without proving achievable safe exposure, a human regimen ranking, a particular target mechanism or an approved indication. prior:functional-drug-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Specimen and assay card. Record donor/site/time, living preparation, transport and processing, initial composition, culture history, assay version, concentrations, exposure duration, replicates and control range. Fixed tissue cannot supply living cells; whether previously frozen material can supply the required viable preparation must be demonstrated for that protocol. Input suitability and recovery must be demonstrated for the method. Testing and endpoint processing use finite material. Output needs units, denominator, normalisation and uncertainty; acceptance criteria must be defined for the actual method. Name whether the preparation is dissociated cells, a fresh fragment or an expanded organoid. Mixed samples include normal neighbours, and expansion can change the represented populations.
evidence.explanation: A controlled laboratory response is useful within its conditions, without proving achievable safe exposure, a human regimen ranking, a particular target mechanism or an approved indication. prior:functional-drug-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Handling evidence is method-specific. Ladan and colleagues collected breast tissue in their specified medium, cut 300 micrometre slices and assessed morphology, proliferation and apoptosis after three-day exposure. This is not a general transport or storage protocol for all screens. Growth-rate methods show why baseline counts and control division affect interpretation. Retain failures and exclusions; failed preparation is not clinical resistance. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4887336/ Medium, drug access and exposure duration can change the result. Mechanism-relevant controls test whether the claimed interaction can occur; absent required cells or unrealistic exposures can make an experiment uninformative even when a numerical response is available. A laboratory concentration is not a safe human dose.
evidence.explanation: A controlled laboratory response is useful within its conditions, without proving achievable safe exposure, a human regimen ranking, a particular target mechanism or an approved indication. prior:functional-drug-testing: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.

A drug target is a biological molecule or structure that a treatment acts on, and the mechanism of action explains how that action produces an effect. The National Cancer Institute describes targeted therapy as treatment that targets proteins that control how cancer cells grow, divide and spread, and says most targeted therapies are small-molecule drugs, which are small enough to enter cells and so suit targets inside cells, or monoclonal antibodies, which are designed to attach to specific targets on cancer cells. It describes antibodies that mark cancer cells for the immune system, antibodies that stop growth or cause self-destruction directly, and antibodies that carry toxins to cancer cells. These are different jobs, so a shared label of targeted does not make the mechanisms interchangeable, and a target that is only an address for delivery need not drive the cancer's growth.

An altered gene or an elevated protein can suggest a target hypothesis; it does not show that inhibiting the target will harm cancer cells selectively, which controlled perturbations of the target test, and safe exposure and appropriate clinical studies answer later questions. Naming a target answers only the first of several questions. Binding is an interaction between molecules and can be shown with a purified protein, which does not show that the compound reaches the protein inside a cell. Target engagement asks whether the interaction occurs in the relevant cells or tissue, and exposure, target location and the cell membrane all bear on it; a blood concentration and a concentration at an intracellular target are different observations. The cellular thermal shift assay of Martinez Molina and colleagues was developed to evaluate drug binding to target proteins in cells and tissue samples, and its authors used it to monitor drug transport and activation, off-target effects and resistance in cancer cell lines. Binding is also different from changing function: a compound can inhibit an enzyme, activate a receptor or deliver a payload, and a binder can leave the target's activity unchanged. Binding assays test an interaction under specified conditions and engagement assays examine the relevant cells or tissue, while a downstream signal measures a biological consequence and is not automatically a direct measure of how much of the target is occupied; growth, death and regrowth assays add further layers. A measured change in signalling, division or survival needs controls that test the proposed explanation, and one positive experiment should not carry the whole claim.

The last step is clinical. Mechanistic plausibility does not show benefit, because the target may also be present in healthy tissue and the useful margin depends on achieved benefit and harm in a stated disease, treatment setting, product and outcome. The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

The National Cancer Institute adds that cancer cells can become resistant to targeted therapy when the target itself changes so the drug can no longer interact with it, or when cells find new ways to grow that do not depend on the target.

Worked example, fictional. An antibody binds protein A on cancer cells, and a growth assay shows no change. Binding is supported under the assay conditions. It has not been shown that protein A drives growth, that the antibody inhibits protein A's function, that a finished payload-bearing product delivers anything, or that the product is safe and beneficial; each of those needs its own evidence. Before saying a drug worked, name the layer that was measured.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Consider an invented repair-gene R example, with measurements attributed to the same pretreatment tissue region except for a derived model. A supported splice-site DNA variant identifies a candidate sequence change. Loss of the other allelic contribution, with the variant assigned to the retained contribution, supports a possible two-hit explanation subject to copy and phase uncertainty. A reproducible abnormal RNA junction in malignant-cell-enriched material adds evidence for a changed transcript product, while reduced staining with suitable controls adds a protein-signal difference in the assigned cells. Neither establishes that every intact protein is gone. A high genomic scar adds evidence about genomic history, not a direct test of present repair. Impaired repair in a suitable model with informative cycling and damage controls addresses function under those conditions. A replicated drug response at specified exposures adds a model-sensitivity hypothesis; it still leaves achievable safe exposure and patient benefit to their appropriate evidence. These are distinct observations, not a requirement to perform every assay before using any established clinical biomarker.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: OlympiA, trial NCT02032823 sponsored by AstraZeneca, NRG Oncology and the Breast International Group and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, showed that a year of the PARP inhibitor olaparib after standard treatment improves survival in women with germline BRCA mutations and high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancer, about eighty percent of whom had triple-negative disease. It randomised 1,836 patients to olaparib or placebo, met its primary invasive disease-free survival endpoint and showed an overall survival benefit that was sustained at six years. It makes germline testing a treatment decision for every such patient, and whether the benefit extends to somatic or non-BRCA HRD alterations is the open question.

A tumour-only BRCA finding or an arbitrary high scar number does not substitute for these conditions.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Biallelic inactivation concerns whether either parental contribution still supplies useful function in the relevant cancer-cell population, rather than simply counting two physical DNA copies or two events somewhere in a tissue. A damaging change plus loss of the other contribution can support it, but phasing, allele-specific copy state, consequence and cell mixture matter. High VAF alone cannot establish this state. Nguyen and colleagues' pan-cancer analysis associated particular biallelic repair-gene alterations with genomic damage patterns; that association does not make every variant in every repair gene functionally equivalent or establish present drug sensitivity.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

Copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity can replace two parental versions with copies of one version without reducing the total copy number, so loss of heterozygosity is not always loss of a physical chromosome copy.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: OlympiA, trial NCT02032823 sponsored by AstraZeneca, NRG Oncology and the Breast International Group and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, showed that a year of the PARP inhibitor olaparib after standard treatment improves survival in women with germline BRCA mutations and high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancer, about eighty percent of whom had triple-negative disease. It randomised 1,836 patients to olaparib or placebo, met its primary invasive disease-free survival endpoint and showed an overall survival benefit that was sustained at six years. It makes germline testing a treatment decision for every such patient, and whether the benefit extends to somatic or non-BRCA HRD alterations is the open question.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

Different layers can share errors; measured, inferred and imputed values, model version, missing inputs and evaluation remain distinct. prior:multi-omic-integration: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Genomic scars are historical patterns in sampled tumor DNA. They can remain after a surviving population restores homologous repair, so a scar result is not a direct measurement of current function or a guarantee of drug benefit. DNA extraction consumes material; purity, ploidy estimation, segmentation, specimen quality and algorithm version affect the reported result. Counts are not percentages of cells whose repair has failed.

Loss of heterozygosity means losing one parental version, with or without a reduction in total copy number. Abkevich 2012 counted LOH regions longer than 15 megabases but shorter than a whole chromosome in epithelial ovarian cancer analyses. Birkbak counted imbalanced regions reaching a telomere without crossing the centromere. Popova studied transitions between adjacent regions at least 10 megabases long in basal-like breast carcinoma. The original LST method estimated counts separately within each chromosome arm, excluding centromeric breaks, after filtering and smoothing variations smaller than 3 megabases. Segment filters and clinical score cutoffs are different rules.

A composite score can sum different scar features. Telli 2016 used the unweighted sum of LOH, telomeric allelic imbalance and large-scale transitions, with a predefined high-score boundary reported as 42 in the abstract, or a deleterious BRCA1/2 finding, in three platinum-containing neoadjuvant triple-negative breast cancer trials. The training population used to choose a boundary, the treated population used to test response, the assay scale and the intended use are different facts. A number on another assay cannot be read against this threshold without validation; a response association is not an interchangeable treatment-selection rule.

In a fictional, already filtered within-arm profile, a 12-megabase segment next to an 8-megabase segment fails the requirement that both neighbors be at least 10 megabases. A 12-megabase segment next to a 14-megabase segment meets that size component. This tests counting, not a 10-megabase deletion rule, present repair function or a clinical response cutoff. The original algorithm filters and validation population still apply.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
RAD51 nuclear foci are assemblies of a protein involved in homologous recombination. Their interpretation depends on the sampled tumour cells, cell-cycle state, damage, staining, scoring and controls. A low count without enough informative cycling cells is uninformative rather than proof that repair is absent. The assay is a functional surrogate, not direct observation of every completed repair event.

Cruz and colleagues in 2018 assessed RAD51 with geminin as an S/G2 marker and gamma-H2AX as a damage marker in patient-derived breast cancer models and retrospective tumour specimens. Castroviejo-Bermejo and colleagues separately compared RAD51 and genomic HRD scores against olaparib response in breast cancer xenografts, then assessed feasibility in archival breast samples, including PALB2-related cancers. The latter clinical samples established feasibility, rather than a randomised benefit from choosing treatment with the assay.

A scar records accumulated genomic changes; a suitably controlled RAD51 result asks about a present repair-related state. Repair-restoring changes and acquired foci were observed in selected resistant BRCA-mutated breast cancers, but those small cohorts do not establish a universal treatment-switch rule. Use the actual assay version, informative-cell requirements and intended-use validation. A research score cannot replace the biomarker, disease and companion-test conditions of a medicine's label.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: OlympiA, trial NCT02032823 sponsored by AstraZeneca, NRG Oncology and the Breast International Group and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021, showed that a year of the PARP inhibitor olaparib after standard treatment improves survival in women with germline BRCA mutations and high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancer, about eighty percent of whom had triple-negative disease. It makes germline testing a treatment decision for every such patient, and whether the benefit extends to somatic or non-BRCA HRD alterations is the open question.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A practical report reading starts with six questions: what specimen, region, date and treatment context were sampled; what object and units were measured with which assay version; whether the result is signed clinical, preliminary, research or model-predicted evidence; which controls or reference support the comparison; what remains unmeasured; and which actual decision could change. A missing field is a question to resolve, not a fact to assume. For fictional pretreatment bulk RNA, high R relative to a stated reference supports captured expression in that mixture. Calling it a surface target remains an interpretation until the contributing cells and accessible protein are established; selectivity, dependence and treatment benefit need their own evidence. Molecular layer and resolution are separate axes. Mapping 500 RNA targets in one section adds location relative to a pooled RNA result, while the measured layer remains RNA. It does not add a membrane-protein or functional measurement.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional comparison, gene R is high in cancer cells, low in fibroblasts and similarly high in normal luminal epithelial cells. The first contrast supports higher expression than fibroblasts, even if it passes a statistical threshold; it does not establish cancer selectivity. The normal epithelial comparison addresses that claim more closely, while leaving other organs, cell states and target accessibility untested. If that reference group is tiny, contaminated or prepared differently, preserve the unresolved comparison rather than declaring selectivity or exact equality. Normal epithelial cells can also contribute familiar lineage markers to a tumour specimen. An image-based tumour mask is an assignment that needs validation for its actual method and specimens, rather than automatic proof that every included cell is malignant.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: KEYNOTE-355, trial NCT02819518 sponsored by Merck and published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022, established pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy as first-line treatment for metastatic triple-negative breast cancer with PD-L1 expression. It randomised 847 patients and met its primary progression-free and overall survival endpoints in tumours with a combined positive score of ten or more, in the prespecified CPS-ten-or-more comparison. This does not prove that the effect is exactly absent in every lower-score group. OnCo links it to triple-negative breast cancer, pembrolizumab, the CPS term, the TNBC roadmap and IMpassion131. Other first-line strategies, including ADC-based regimens, are separate comparisons; this trial alone cannot rank them.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: KEYNOTE-522 randomised 1,174 people with previously untreated stage II or III triple-negative breast cancer to a whole pembrolizumab or placebo strategy before and after surgery, with the same chemotherapy backbone. The first-602 pCR analysis reported 64.8% versus 51.2%. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Germline testing examines DNA from an appropriate non-tumour specimen, often blood or saliva, for constitutional variants. Many are inherited; a constitutional change can also arise newly. Tumour sequencing can reveal a finding that needs germline confirmation, but it does not establish its origin. A multigene panel and a targeted test for a known family variant answer different questions.

Testing includes consent, review of personal and family history, specimen collection, laboratory analysis and interpretation. A pathogenic or likely pathogenic finding may inform care and testing of relatives. It does not guarantee that cancer will occur or that a particular treatment will work. A variant of uncertain significance is not a pathogenic result and should not direct clinical management. A negative result must be interpreted against the genes and variant types the assay could detect and whether a causative family variant is already known.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.
evidence.explanation: Malignant-profile RNA for presentation components does not establish assembled class-I or class-II display, a particular peptide or recognition. B2M is scoped to class I. Peptide measurement has cell-attribution/sampling limits and remains peer-only where held in the pending record. prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. This is stronger evidence of natural presentation in the sampled material than a binding prediction alone. The analytical observation still has a defined specimen and workflow. It does not automatically establish the abundance of a ligand on every cancer cell, receptor recognition or a treatment effect. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019). Capture starts from mild-detergent solubilised lysates (Chong and colleagues, 2018; Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020 immunoprecipitated HLA from soluble lysates), so a lysate is not a surface-only survey, and in multi-allele samples a peptide was assigned to the best-scoring allele or alleles by computation (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). Identification depends on the analysis: a deep-learning model trained on more than 300,000 synthetic peptides improved HLA peptide identification up to 7-fold and indicated that 87 per cent of the proposed proteasomally spliced HLA peptides may be incorrect (Wilhelm and colleagues, 2021). A quantitative tissue study isolated peptide-HLA complexes from snap-frozen tissue and used formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks only for histology (Science Translational Medicine, 2022).

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.
evidence.explanation: Recovered immune programs, tissue position, assembled presentation, recognition and killing retain separate evidence requirements; an expression label is not a functional assay. prior:cold-vs-hot: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt: TIL is a location label, CD8 is a phenotype and antigen specificity is another property. Simoni found bystander CD8 cells recognizing viral rather than cancer epitopes in human lung and colorectal tumours; the study’s CD39 associations are not a universal test of every cell’s target. A functional assay compares defined effectors and targets with recognition and target-survival controls. Neither presence, cytokine release nor one killing assay reproduces every access barrier or establishes clinical benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.
evidence.explanation: Malignant-profile RNA for presentation components does not establish assembled class-I or class-II display, a particular peptide or recognition. B2M is scoped to class I. Peptide measurement has cell-attribution/sampling limits and remains peer-only where held in the pending record. prior:hla: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In cancer, class I HLA shows peptides to CD8 T cells and is also the main ligand for inhibitory receptors on natural killer cells, so losing it can hide a tumour from T cells while removing a brake on NK cells. HLA-E and HLA-G are nonclassical and vary little between people; HLA-E presents leader peptides from other class I molecules and binds the NK receptor CD94/NKG2A (Braud et al., 1998, with HLA-E tetramers). Tumours can lose a presenting allele (HLA loss of heterozygosity), alter processing or reduce expression, and allele-specific loss differs from complete loss of conventional class I display; targets on retained alleles may remain possible. Tran et al. (2016) documented a colorectal cancer lesion that progressed after T-cell therapy against mutant KRAS G12D, which had lost the chromosome 6 haplotype encoding the restricting HLA-C*08:02; this shows escape in one patient, not a rate. Typing, protein expression, recovered peptide, recognition and killing are different observations, and a conventional surface-target engager avoids peptide-HLA dependence while a peptide-HLA-directed engager keeps it.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A primary melanoma study used mass spectrometry to identify HLA-associated peptides from native tumor tissue and then evaluated selected mutated peptides with immune assays. This is stronger evidence of natural presentation in the sampled material than a binding prediction alone. The analytical observation still has a defined specimen and workflow. It does not automatically establish the abundance of a ligand on every cancer cell, receptor recognition or a treatment effect. A published protocol isolates MHC-peptide complexes by immunoaffinity capture, dissociates the peptides by acid denaturation, fractionates them by HPLC and identifies them by nano-UPLC tandem mass spectrometry, from cell lines and tissues (Purcell and colleagues, 2019). Capture starts from mild-detergent solubilised lysates (Chong and colleagues, 2018; Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020 immunoprecipitated HLA from soluble lysates), so a lysate is not a surface-only survey, and in multi-allele samples a peptide was assigned to the best-scoring allele or alleles by computation (Sarkizova and colleagues, 2020). Identification depends on the analysis: a deep-learning model trained on more than 300,000 synthetic peptides improved HLA peptide identification up to 7-fold and indicated that 87 per cent of the proposed proteasomally spliced HLA peptides may be incorrect (Wilhelm and colleagues, 2021). A quantitative tissue study isolated peptide-HLA complexes from snap-frozen tissue and used formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded blocks only for histology (Science Translational Medicine, 2022).
evidence.explanation: Malignant-profile RNA for presentation components does not establish assembled class-I or class-II display, a particular peptide or recognition. B2M is scoped to class I. Peptide measurement has cell-attribution/sampling limits and remains peer-only where held in the pending record. prior:immunopeptidomics: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
An inflamed or hot pattern has specified immune cells within sampled tumour regions. In an excluded pattern, cells concentrate in surrounding stroma or at a boundary with less entry into malignant nests. A desert has few relevant cells in the examined regions. Cold is used for desert alone or for both desert and excluded patterns, so state the definition. A macrophage-rich sample is not automatically T-cell inflamed.

These are observations about identity and location. Some infiltrating T cells recognize viral or other non-cancer antigens; others restrain responses. Region, specimen, disease site and sampling time matter, and treatment can change the pattern. Neither a small biopsy nor a pattern label describes every site in a person or selects an immunotherapy. Exclusion suggests questions about recruitment, vessels, matrix and local cells, rather than proving one causal wall.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The original RNA Integrity Number method summarized electrophoretic features to standardize quality assessment. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) is the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) system, with two main classes of peptide-display molecule. Classical class I (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) has a heavy chain, beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) and a bound peptide, is found on most nucleated cells, usually displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell and is read by CD8 T cells. Class II (HLA-DR, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) has alpha and beta chains with a bound peptide, is mainly on professional antigen-presenting cells (expression can be induced elsewhere), usually displays proteins processed in vesicles, often acquired from outside, and is read by CD4 T cells. These are common routes, not exclusive lists: cross-presentation puts externally acquired antigen on class I without making it class II, and a CD4 response is not proof of matching class I tumour display. CD4 and CD8 are coreceptors and usual recognition partners, not guarantees of cell function. Structural work shows the T-cell receptor lying across the peptide and HLA together (Garboczi et al., 1996), CD8 contacting the class I alpha2 and alpha3 domains and B2M (Gao et al., 1997) and CD4 engaging a separate class II region (Yin et al., 2012); these constructs do not define universal angles or functions.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
A conventional alpha-beta T-cell receptor uses paired chains to recognise a peptide-HLA surface. Its recognition chains assemble with CD3 signalling partners, as demonstrated in the human TCR-CD3 structural study. CDR3 is an informative variable region, but neither a beta-chain sequence nor CDR3 alone specifies the complete paired receptor or its function.

Particular receptors can cross-react across peptide and HLA contexts; that does not establish a universal cross-reactivity rate. Paired receptor identity, binding, activation, target-cell death and clinical benefit require different evidence. A response by one reconstructed pair to peptide-loaded cells does not establish that another alpha-chain pairing recognises the same target, or that either kills naturally presenting tumour cells. Use irrelevant-target, HLA and target-only viability controls. Peptide loading can bypass natural processing, and contact diagrams are not healthy-tissue safety tests.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Replication makes DNA from DNA. Transcription uses a DNA template to make RNA. Translation reads the coding sequence of a message in three-base codons to build a polypeptide; the transcript and reading frame matter. Functional noncoding RNAs do not need to become protein. Reverse transcription copies RNA into DNA in relevant viral and retrotransposon contexts. This information-flow map is not a guarantee that every DNA change produces a measured RNA or protein change.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Epithelium forms linings, coverings and glands; an epithelial cell is not necessarily malignant. A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath an epithelium, distinct from each cell’s lipid membrane. Stroma includes supporting cells, extracellular matrix and vascular structures, rather than only collagen or fibroblasts. Immune cells and other nonmalignant cells can contribute to a tumor specimen. The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. Combining layers can reveal agreement, competing explanations, missing evidence or a sample mismatch, and it does not by itself show that a matching treatment will help: the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets (2018) grades alterations in six levels of clinical evidence by their implications for patient management, from targets ready for routine decisions to investigational targets that need more data (Mateo and colleagues, 2018; a second version appeared in 2026). For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
The study profiled 104 primary TNBCs across assays: copy-number arrays in 104, RNA sequencing in 80, and genome or exome sequencing in 65. Deep re-sequencing validated 2,414 somatic single-nucleotide variants for the mutation analysis. The cancers showed a wide, continuous spectrum of genomic evolution; 36% of the validated somatic single-nucleotide variants were observed in the compared transcriptome sequence. Non-detection in those data does not establish biological silence in every cell. Basal TNBC showed more variation in clonal frequencies than non-basal TNBC. TP53, PIK3CA and PTEN mutations were clonally dominant compared with other genes, though in some tumours their frequencies were incompatible with founder status; mutations in cytoskeletal, cell-shape and motility genes occurred at lower clonal frequency, suggesting later acquisition.

The cohort is deposited as brca_bccrc (British Columbia, Nature 2012) on cBioPortal.
