evidence.supportingExcerpt: A DNA change, an RNA count and a protein or phosphorylation measurement answer different questions, so integration starts with an evidence record for each measurement: the patient or experimental unit, specimen, collection time, tissue region, method, units and quality limits. Measurements from one specimen are paired; measurements from separate cohorts are not, and even adjacent tissue sections do not hold identical cells. Three reports that copy one DNA call add no new layer, and a value predicted by a model, such as RNA imputed from an image, must stay labelled as imputed beside measured values. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (Argelaguet and colleagues, 2018) is one research method: it infers hidden factors that capture biological and technical sources of variability, separates axes shared across data types from axes specific to one, and can impute missing data; the authors applied it to 200 samples of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia profiled for somatic mutations, RNA expression, DNA methylation and ex vivo drug response. A factor is a statistical pattern, not a mechanism or a validated test. Technical variation needs its own handling: Risso and colleagues (2014) showed that usual RNA sequencing normalisation mostly accounts for sequencing depth and fails to correct library preparation and other unwanted technical effects, and where treatment time and processing method always change together, those data alone cannot separate their effects. In a proteogenomic study of 105 genomically annotated breast cancers, 77 of which gave high-quality data, pathway analysis of the phosphoproteome identified a G-protein-coupled receptor cluster that was not readily identified at the mRNA level (Mertins and colleagues, 2016), an example of layers adding different information. Correlation between layers is not a tested dependency, and a controlled intervention addresses a different question. Layers need not agree numerically, and disagreement is not automatically an error: bulk RNA from a mixed sample can be high for a gene whose protein, on a tissue image, sits mainly in normal vessel cells, so averaging the two into one confidence score would hide whether malignant cells carry an accessible target. For a prediction model, a patient who appears in several layers must stay on one side of a patient-level split, and many cells from one biopsy are not many patients.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.
evidence.explanation: Model establishment and preparation select cells while spatial/cellular methods sample bounded material; fidelity must be assessed rather than inferred from method names. prior:spatial-transcriptomics: inherited evidence depth; no fresh whole-owner certification

review.auditor: GPT-6.1 Sol coordinator; semantic and source assessment at stated primary/inference scope, not blind, expert, learner or language acceptance

points.requirement: Insertional mutagenesis = integration that disrupts a gene or its regulation with consequence; integration is the event; most insertions do not cause cancer; clonal expansion != malignancy (useful responses expand clones).

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Three primary reports show why the setting matters. After retrovirus-mediated gamma-c gene transfer into autologous CD34-positive bone marrow cells for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, 9 of 10 patients were corrected, but almost three years later the two youngest developed uncontrolled clonal proliferation of mature T cells; both clones carried vector integration near the LMO2 proto-oncogene promoter with abnormal LMO2 expression, which the authors attributed most likely to retrovirus enhancer activity (Hacein-Bey-Abina et al., 2003). In a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia given CD19 CAR T cells, 94 per cent of CAR T cells at the peak of response came from one clone in which lentiviral insertion had disrupted TET2, the patient's second TET2 allele carried a hypomorphic mutation, and the clone showed a central memory phenotype alongside complete remission: an expanded clone linked to benefit, not a new cancer (Fraietta et al., 2018). In 724 patients treated with T-cell therapies at one centre, a lethal T-cell lymphoma followed axicabtagene ciloleucel for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; the tumour, the CAR T cells and the patient's normal blood cells were profiled in depth, both lymphomas were Epstein-Barr virus positive and linked to DNMT3A and TET2 mutant clonal haematopoiesis, and no evidence of oncogenic retroviral integration was found with multiple techniques (Hamilton et al., 2024). The first is a specific stem-cell regimen and the others are single-centre or single-patient observations, so none is an incidence estimate for a vector or product.

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: To attribute a malignancy after engineered-cell therapy, investigators ask whether the therapeutic sequence is present in the malignant cells, where the integrations are, whether they alter relevant genes, whether related clones were detectable earlier, and what prior therapy, underlying disease and pre-existing genetic changes contribute. Integration-site sequencing maps insertion locations, quantitative DNA assays estimate vector copies per cell, and flow cytometry, gene-expression measurement and pathology answer different questions about identity, function and malignancy; the sample is consumed by testing. Average vector copy number cannot show the position or effect of each insertion, a clone's frequency depends on the sampled cells, assay sensitivity and time, and blood may not represent every tissue. This record gives no copy-number or clone-frequency threshold because none of the sources read sets one. Messenger RNA delivery that does not integrate does not use genomic insertion as its route, which does not remove its other risks.

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Three primary reports show why the setting matters. After retrovirus-mediated gamma-c gene transfer into autologous CD34-positive bone marrow cells for X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency, 9 of 10 patients were corrected, but almost three years later the two youngest developed uncontrolled clonal proliferation of mature T cells; both clones carried vector integration near the LMO2 proto-oncogene promoter with abnormal LMO2 expression, which the authors attributed most likely to retrovirus enhancer activity (Hacein-Bey-Abina et al., 2003). In a patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia given CD19 CAR T cells, 94 per cent of CAR T cells at the peak of response came from one clone in which lentiviral insertion had disrupted TET2, the patient's second TET2 allele carried a hypomorphic mutation, and the clone showed a central memory phenotype alongside complete remission: an expanded clone linked to benefit, not a new cancer (Fraietta et al., 2018). In 724 patients treated with T-cell therapies at one centre, a lethal T-cell lymphoma followed axicabtagene ciloleucel for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; the tumour, the CAR T cells and the patient's normal blood cells were profiled in depth, both lymphomas were Epstein-Barr virus positive and linked to DNMT3A and TET2 mutant clonal haematopoiesis, and no evidence of oncogenic retroviral integration was found with multiple techniques (Hamilton et al., 2024). The first is a specific stem-cell regimen and the others are single-centre or single-patient observations, so none is an incidence estimate for a vector or product.

evidence.explanation: Integration, gene dysregulation, clonal expansion and malignancy are separated using LMO2, TET2 and the Hamilton case at their own scopes.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: To attribute a malignancy after engineered-cell therapy, investigators ask whether the therapeutic sequence is present in the malignant cells, where the integrations are, whether they alter relevant genes, whether related clones were detectable earlier, and what prior therapy, underlying disease and pre-existing genetic changes contribute. Integration-site sequencing maps insertion locations, quantitative DNA assays estimate vector copies per cell, and flow cytometry, gene-expression measurement and pathology answer different questions about identity, function and malignancy; the sample is consumed by testing. Average vector copy number cannot show the position or effect of each insertion, a clone's frequency depends on the sampled cells, assay sensitivity and time, and blood may not represent every tissue. This record gives no copy-number or clone-frequency threshold because none of the sources read sets one. Messenger RNA delivery that does not integrate does not use genomic insertion as its route, which does not remove its other risks.

review.auditor: Coordinator intake; not expert sign-off
review.rationale: Canonical census and review support a generic on-target/off-tumour record distinct from lymphoma lineage costs. Its definition and the therapeutic-index lead are corrected; broader older lineage and class assertions are not all re-verified.

evidence.explanation: Intended-target recognition in healthy tissue differs from unintended peptide recognition, CRS and binding specificity; the two cases and complementary tests retain their limits.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: On-target, off-tumour toxicity is injury from recognition of the intended target on healthy tissue. It differs from recognition of an unintended molecular target. The predictable, lymphoma-specific consequences of aiming at lineage antigens (B-cell aplasia, low immunoglobulin, and the effects of CD52, CCR4 and CD47 targeting) are described in the record on the cost of aiming at a lineage antigen, which this record does not repeat.

evidence.explanation: Intended-target recognition in healthy tissue differs from unintended peptide recognition, CRS and binding specificity; the two cases and complementary tests retain their limits.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Many candidate cancer targets are normal proteins found at different levels or places in the body, so tumour-associated does not mean tumour-exclusive. A treatment that recognises its intended target wherever it is accessible, such as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell, can harm any healthy tissue that displays it, and tissue location, target density, receptor properties and exposure all shape the outcome. This differs from off-target cross-reactivity, in which the receptor recognises an unintended molecule, and from cytokine release syndrome, which is systemic inflammatory activation; the three can occur together. It also differs from payload toxicity in an antibody-drug conjugate: a pooled analysis of ADC trials found the key grade 3 to 4 toxicities grouped by payload and concluded they were likely off-target and related to the payload (Masters et al., 2018). Binding specificity is not tissue selectivity, and experience with an antibody against a target does not automatically carry over to a living cell with a different recognition and signalling system.

evidence.explanation: Intended-target recognition in healthy tissue differs from unintended peptide recognition, CRS and binding specificity; the two cases and complementary tests retain their limits.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: Two primary reports show the contrast. A patient with colon cancer metastatic to the lungs and liver received 10 billion autologous T cells expressing a trastuzumab-based CAR against ERBB2 (HER2), the largest number permitted in the first dose-escalation cohort, the day after a lymphodepleting regimen of cyclophosphamide (60 mg/kg daily for 2 days) and fludarabine (25 mg/m2 for 5 days). Within 15 minutes the patient had respiratory distress, chest imaging showed pulmonary oedema, and the patient died 5 days after treatment, with marked rises in interferon-gamma, GM-CSF, tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-6 and interleukin-10. At autopsy multiple organs showed systemic ischaemia and haemorrhagic microangiopathic injury and the lungs diffuse alveolar damage; histological examination of autopsy tissue found ERBB2 at 3+ in liver metastases and 2+ in lung metastases and much lower levels in normal lung parenchyma, normal liver and normal breast. The authors hypothesised that highly active ERBB2-directed T cells recognised ERBB2 on normal lung cells on first pass through the lung and released inflammatory cytokines that began a cascade ending in multiorgan failure; the autopsy findings were read as initial lung injury followed by days of hypotension and ischaemia, and the authors call the significance of the cells' reactivity against cultured primary cells unclear. This is a single case, with a stated dose and conditioning, whose mechanism is the authors' hypothesis and which gives no incidence for any CAR product (Morgan et al., 2010). In a trial of an affinity-enhanced T-cell receptor against HLA-A*01-restricted MAGE-A3 in myeloma and melanoma, the first two patients developed cardiogenic shock and died within days; no MAGE-A3 expression was detected in heart tissue at autopsy, and beating cardiomyocytes made from induced pluripotent stem cells triggered T-cell killing through recognition of an unrelated peptide from titin. That is off-target recognition of an unintended molecule, not the intended target in the wrong tissue (Linette et al., 2013).

evidence.explanation: Intended-target recognition in healthy tissue differs from unintended peptide recognition, CRS and binding specificity; the two cases and complementary tests retain their limits.
evidence.supportingExcerpt: How the question is asked before and during trials. FDA's CAR T-cell development guidance says to assess both undesired targeting of healthy tissue that expresses the intended antigen (on-target/off-tumour) and unintended targeting of other antigens, using examples such as tissue cross-reactivity studies with an antibody carrying the same recognition domain, protein arrays, cytotoxicity and cytokine-release testing on panels of primary cells, cell lines or stem-cell-derived organ systems, and relevant animal models, and encourages a combination of methods; antigen recognition domains can differ in affinity or avidity or recognise a different site, which should be evaluated, and CAR T cells can carry added components such as suicide genes. In practice a readout is a staining intensity or positive fraction, a binding profile, killing or cytokine release by healthy cells at a named time, and finally organ injury in the treated population; stained fixed tissue does not show a living organ's accessibility, an animal model may lack the human target, and a negative result in one panel is not a safety certificate. No universal expression cut-off is given here because no source read gives one. Whether affinity tuning, recognition logic or control switches improve safety for a particular design needs that design's own evidence. The 2026 ASTCT consensus abstract lists on-target, off-tumour toxicity among the toxicities for which it considered definitions and grading; its criteria were not readable.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A recycling station can hold a large pile because more material arrives or because processing has slowed. The pile is an amount; material processed over time is a rate. Neither alone tells you whether the city depends on that station.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Yamamoto and colleagues found that the cargo receptor NBR1 helped direct MHC-I proteins to lysosomes through an autophagy-dependent route in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma models. This lowered the amount of MHC-I at the cell surface, where it displays antigens to CD8 T cells. In mouse experiments, reducing MHC-I or depleting CD8 T cells reversed tumour control after genetic autophagy inhibition. Chloroquine increased surface MHC-I but, alone, did not significantly reduce tumour weight in the reported experiment; its effects on lysosomes are broad. These model results do not establish that every KRAS-driven cancer depends on autophagy or that blocking it benefits patients.
